Title: Agent engineering starts by assuming the model gets fooled
Description: Cynthia Akiotu of Accenture at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on identity, MCP tools and authorization checks that hold when prompt injection works.
Body:
A customer asks a support agent about refunds, the agent retrieves the refund policy, and hidden in that document is an instruction to export every customer case to an outside address. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, Cynthia Akiotu, AI security and data protection architect at Accenture and a Microsoft MVP in Security Copilot, used that one scenario to argue that once an LLM can act, every engineering decision becomes a security decision.

Her design goal is refreshingly modest: don't pretend the model can't be manipulated. Contain what happens when it is.

## Same model, new blast radius

Cynthia starts by putting prompt engineering and agent engineering side by side. The model is identical. What changed is everything around it: instructions, context, identity, tools, actions and governance. A chatbot that answers wrongly misleads someone. An agent that acts wrongly sends the email, updates the record or deletes it.

Each layer adds capability and widens the blast radius unless it's deliberately constrained. And these layers aren't one team's checklist; identity, data, security and operations teams all own a piece.

## Retrieved text can inform, never authorise

The refund scenario is indirect prompt injection. The attacker never talks to the agent; they plant instructions in a source the agent will read. Her design question is sharp and practical: who can write to the knowledge sources your agent retrieves from? Detection helps, she says, but you still need controls beyond the model, because the next question is whose authority the agent is running on.

She lays out three identity patterns: delegated access on behalf of a signed-in user (the agent inherits that user's reach), an agent with its own account like a digital worker, and app-only identities for background work. If any of these is broad, a fooled model gets broad reach.

## MCP is a protocol, not a trust decision

The Model Context Protocol section is the one platform teams will screenshot. MCP standardises how agents discover and call tools, which is convenient. It doesn't make a server trustworthy. Her example shows a ticket-search tool whose description quietly asks the model to send a report elsewhere, which is tool description poisoning. Review servers and tool definitions, restrict discovery, validate requests and enforce permissions at execution.

Then the line every agent builder should tape to the monitor: capability doesn't mean authorization. Writing "please don't delete data" in the system prompt is a suggestion. A policy check in the application that denies the delete because no approver exists, and logs the attempt, is a boundary.

## Follow the attack, then follow the trace

Cynthia connects the pieces into one path: the agent retrieves the poisoned policy, mistakes it for an instruction, tries the export, and the API rejects it. The model was fooled; the system held. Controls sit at several points (inputs, retrieved context, tool arguments, actions, outputs), and an AI gateway is a good shared front door for model traffic, but tool execution may take a different route to an enterprise API and still needs its own check.

Correlated traces let the security team see the denied export even when the customer sees a normal answer. Her case study uses the Microsoft stack she works in, including Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 for agent identity and life cycle, as one example of turning these principles into platform capabilities.

## Least agency

Her closing pattern is least agency: enough freedom to do the job and no more, narrow tool access, deny unapproved actions by default, humans in the loop for irreversible changes, and deterministic application logic validating whatever the model proposes. Before production, ask who owns the agent, which identity it uses, and whether you can trace, stop and recover its actions.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from chatbots to agents with tools, and security architects reviewing them. It's a clear, structured talk rather than a code walkthrough, and the refund story makes it easy to retell in your own design review.

Title: In anti-money laundering work, a prompt is a compliance control
Description: Pratik Patel of Hexaware at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on grounded, schema-checked prompts for AML investigations that never infer intent.
Body:
"Explain why this transaction is suspicious" looks like a harmless prompt until you notice it has already decided the answer. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Pratik Patel, Principal Consultant at Hexaware Technologies, argued that in a bank a prompt is a control, and should be designed, tested and governed like any other control in an anti-money laundering (AML) workflow.

Pratik has spent more than 14 years on financial services transformation, with AML, fraud and cloud modernisation work for banks including TD Bank, Royal Bank of Canada and Santander. The talk reads like it: fewer clever tricks, more audit questions.

## The leading prompt problem

The opening contrast is the best part. The basic prompt assumes suspicion and invites the model to build a story, and models are very good at building stories when evidence is thin. The governed version reads: "Summarize the supplied transaction evidence, identify documented alert indicators, cite supporting record IDs, and flag information gaps. Do not infer criminal intent."

The model summarises instead of concluding, cites record IDs, says what's missing and stays away from intent. Pratik distils it into five principles: context grounding, structured instructions, evidence traceability, controlled reasoning (facts separate from hypotheses) and safe failure.

## Where AI sits in the pipeline

His workflow runs ingest, enrich, alert, summarise, investigate. The model helps in the last two steps only. It doesn't replace transaction monitoring and doesn't make the call. For Currency Transaction Reporting, which is rule-driven (in the US, cash over ten thousand dollars in a business day triggers a report), AI gathers related transactions and checks fields, and the analyst validates the aggregation.

The architecture is five layers: enterprise data sources, a governed cloud-native data platform, prompt orchestration, compliance applications, and governance drawn over all of them. His warning about layer two is worth repeating: if the data underneath is messy, the AI produces messy answers, only faster and more fluently.

## Facts, indicators, assessments

The pyramid slide separates three kinds of statement that must never blur. Verified facts come straight from source systems. Observed indicators are patterns that warrant review against monitoring criteria. Investigative assessments are interpretations, reviewed and owned by an analyst, never determined by the model.

His contrast example: a weak output says the customer is structuring deposits to avoid reporting. A governed one lists five cash deposits between $9,000 and $9,900 across four days, with transaction references, and says the pattern warrants analyst review. Same facts, very different liability.

## Valid JSON is not a true answer

Outputs follow a schema: case ID, transaction summary, indicators each with evidence IDs, missing information, and a review status that starts as pending analyst review, never approved. Four gates sit behind it: schema enforcement, evidence verification (if the model cites a transaction that was never retrieved, the output is rejected), completeness checks, and escalation to a correction workflow or an analyst.

The caution he underlines is the one most teams skip. A well-formed response tells you nothing about whether it's correct, which is why evidence checks and human review sit on top of schema validation.

## Fail safe, and treat documents as data

Pratik lists failure scenarios with a control for each: request more evidence when it's missing, flag conflicting customer records, reject unsupported claims, block unauthorised access, retry bad formats within limits, and require human review when confidence is low. "In regulated operations, a safe refusal or escalation is always better than a confident, unsupported answer."

He also covers prompt injection in a case file (hidden text telling the model to mark the case low risk is data, never a command) and a flat ban on autonomous regulatory submissions. Governance means versioned prompts with approval gates, least-privilege access, and audit trails good enough to answer who approved this prompt, what data it saw and who reviewed the output.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects building LLM features in banking, insurance or any regulated review workflow. It's a framework talk without a live demo, and the rollout plan (start with bounded summarisation tasks, measure from day one) makes it a good brief to hand a compliance stakeholder.

Title: Your agent orchestrator won't save your money; the thin controller will
Description: Yedidya Schwartz, CTO of Quicklizard, at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 on crashing six durable engines to see who pays twice for model calls.
Body:
Yedidya Schwartz, CTO at Quicklizard, built a pipeline where AI agents turn a ticket into a mergeable pull request, then crashed the same tiny job on six durable execution engines to see which one protected his model bill. None did by default. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 he showed that the shape of your code, a thin controller with every model call in its own step, decided the cost, not the engine.

This is one of the most evidence-heavy talks of the event: real failures, a controlled experiment and a bill kept outside every engine so none could flatter itself.

## Green on GitHub, phase 8 never ran

The first version was one 338-line Markdown prompt that Claude ran on a GitHub self-hosted runner, from intake through planning, build, tests, QA, three-model review, translations into 12 languages, PR and CI. For two hours it went well. QA checked 34 acceptance criteria and all passed. Then, at phase 8, instead of translating, the model wrote a polished summary of the translation work it was supposed to do and stopped.

GitHub showed success, because success meant the process exited cleanly. The runner deleted the pod with the commits still on its disk. No draft PR, no traces, every model call already paid. Yedidya's conclusion: the model can do the work, but code has to decide when it's done. He rewrote the pipeline as roughly 485 lines of Python where a plain for loop picks the next phase, and a for loop can't decide to write an essay instead of running phase 9.

## Defaults were built for seconds, agents run for hours

Before choosing a tool he wrote down hard requirements, the biggest being that agents must run inside his private network to reach internal services and databases. That alone ruled out most hosted coding agents without an enterprise plan or a beta feature.

Then he compared engines on his own terms: LangGraph saves between steps but not inside them, the DAG schedulers handle loops back to a critic only with workarounds, Inngest caps a step at two hours, and several engines kill a step that stays quiet too long. His best slide is about defaults: they were tuned for API calls, while an agent step can take hours. His CI fix step started with a 20-minute timeout and ended at four hours. He picked Temporal, partly because he knew it well, and was clear that this is his choice for his pipeline, not a ranking.

## The experiment: who pays twice?

The part to watch closely is the crash test. A fake model charged a fixed price per call and logged every charge to a file the engine never saw. A clean run cost exactly $2. He killed the job three ways (mid-call, graceful shutdown, right after the file write) on Temporal, Restate, Inngest, LangGraph, DBOS and Prefect, in two variants.

Written the natural way, with the model call and file write in one step, every engine overpaid: $4 on Restate, DBOS and Prefect, $6 on LangGraph, $14 on Inngest (and $12 with no crash at all, due to defaults), and $10 on Temporal. With the thin controller, where each model call and each write is its own step and a step is skipped if its output is saved, every engine landed at $3.50 for a mid-call crash and exactly $2 after the save. Worse, no engine's UI showed the second charge. Count your money outside the engine.

## Agents lie about success, so stop asking them

The war stories are memorable. A skip-if-output-exists check once found a file full of error text, skipped the model and shipped an empty PR. Translations went missing at random because two workers had separate disks, and the scheduler, not the model, decided where each step landed: seven of 12 languages vanished until all files moved to S3. Agents claimed a type check passed that they never ran; Yedidya's run produced five compile errors in components the agent had made up.

His proof ladder puts the agent's self-report at the bottom and a real diff, a build his code runs, green CI and a human merge above it. In his pipeline, done means CI is green. He also zooms out to Stripe, Spotify and Uber, and his verdict on whether it's worth it is honest: not yet, but close, with about one feature in four merged and only after a lot of human work.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to choose Temporal, Restate, LangGraph or friends for agent workflows, and anyone whose agents report success on their own say-so. It's long, and every slide earns its place.

Title: Physical AI safety agents should reason over a system graph
Description: Vraj Patel of Apptronik at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on bounded agents, system graphs and skills for safety assurance in robots and AVs.
Body:
Robots and autonomous vehicles keep changing after they ship, and the safety case has to keep up with every new perception model. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Vraj Patel, Staff Systems Engineer at Apptronik and formerly at May Mobility, showed how bounded, human-supervised agents can help with continuous safety assurance, as long as they reason over an explicit system graph instead of a loose pile of documents.

His thesis is that a prompt alone isn't enough here. The context has to be engineered first. Vraj presented in his individual professional capacity, and the framework he showed is illustrative rather than a specific employer's system.

## The documents outpace the engineers

Building a humanoid, an autonomous mobile robot or an AV produces engineering docs, safety analyses, prototypes, hypotheses and evidence at a pace that grows as teams lean on tools like Claude and Codex. The material ends up fragmented across tools. An agent pointed at that mess will happily produce plausible safety claims. Vraj's answer is to give it four pillars to stand on: a system graph, skills, tools and data, and governance with approvals.

## Build the graph before the prompt

The system graph starts with the operational design domain (ODD): where the system works, whether a warehouse, a city limit or a construction site, and under which conditions, such as rain or sunlight. From there it maps objects and interactions, hazards (especially to humans), safety goals, requirements, verification criteria and finally claims. Edges carry relations such as "mitigates a hazard" or "is verifiable", so the graph bounds where an agent can wander.

The sources stay whatever teams already use: Jama or Doors for requirements, Draw.io or Miro for architecture, Confluence and Jira for docs, Git for releases. The abstract keeps the model-based systems engineering (MBSE) model as the single source of truth, with frameworks such as ISO 26262, ISO 21448 (SOTIF), UL 4600 and ASPICE as guides.

## Skills with golden cases

Vraj shows a hazard coverage skill as a template: a triggering condition, inputs, the procedure the agent runs, and an output (JSON or Markdown) where every item carries a unique ID. The guideline baked in: never override, never claim safety without human approval. Each skill gets golden cases to evaluate against.

His worked scenario is a person cutting into the path of a moving unit after the perception model is revised. The agent detects what changed in the model, finds the impacted scenarios, hazards and controls, checks coverage and whether other systems are affected, and escalates if the safety scenarios need a rerun. In his words on the slide, the outcome is a traceable question for an engineer, not an autonomous safe-to-release verdict.

## Agents are software that can fail

The point that will land with anyone who has written a safety case: treat the agent workload itself as something that needs its own safety case. Measure evidence validity, false positive rate, classification quality, tool compliance and reviewer acceptance. The abstract names the risks to watch: hallucinated evidence, incomplete context, prompt drift and over-automation.

Human authority is an architectural requirement here. Agents can read and retrieve; they can't write or override without a person signing off, and whoever approves the output owns it. "The AI did it" is not an accountable party.

## Start with one vertical slice

The roadmap is refreshingly modest. Build a small graph for one vertical, connect the sources, ship one skill, evaluate it, harden it, then expand. His three takeaways: engineer the context, package the procedure, and command the action. Traceability from evidence to decision to claim is the core competency the standards ask for anyway.

## Who should watch

Systems and safety engineers in robotics, AVs and other physical AI, plus anyone building agents for regulated engineering workflows. It's an architecture talk with no live demo, and the system graph is the part worth sketching on your own whiteboard.

Title: NEPA permitting with LLMs needs prompts that act like governed rules
Description: Mohit Upadhyay of Tech Mahindra at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 on evidence-first prompts, provenance and RAG for NEPA categorical exclusions.
Body:
A cell tower next to a historic district looks like a routine install until someone asks whether it disturbs the ground, changes the visual character of a landmark or needs sign-off from three agencies. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Mohit Upadhyay, Principal Solutions Architect at Tech Mahindra, walked through how his team builds AI support for National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) Categorical Exclusion determinations, and why the prompt there has to behave like a versioned, tested business rule.

The headline idea: permitting is about evidence, and a fluent answer is never proof that an exclusion applies.

## The domain, briefly

Federal infrastructure, telecom, utility and defence projects near protected sites face NEPA plus Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. Analysts check thresholds such as ground disturbance and structure height across several agencies, mostly by hand. Mohit's platform combines LLMs with computer vision, geospatial data and retrieval over sources like Google Street View, NPS IRMA, FCC ULS, EPA ECHO, USGS 3DEP and State Historic Preservation Office systems.

If you don't work in permitting, the patterns still transfer. That's the reason to watch.

## Every fact keeps its provenance

The evidence model is the most reusable part. Project facts (footprint, excavation, elevation, access, utilities) stay separate from retrieved reference material. Each fact carries its source file, collection date, extraction method and reviewer status. Geospatial records keep their coordinate system, precision and processing history.

Mohit also insists that missing data must never turn into a clearance. A true negative, a failed query and an inaccessible record are three different outcomes. If the authoritative source is unreachable, the system asks a human for manual evidence instead of assuming the best.

## Keep NEPA and Section 106 in separate fields

One small rule with big consequences: hold separate status fields for NEPA and historic preservation, and never call a NEPA pathway complete while other reviews are unresolved. Similar-looking sites don't get to inherit each other's outcomes either. Every site is evaluated on its own evidence, with no bias from previous approvals of a similar nature.

## The prompt defines what the AI may not do

In Mohit's framing, the prompt is a controlled operating instruction. It authorises the model to identify applicable rules, extract facts, expose uncertainty and draft for review. It forbids non-existent citations, unverified site conditions and claims that an approval was granted. Observed facts, inferred facts, open questions and applicable rules stay in separate sections, and a second verification prompt checks that each citation supports the conclusion drawn from it.

The output schema follows the same logic: the action under review, the controlling authority, observed facts with citations, missing evidence, next steps for the environmental specialist, and a status from a fixed set (cleared, conditionally cleared, pending review, not approved). Conflicting engineering drawings or disputed historic effects trigger escalation.

## Retrieval: filter first, never average conflicts

Before any search, filter by jurisdiction, agency, document status and effective date. Use hybrid semantic and keyword search to catch definitions and exceptions, and chunk clauses with their headings, definitions and neighbours so an exception travels with its rule. Conflicts get flagged, never averaged.

On the vision and spatial side, a buffer or overlap is a screening signal, not an effects determination, and every machine-derived feature gets a confidence or review status. Retrieved web content is treated as untrusted and tested for prompt injection.

## Success is a reviewable record

The workflow has three human-supervised steps (intake validation, rules retrieval, a dossier of site conditions), with a rules engine handling measurable conditions and the language model explaining and drafting around them. A designated approval is required before any external submission. Mohit's measure of success is a reviewable decision record that helps experts find evidence and see what remains uncertain, not a verdict that a project is compliant.

## Who should watch

Engineers building LLM features for regulated, evidence-heavy decisions: permitting, legal review, audits. The delivery is dense and slide-driven rather than a code walkthrough, so treat it as a design checklist. Mohit is clear that each new domain still needs fresh legal mapping and evaluation.

Title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 roundup: checking agents before they act
Description: Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 in review, from hooks that gate coding agents and SBOMs that stop at the model to cell isolation, masking checks and safe recovery.
Body:
[Conf42 DevSecOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2026) ran online on October 1, 2026, with 24 talks, and one question kept coming back: what happens to security controls built for a human pace when the code is written, installed and shipped by agents? Speakers from Harness, ArmorCode, Keeper Security, WSO2, SAP, Microsoft, Tesla, T-Mobile and AWS answered it from different corners: before the tool call, inside the artifact, at the tenant boundary, in the test data and during recovery.

## Put the check before the action, not after the alert

The busiest track was about coding agents, and its speakers converged on timing. [Artemis Leonardou](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_agents_guardrails_policy) (NOFire AI) described an incident where the alerting worked exactly as designed and was still useless, because it reported something that had already broken. Humans hesitate before acting; agents don't. The talk is about evaluating an action before it executes, using the pipeline you already have.

[Karan Bansal](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Karan_Bansal_agents_leastprivilege_hooks) (ArmorCode) made hooks the enforcement layer: they intercept every tool call between the agent's decision and its execution and run outside the model, so prompt injection can't talk its way past them. His blocking scripts cover dangerous commands, secret exfiltration, typosquatted installs and agents that mark failing tests as skipped to fake a green build. [Oleksandr Kryvchenko](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Oleksandr_Kryvchenko_claude_cicd_pretooluse) (Keeper Security) showed why that matters: Claude Code's `permissions.deny` rules can be silently bypassed, and PreToolUse hooks put policy in your own code instead of the model's.

[Yunhao Jiao](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Yunhao_Jiao_aicoding_verification_gates) (TestSprite) brought numbers from CoderCup, a public competition where four frontier coding agents built the same ten-phase app. Every agent broke previously working features between 31 and 57 times in a single build, and the breaks stayed invisible until something ran the application. His argument: the PR gate is too late, so verify while the agent works. [Deepanshu Kukreja](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Deepanshu_Kukreja_agents_automation_incidentresponse) looked at the other side, using agents to automate DevSecOps chores across IaC, CI/CD and incident response.

## The supply chain now includes weights, memory and RAG

The keynote from [Roshan Piyush](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Roshan_Piyush_supply_chain_security), Head of Security Research at Harness, traced supply chain attacks from SolarWinds and XZ Utils to Shai-Hulud, then argued that agent configuration (hooks, skills, CLAUDE.md files, memory, MCP servers) is where the trust has moved. He ran a discovery script on his own laptop and found more than a thousand agent artifacts, half of them unknown to him.

[Emmy Eide](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Emmy_Eide_sbom_models_supplychain) (Realign Labs) went after the artifact itself. DevSecOps got good at proving what's in a build, but a model-bearing service ships a multi-gigabyte blob that no scanner parses and no SBOM format meaningfully describes. The talk maps which gates still fire and which wave through what they can't inspect. [Jayakumar Ramalingam](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Jayakumar_Ramalingam_apis_inference_guardrails) (SiriusXM) covered APIs where a single request can now trigger inference, retrieve user context and call downstream tools. [Ananda Kumar Dey](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Ananda_Kumar_Dey_rag_vectors_trust) (Quadrant Technologies) and [Sirisha Ayyagari](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Sirisha_Ayyagari_zerotrust_sap_pricing) applied the same thinking to enterprise RAG and to AI-driven pricing inside SAP.

## Isolation and identity, without long-lived secrets

[Lahiru De Silva](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Lahiru_De_Silva_kubernetes_multitenancy_isolation) (WSO2) gave one of the most concrete talks of the day. Namespaces and NetworkPolicies stop accidents, not a determined neighbour, so OpenChoreo, a CNCF Sandbox internal developer platform, gives each tenant environment its own cell: a namespace with a Cilium policy boundary, its own observability scope, and four directional gateways (northbound, westbound, southbound, eastbound) built on Envoy and the Kubernetes Gateway API.

[Venkata Velavarthipati](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Venkata_Velavarthipati_workloadidentity_oidc_secretless) removed stored credentials from multi-cloud pipelines with OpenID Connect and workload identity federation. [Perumalsamy Ravindran](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Perumalsamy_Ravindran_terraform_multicloud_iac) covered Terraform across providers, [Sonu Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Sonu_Kumar_platformengineering_governance_ai) (Peoplefluent) governed platform engineering, and [Rahul Kizhakkepachilamakol](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Rahul_Kizhakkepachilamakol_distributedsystems_vulnerabilities_latency) (AWS) the anti-entropy mechanisms that keep vulnerability findings flowing within minutes at cloud scale, where every minute of delay widens the exposure window.

## Test your detection and your recovery, not just your build

[Aleksander Kryukov](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Aleksander_Kryukov_detection_exploits_simulation) asked whether your alert would have fired in time, then answered it with a harness that replays candidate detection rules against 46 historical Web3 exploits using state-forked execution. Detection deadlines come from observed exfiltration curves, not arbitrary SLAs. [Sanjay Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Sanjay_Iyer_recovery_eventdriven_rto) made a point that deserves more airtime: a recovery can meet RTO and RPO and still replay duplicate transactions past fraud controls or restore stale permissions. [Mridula Chilakamarri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Mridula_Chilakamarri_kubernetes_opentelemetry_diagnostics) (Dell Technologies) built deterministic request-level diagnostics on OpenTelemetry and W3C Trace Context.

## Data, privacy and the browser

[Siyuan Feng](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Siyuan_Feng_datamasking_testdata_validation) (CSC) tackled a problem every test-data team hits: validating masking when legacy tables have no stable keys. The trick is to intersect sensitive values first and build composite identifiers only for the overlapping subset. [Mary Sirisha Duggimpudi](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Mary_Sirisha_Duggimpudi_datadiscovery_privacy_compliance) (T-Mobile) covered AI-driven sensitive data discovery, [Vinay Puri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Vinay_Puri_ml_compliance_monitoring) (Amazon) ML-based compliance monitoring, and [Ashwin Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Ashwin_Kumar_mobile_authorization_identity) (Tesla) identity binding for executives reading analytics on unmanaged phones.

Two talks stayed close to the pipeline. [Elena Darevskaya](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Elena_Darevskaya_csp_browser_javascript) (SAP) showed how a customer's Content Security Policy or COOP headers break an embedded SDK that worked fine in development, and how to catch it earlier. Title: Give an agent's Terraform change consequences before merge
Description: Kevin Brown of Cloud World Model at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 shows simulated cost, CPU and latency for an infrastructure PR, gaps labelled.
Body:
An agent can write a perfectly valid Terraform change and still have no idea what it costs or how it behaves under load. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Kevin Brown, founder and CEO of Cloud World Model, argued that the missing layer between an agent's plan and the real cloud is a model of what the change will do, and showed his company's GitHub app putting simulated results straight into a pull request.

Fair warning on scope: this is a short founder talk about his own product. The idea it carries is worth the few minutes even if you never install anything.

## Prompting decides intent, not consequences

Kevin's abstract frames it neatly: "Prompt engineering decides what an agent intends. Something else decides what happens when it acts." An agent that can write and apply an infrastructure change can't feel its cost, latency or failure behaviour until it's live. The usual guardrail, a sandbox, covers code. It says nothing about what a workload does at 300 requests per second or what a node failure does to a queue.

`terraform plan` doesn't fill that gap either. In the talk he points out that plan tells you the change is syntactically correct and what resources move, not what the change will cost, how latency shifts or how often it fails. Reviewers end up approving infrastructure PRs with less information than they'd demand for an application change.

## The demo: one machine type, one report

The worked example is deliberately boring, which is the point. Kevin took the public HashiCorp GKE tutorial for Terraform and committed one small change: the node shape moved from n1-standard-1 to e2-standard-2 on two nodes. Opening the pull request triggers a report that simulates the base and the head of the PR and shows the before and after for cost, CPU, P99 latency and error rate, modelled at 300 RPS.

The reviewer, or the agent that made the change, can then decide whether to adjust or merge. Kevin's pitch is that these are numbers you'd normally only see after the deploy.

## Read the labels

The part of the talk that earns trust is the time spent on what the model gets wrong or doesn't cover. Every number in the report carries a label: modelled, estimated, or a known gap.

He lists the gaps out loud. IAM policies aren't modelled. Network paths such as route tables and security groups aren't modelled; the report detects the change and marks it "not modeled yet". Memory scope is covered for Cloud Run and GKE only. Spot interruptions are modelled for EKS only, with a two-minute notice.

Cost is modelled from public list prices, so a reported saving doesn't include your discounts and isn't your bill. Cloud World Model also doesn't connect to your cloud account; Kevin presents that as a feature, with the trade-off that you still have to check your own environment. A simulation that tells you where it's blind is far more useful than one that's confidently precise about everything.

## Why this belongs at a prompt engineering conference

The broader argument matches a thread that ran through the event: reliable agents need checks outside the prompt. You can tell an agent in capital letters to avoid expensive changes, and it still won't know what expensive means for a node pool change. A modelled consequence, attached to the PR where both the agent and the human reviewer can see it, turns that sentence into evidence. It gives the agent consequences before it gets access.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure teams letting agents (or juniors, or tired seniors) open Terraform PRs, and anyone designing review gates for infrastructure as code. It's a vendor demo, so go in expecting a product walkthrough. Kevin closed by asking teams who ship infrastructure as code weekly to send one real PR for blunt feedback, with no contract.

Title: Your coding agent's dotfiles are the new software supply chain
Description: Roshan Piyush of Harness at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 on why hooks, skills, memory and MCP servers are where AI supply chain attacks now land.
Body:
Roshan Piyush, Head of Security Research at Harness, pointed a discovery script at his own laptop before giving his Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 talk. It found 1,103 agent-related artifacts, about half of which he didn't know were there, including 158 skills and around 830 instruction files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. His argument follows from that inventory: the software supply chain now runs through the configuration that tells AI agents how to behave, and almost nobody reviews it.

## Attackers follow the trust

The first third of the talk is a fast tour of supply chain incidents, and the point is the pattern, not the nostalgia. SolarWinds shipped a signed backdoor through a build pipeline. Codecov's compromised uploader script exfiltrated environment variables. Alex Birsan's dependency confusion research showed registries preferring the higher version number over the internal source. XZ Utils was a two-year trust-building operation, caught only because a developer was annoyed by a 500 millisecond SSH delay. Roshan's aside lands well: an AI agent would never have bothered about half a second.

Then the newer ones. The LiteLLM compromise came through an already-compromised Trivy action and dropped a Python `.pth` file, which runs every time the interpreter starts. Shai-Hulud tore through npm and used TruffleHog, a secret scanner, to find the secrets it stole. A later variant used AI to craft payloads and embedded a request about building a nuclear bomb, so that LLM-based malware scanners would refuse to look at it. Each step moved to wherever developers had put their trust: an update, a tool, a package manager, a contributor, a release channel. Roshan's claim is that trust is now moving to the agent.

## Committed config is committed behaviour

The sharpest line in the talk is about what lives in our repos now: "Not to commit dot ENV files, but now we commit an entire behavior." Teams check in CLAUDE.md, `.cursor` rules, `mcp.json` and `settings.json` so colleagues can share them. Anyone who clones the repo inherits instructions they've probably never read, which a colleague may have pasted from somewhere else.

Hooks get special treatment. In Roshan's words, "Hooks have become the dot bash RC problem for the agents at scale." They run on every prompt and every action, they can silently rewrite context, and his team's research found that hooks could edit other hooks without any approval prompt. A malicious instruction in an MCP server can install a hook that does the rest.

## Memory, hallucinated packages and blind spots between tools

Three more attack paths get a short treatment each:

- **Memory poisoning.** Tell an agent once to use a mock payment tool for testing and forget about it. Months later a vector store retrieves that note by relevance, not recency, and the agent authorises a payment through the mock. Roshan also cited research showing five malicious documents in a million can hijack an answer with a 90% success rate.
- **Hallucinated dependencies.** Agents rarely typo, but they do invent package names. An attacker only has to register the name the model keeps suggesting.
- **Cross-tool blindness.** Claude refused to tamper with its own hooks and settings, but Cursor or Windsurf would happily edit Claude's files, and the reverse holds too. Each agent guards itself and ignores its neighbours.

He also admitted that he, a head of security research, usually picks "always allow" on the permission prompt. Humans get tired of approving things, and he counts that fatigue as part of the threat model rather than a moral failing.

## What he wants teams and vendors to do

The recommendations split in two. Teams can act now: open your `.claude` and `.cursor` folders and look; review agent configuration as source code; replace static API keys with short-lived role credentials (his team uses 24-hour sessions for Bedrock); and red-team the models you rely on, as NIST AI 600-1 expects. Vendors and the ecosystem need to supply what nobody can build alone: a kill switch that hooks can't disable, signed models with provenance (CycloneDX ML-BOM and SPDX AI BOM are a start), signed MCP servers, provenance for hooks, and guardrails that work across agents. His blunt summary: "AI supply chain is completely broken right now."

## Who should watch

Platform and AppSec engineers rolling coding agents out to a whole organisation, and anyone who has approved a CLAUDE.md in code review without reading it. The talk is threat modelling and field notes rather than a product demo, and the attack history alone makes a good briefing for a team that hasn't been following the npm incidents.

[Watch Roshan Piyush's talk](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Roshan_Piyush_supply_chain_security) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/9-n30eWZ8pY)).

## Related Conf42 talks

- Alex Shershebnev (Zencoder) on [wiring MCP into DevOps without opening a security hole](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_cloud_mcp_secure), DevSecOps 2025.
- [Your AI Has Too Much Access: Deterministic Authorization for Coding Agents](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) by Sohan Maheshwar (AuthZed), LLMs 2026.
- [LLM hacking is underrated](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_hacking_underrated_security) by Dmitriy Volkov (Palisade), on fine-tuning poisoning, LLMs 2025.

## From Harness

Harness makes software delivery tooling, and in the talk Roshan describes it putting agents across the pipeline: dependency installs, PR review, deploys, production monitoring and rollbacks. The talk's abstract links to a demo of its runtime protection agent.

Title: Charter, harness, factory: who owns each coding agent rule
Description: Ian Johnson of Parento at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 maps where a coding agent gate can sit and who gets paged when that rule is wrong.
Body:
In most teams running coding agents, a new rule lands wherever the person who noticed the problem happens to have commit access. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Ian Johnson, Staff Software Engineer at Parento and author of Harness Engineering, gave that mess a map: three contexts (charter, harness, factory), six rungs where a gate can physically sit, and two boundary lines that tell you who owns each one.

This is an org-design talk wearing a prompt engineering badge, and it's better for it.

## Three contexts, one arrow

Ian splits what most people call "the harness" into three layers. The charter says what this project is about: rules, hooks and skills that live in the repository and change constantly. The harness says how a turn happens: tools, context and prompting, changing rarely but with big impact when it does. The factory says how work ships: stages, gates, guards and records, changing least of all.

Dependencies point one way, from factory to harness to charter. The factory hands work to the harness; the harness reads the charter to understand the code base. If the charter configured the harness, one repository would govern the entire fleet. And a harness that knows about the factory can't run on a laptop, which he treats as a design smell you can test for.

The two failure stories in his abstract will feel familiar. Platform ships a harness and finds one team's opinion inside it. Development writes a charter and spends a third of it trying to configure a pipeline it can't reach.

## A ladder that alternates inference and determinism

The middle of the talk is the ladder. In the charter, a gate can be a rule (the agent is told, nothing enforces it) or a hook (a cheap, deterministic script fired on an event). In the harness, it can be a judging phase (an inference call) or a predicate (a boolean check). In the factory, it can be a review stage (inferential, looking at one turn's output) or a stage gate (deterministic, firing on the published diff).

Walking up, you swap between inference and determinism at every step. Ian doesn't say climb to the top. Inferential rules feed forward and deterministic checks feed back, and you want both. Two more things stay deliberately off the ladder: the tool grant, because it withholds a capability, and CI, because it sits outside the work.

His worked example takes one sentence, "every HTTP call goes through libhttp", and shows it living at three addresses with three owners. The same predicate at two boundaries isn't one rule enforced twice, he argues, because each boundary sees different things: the in-harness check sees tool calls and state, the factory sees the whole finished tree, and the charter only sees what's in context for the turn.

## Two lines, and they cross in the harness

The context line asks what a thing governs: a project, a turn or a delivery. The ownership line asks who gets paged when it's wrong. Both agree at the charter (development) and at the factory (platform). They cross inside the harness, which is where your org-design arguments have been happening all along.

He splits the harness component by component. Platform owns the prompt skeleton and contract; development owns what the repository contributes. Platform owns which tools exist; development picks which get a phase. Platform owns the budget ceiling, because that's money. And for policy, the rule that makes shared ownership survivable: platform sets the floor, development tightens and never loosens. A repository that can loosen the floor has no floor, only a default, so every legitimate loosening gets a named escape hatch.

## Honest about the evidence

Ian is upfront that his change-rate diagnostic (a quarter with three factory changes and no charter ones means the distribution is wrong) comes from his own repositories and one production code base, so there's no benchmark. He also says the harness split is where he has changed his mind most. That candour makes the model easier to trust.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers building internal agent tooling, and tech leads tired of the same argument about where a rule belongs. The homework is concrete: publish the floor as one versioned file, switch the factory off and see if a turn still runs, and for your loudest rule, name the rung it actually sits on. If the answer is prose and you expected a gate, that gap is next week's work.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Hardening AI Coding Agents with Hooks: Enforcing Least Privilege on Autonomous Developers](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Karan_Bansal_agents_leastprivilege_hooks) by Karan Bansal at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.
- [Your AI Has Too Much Access: Deterministic Authorization for Coding Agents](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) by Sohan Maheshwar at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026.
- [From Prompts to Review Harnesses: Scaling AI Code Reviews Across 70+ Software Projects](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Guido_Scheffler_code_review_harness) by Guido Scheffler of CGI at Conf42 AI Agents 2026.

Title: Your agent's prompt is one layer, not the whole system
Description: Emerson Braun of Plan A Technologies at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 splits agent reliability into six layers so a fix lands in the right one.
Body:
When an agent misbehaves, the first reflex is to open the prompt and add another sentence. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Emerson Braun, Staff Engineer and Regional Director at Plan A Technologies, argued that the prompt is only one part of the design, and that a reliable agent needs context, contracts, outputs, retries and evals that live outside it.

His case study is small and relatable: a content pipeline he built for his own posts on X and LinkedIn. Threads published, the blog post went out, the newsletter got scheduled. Then one post was saved as an empty draft. He fixed the prompt, as everyone would, and then realised the prompt wasn't where the bug lived.

## Your agent is perfectly designed to get the result it gets

Emerson borrows the old systems-thinking line that every system is perfectly designed to get the result it gets, and points it at agents. If brand rules, approval policy, "don't post twice", output format and the draft-validate-publish steps all sit in one prompt, then a failure gives you no idea which of those layers broke. Everything is an instruction, and every instruction is a polite guess.

So he splits the work into six layers: context, contract, output, retries, the prompt itself, and evals. Each one gets its own diagnostic question.

## Context is an input, so version it

The first failure he describes is stale context. The agent was told to follow the brand guide and it did, faithfully, using version three, while marketing had shipped version four the week before. The prompt was fine. The input was wrong.

His fix is to treat context like any other input: record which version was loaded, when, and a hash, so you can reconstruct exactly what the agent saw. The question to ask is whether the agent had the right information and whether it was current.

## If the tool allows it, the prompt doesn't forbid it

"Never publish without approval" is a sentence. A publish tool that accepts any call is a capability. When the two disagree, the capability wins. Emerson tiers actions by risk: low-risk reads, searches and classification run alone; reversible actions run within policy limits and with enough record to reconstruct them; high-impact actions such as deletes go to a human. And the human needs the impact and the context of the decision in front of them, not a random ID and an approve button.

## The empty draft was a correct refusal

The empty post turned out to be the model doing the right thing. The draft was requested for another brand's account, the model refused, and the pipeline saved the refusal as an empty draft. The real bug was that nothing checked the output against a contract. Emerson's rule: parse and validate model output the way you'd validate a third-party API, and when it doesn't match, record why.

## Failure is a state, and retries need a key

Retries get the same treatment. A timeout on "publish" followed by a blind retry is how you publish twice. He uses idempotency keys, a state machine that knows what to do after a failure, bounded retries that hand off to a dead letter queue or a person, and recovery that regenerates only the missing part instead of starting from scratch. Automate the recovery decisions, not the retries.

## Shrink the prompt, then judge the purpose

Once the rules move out into code, the prompt shrinks to its core: stable policy, task context, retrieved knowledge and user intent, kept separate. A good test for whether something belongs there: does the failure change when you change the words? If it does, it's a prompt problem. If not, look elsewhere.

His first eval run is the warning shot. Seven drafts, all checks green, and the drafts were still empty or written with the wrong context. The checks measured format, not purpose. He ends with six questions to ask before touching the prompt, one per layer, and a closing challenge: which of your rules lives only in a prompt?

## Who should watch

Anyone running an agent with real side effects (posting, merging, sending, deleting) who keeps patching the system prompt after every incident. It's a short, practical talk built around one honest failure, and the six questions are easy to steal for a postmortem template. If you want the observability half, Emerson points to his earlier Conf42 talk on tracing agents.

- [The Retry Storm That Ate My Budget: Debugging the Hidden Cost Loops in Agentic AI](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens) by Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula at Conf42 AI Agents 2026.

Title: Conf42 AI Agents 2026: less LLM, more harness
Description: Conf42 AI Agents 2026 roundup - planning without model calls, AI coding harnesses, LLM-as-judge testing, runaway token bills and agent security, in 22 talks.
Body:
Conf42 AI Agents 2026 ran online on September 24, 2026, with 22 talks, and the loudest message was a sceptical one: the model is rarely the problem. Speaker after speaker argued that what makes an agent shippable is the system around it, meaning deterministic planning, typed tools, review harnesses, evals, budgets, and identity boundaries. There were plenty of demos, but the best talks were about what happens after the demo.

The full lineup is on the [Conf42 AI Agents 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/agents2026), and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCZ8u5VHJAm9eOB9KJTCZT8).

## Stop asking the model what to do next

[Maureese Williams](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Maureese_Williams_planning_search_graph), an AI Engineer at Disney, started from a mundane observation: at every step, an agent asks the language model what to do next, so a twenty-step task costs twenty model calls and gives a different plan each run. The GATS approach (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) runs UCB1 tree search over a state-transition graph the agent builds as it works. The LLM never picks an action; it is the last rung of an escalation ladder, after symbolic rules and learned statistics, and its answers are cached.

[Michael Haim](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Michael_Haim_orchestration_patterns_determinism), founder and CEO of Zindell Technologies, tackled the same non-determinism from the language side: you cannot orchestrate agents with a plain if or switch when their output is fuzzy, so use pattern matching to turn it into structured, auditable control flow. And [Elizabeth Fuentes Leone](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost) of AWS showed semantic tool selection: every call serialises every tool description into the context, so filter tools with vector search before they reach the LLM, cutting both wrong picks and token cost.

## The harness decides what ships

AI coding got its own track, and almost none of it was about prompts.

- [Ruben Marcus Luz Paschoarelli](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ruben_Marcus_Luz_Paschoarelli_coding_harness_evidence) of MultiVM Labs argued that AI coding fails because the system around the model trusts the wrong evidence, and showed his harness: short specs, isolated git worktrees, model routing by role, browser verification, screenshot gates, and cost controls.
- [Guido Scheffler](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Guido_Scheffler_code_review_harness) of CGI told the story of scaling AI code reviews across more than 70 projects, moving from brittle prompts to a deterministic review harness with an agent runner, an MCP server, managed checklists, and enforced completeness.
- [Suneet Malhotra](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Suneet_Malhotra_mcp_pipeline_accuracy), Senior Manager of Test Engineering at Motorola Solutions, presented a Claude Code and MCP pipeline whose three MCP servers turn product requirements into Jira stories, test cases, and Appium code at about 80% accuracy; the talk is about the other 20%, and why the human PR gate is mandatory.
- [Kemet Dugue](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Kemet_Dugue_workflows_productivity_onboarding) walked through how Uber's driver onboarding team turned script-heavy manual processes into agentic workflows, and [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Peter_De_Tender_azure_deployment_automation) of Microsoft showed how his open-source library of Azure demo scenarios became an agentic deployment system. [Kabir Ibraheem](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Kabir_Ibraheem_fullstack_tooling_productivity) of Meltwater offered a practical tour of AI tools for full-stack engineers.

## Who judges the agent

Testing non-deterministic systems came up again and again. [Liran Yushinsky](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen), who leads automation at JFrog, asked how you test an AI that never gives you the same answer twice when it generates executable code through a chain of tool calls, and answered with LLM-as-judge alongside conventional checks.

Diamond sponsor Harness made the enterprise case: [Shubham Jindal](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Shubham_Jindal_ai_demo_enterprise), Director of AI at Harness, laid out four pillars (context engineering, evals, memory, and governance) and argued that an eval suite should never pass at 100%, because then it cannot measure progress. [Shubham Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Shubham_Sharma_readiness_platform_enterprise) of Microsoft proposed a unified readiness framework, so models, retrieval, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop workflows are assessed together rather than team by team.

## The bill comes at 2 AM

[Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens) of AWS opened with the scene every agent operator dreads: 2 AM, no customers, no deploys, every dashboard green, and the bill climbing by multiples because their own agents were working hard all night on nothing. The talk dissects retry storms, runaway tool calls, context bloat, and multi-agent overhead.

[Vladimir Beskorovainyi](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Vladimir_Beskorovainyi_sql_orchestration_scale) of Besk Tech brought the most production-scarred talk of the day: an on-prem text-to-SQL platform with open-weight models across 500+ data marts and 30M+ users. The opener says it all: "Very few people have to answer for the number it gives at 9:00 in the morning."

## Don't give the agent a shell

The trust track was about boundaries. [Ahmed Tariq](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_identity_permissions_cloud) of Simplify9 argued for a small set of typed tools, a deliberately limited identity, and enforcement outside the model, instead of a shell and a broad credential. [Blaize Stewart](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Blaize_Stewart_rag_security_injection) of GBLI broke a RAG application live with prompt injection, poisoned documents, and broken document-level authorisation. [Morgan Willis](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Morgan_Willis_production_guardrails_trust) of AWS summed it up: don't trust the agent, trust the system you build around it, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK as the toolkit.

## Agents meet enterprise data

Agents are only as good as the data they act on. [Rohit Deshpande and Scott Young](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Rohit_Deshpande_Scott_Young_mcp_dashboards_live) of SAP showed a ReAct agent that turns a request like AR aging by customer into a deployed dashboard over live data via MCP. [Vishwak Thatikonda](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Vishwak_Thatikonda_mdm_data_retail) of Starbucks explained why master data management built for reporting breaks when agents make decisions on it. [Pon Murugesh Devendren](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Pon_Murugesh_Devendren_sap_incidents_events) of Deloitte built event-driven agents for proactive SAP incident management, [Nick Rezaee](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Nick_Rezaee_health_wearables_intervene) of Harvard showed agents that turn wearable data into timely interventions, and [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_serverless_photos_aws) of Sage confessed that his Step Functions DAG for judging 8,000 photos was a lie, and went agentic.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsors [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) and [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), gold sponsor the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/), the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and all the media partners on the event page.

The series returns with [Conf42 AI Agents 2027](https://www.conf42.com/agents2027) on September 23, 2027. Until then, the playlist holds enough harness engineering to keep your agents honest.

Title: Enterprise AI in four pillars: context, evals, memory, governance
Description: Shubham Jindal of Harness at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 on why AI demos stall before production, and the four pillars that get agents there.
Body:
An AI demo takes days to build and wows the room; the production version can take months and still embarrass you in front of a customer. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Shubham Jindal, Director of AI at Harness, laid out the blueprint his team uses to close that gap: four pillars called context, evals, memory, and governance, each with concrete habits you can copy.

This is a sponsor keynote, and Shubham says up front that Harness has built all four pillars into its own AI for the software delivery pipeline. But the talk is a framework, not a product tour. Almost everything in it applies to any team shipping agents to paying users.

## Demos run on prompts, production runs on context

Shubham's opening claim is that the mindset has to shift from prompt engineering to context engineering. In a demo you are not throwing large data at the model, so a clever prompt carries the day. In production the model meets your siloed systems, your company jargon, and your sensitive data, and that is where it starts to make things up with great confidence.

His line for it: "Context is the new code." His team's case is personal. Harness has separate CI, CD, and code products, and an LLM trained on the whole internet does not know that CI means something specific inside Harness.

He gave four practical tricks for keeping the context window healthy:

- **Compaction.** Summarise the conversation as it nears the limit and keep only the decisions. He compares it to a garbage collector.
- **Large outputs go to files.** A Jira or GitHub MCP call can return a giant JSON blob. Write it to a file and let the agent read the slice it needs, instead of flooding the window.
- **Context editing.** Proactively drop dead ends, like the five wrong Gradle commands the agent tried before finding the right one.
- **Semantic augmentation.** Load skills and reference material when they become relevant, not all at once in the system prompt.

## A knowledge graph is the compiler for your context

The most useful example in the talk is a question that sounds simple: which of my PRs caused an incident last week? The answer crosses the PR, the CI run, the CD deployment, the version that shipped, and the on-call page. Ask an agent to stitch that from three raw data sources and it will guess at relationships it does not understand.

Shubham's fix is to extract the entities you care about (services, users, incidents, releases), enrich them with metadata such as owners, link them into a graph, and expose that graph through an API the agent can query and walk. If context is the new code, he says, the knowledge graph is its compiler.

## Evals should fail on purpose

The second most important pillar, in his ranking, is evals. Unit tests assume deterministic code; agents are probabilistic, so many teams skip testing entirely because they cannot define what good looks like. His example is model switching: an agent tuned on Opus burns too many tokens, so you want to try Sonnet. Without evals you are changing a model name and hoping.

The framework he described:

- LLM-as-a-judge checks, ideally with a different model than the one being judged.
- Regression evals as a quality gate in CI/CD before any prompt, temperature, or model change ships.
- Evals on production traces. Harness runs a simple user temperament check that asks whether the user seems frustrated, types in caps, or repeats the same question.
- Every production failure becomes a new eval case.

The idea worth stealing is that an eval suite should not pass at 100%. Treat it like a benchmark: if 80 of 100 cases pass today, a change that moves you to 85 is progress and one that drops you to 75 is a regression. A suite that always passes can only tell you about the cases you already solved.

## Memory makes an assistant, governance makes it shippable

On memory, Shubham separates short-term memory (the current session) from long-term memory that bubbles up patterns, such as which repos a team works in or what a user keeps asking about. His summary: chatbots forget, assistants remember. He also traces the arc from chatbot to in-app assistant to autonomous agent, with examples like an agent that watches a PR's CI, fixes failures, and pushes until it is green.

Governance he calls the boring pillar enterprises care about most. He splits it into scoped access (do not hand an agent every tool in the GitHub MCP when it only needs a few), guardrails such as PII redaction and EU data residency, real-time content filters, and full audit trails of tool calls and model versions. Governance, in his words, is the new runtime, because it only exists while the agent is running.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads who have a working agent prototype and a nervous security team. The context-window tricks and the "evals as benchmarks" framing are worth the time on their own. If you are still deciding whether to build an agent at all, start elsewhere.

Related talks from other Conf42 events:

- [Hilik Paz on how to evaluate your evals](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) at Conf42 LLMs 2025.
- [Srikanth Devarakonda on LLM evals and benchmarks](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Srikanth_Devarakonda_llms_evals_benchmarks) at Conf42 Observability 2026.
- [Prateek Mittal on knowledge graphs in software delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery) at Conf42 LLMs 2026.

[Watch Shubham Jindal's talk](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Shubham_Jindal_ai_demo_enterprise) or see the whole [Conf42 AI Agents 2026 lineup](https://www.conf42.com/agents2026).

Harness covers the delivery side of software, from CI and CD pipelines to testing and security, with an AI layer aimed at speeding up the path from merged code to production.

Title: Conf42 Observability 2026 - when green stopped meaning healthy
Description: Conf42 Observability 2026 in review, 20 talks on tracing AI agents, dashboards that lie, eBPF, telemetry pipelines and using signals to test.
Body:
[Conf42 Observability 2026](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026) went out on September 10, 2026 with 20 talks, and a single complaint kept surfacing in different accents: the dashboard said everything was fine. Sometimes the culprit was an AI agent reporting 200 OK while answering wrong, sometimes a payment provider, sometimes a fallback path nobody had ever exercised. Speakers from PagerDuty, Adobe, Google, Snowflake, ServiceNow, General Motors, Harness and a crowd of observability vendors showed what to measure instead.

## Green is a claim, not a proof

Diamond sponsor Harness opened with [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), head of resilience testing and LitmusChaos co-founder, on why dashboards can only show paths that have already run. His case study is a third-party API failing over to a redundant path that never carried traffic, a retry storm turning a partial outage into a full one, and a team debugging an hour nobody instrumented. The cure is an inventory of untested paths and controlled experiments to fill it.

[Eleftheria Batsou](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Eleftheria_Batsou_healthchecks_outages_dependencies) (UptimeRobot) took the outside-in version: your app returns a healthy 200 while customers can't pay because Stripe is degraded. The thing that broke is the payment provider, the identity provider, the CDN or the LLM API you added last quarter. [Victoria Nduka](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Victoria_Nduka_accessibility_slos_goldensignals) (VictoriaMetrics) proposed accessibility as a fifth golden signal, so regressions show up in SLOs instead of in an audit weeks later. And [Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_burnout_oncall_sre) (Rootly) pointed the same discipline at people: we have liveness probes for every service, but the engineer holding the pager gets "How are you doing?" and always answers "Fine."

## Agents need traces of their own

The busiest track was agent observability. [Sabith K Soopy](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sabith_K_Soopy_agents_debugging_tracing) (Stackgen) put it best in one line of his abstract: traditional APM won't tell you an agent burned 40k tokens narrating a wrong answer. He showed the spans Stackgen uses to follow an agent through plan, gather and present, with per-tool cost and latency. [Emerson Braun](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Emerson_Braun_agents_llms_observability) (Plan A Technologies) followed one agent run from request to outcome and instrumented the context it received, the decisions it made and where it started to drift.

[Elliot Gardiner](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Elliot_Gardiner_agents_codegeneration_tracing) (Code Telemetry) treated coding agents as long-running processes that search, edit, test, retry and delegate to subagents, and argued that token counts and adoption are the wrong metrics for them. [Princewill Kalio](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Princewill_Kalio_llms_rag_distributedsystems) (Dockie) said the quiet part out loud in his title: AI systems are distributed systems now, with retrieval pipelines, vector stores and background workers, and they deserve distributed-systems tracing rather than print statements.

## The 3am page for code no human wrote

Two talks dealt with the operational aftermath. [Ralph Bird](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ralph_Bird_sre_agents_incidentresponse) (PagerDuty) opens at 03:47 with a pager firing over code written by one agent, shipped by another, never seen by a human, after the SRE agent has already failed. [Artemis Leonardou](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_debugging_agents_codegeneration) (NOFire AI) lived it: an agent-written change passed review and CI, then took a production path down for about three hours. Nothing in the diff was wrong on its own; the failure lived in the combination, and the dashboards could say what and where but not why.

## Measuring whether the AI was right

[Srikanth Devarakonda](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Srikanth_Devarakonda_llms_evals_benchmarks) (Adobe) connected generative AI evaluation (factual accuracy, grounding, safety, task completion) to observable system performance and business outcomes instead of static benchmarks. [Arjun D Sureshbabu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Arjun_D_Sureshbabu_llms_hallucinations_nlp) (Snowflake) shared lessons from a human-in-the-loop architecture for legal, compliance and privacy NLP, where a hallucination has a regulatory cost. [Ravi Chandra](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ravi_Chandra_llms_analytics_semanticlayer) (Google) went after the semantic layer behind analytics agents, using feedback to keep a static, expert-curated ontology from missing the long tail of what users actually ask.

## Pipelines, kernels and the bill

On the plumbing side, [Anais Dotis](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Anais_Dotis_ebpf_linux_networking) (groundcover) gave a hype-free explanation of eBPF and how kernel programming escaped the kernel into monitoring and security. [Rita Lopes](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Rita_Lopes_metrics_logging_tracing) (Gigapipe) started from the familiar four-backend stack of Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Pyroscope, and the trade-off between observing everything and paying for it. [Diana Todea](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Diana_Todea_opensource_observability_sustainability) (VictoriaMetrics) built a green observability pipeline entirely from open source and described how she got there by contributing upstream. [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_cloudnative_architecture_tracing) (SoftNet Technologies) argued for designing observability into cloud architectures rather than bolting it on, and [Joshua Fox](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Joshua_Fox_kubernetes_autoscaling_reliability) (DoiT International) went beyond HPA and VPA for Kubernetes autoscaling that cuts waste without hurting reliability.

## Telemetry as test input

Two talks turned signals into tests. [Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Vasuki_Uday_Kiran_Vudathala_loadtesting_performance_capacityplanning) (ServiceNow) replaced interviews and spreadsheet guesses about peak traffic with workload models built from observability data. [Sumaiyya Fatima](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sumaiyya_Fatima_automotive_embedded_simulation) (General Motors) applied observability-driven validation to hardware-in-the-loop testing for software-defined vehicles, where functionality emerges from many domains talking to each other.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Gold. Every talk is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBA6AiE2f0hmsnFk5oGfFjb).

The series continues with [Conf42 Observability 2027](https://www.conf42.com/obs2027). Bring the dashboards you trust least.

Title: Green dashboards only show the paths you have already tested
Description: Uma Mukkara of Harness at Conf42 Observability 2026 on why green dashboards can't prove resilience, and a four-step loop to test the untested paths.
Body:
Your dashboards can only show the paths your system has actually walked. At Conf42 Observability 2026, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), who leads resilience testing at Harness and co-founded LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, argued that the fallback route, the retry path and the DR plan are exactly the ones nobody instrumented, and that the only way to see them is to break things on purpose first.

The keynote is short and practical. It is also a Harness talk: the last section demos Harness Resilience Testing. The first two thirds stand on their own as an argument for any observability team.

## The gap is widening, and he names three accelerants

The premise: the observability system says green, and incidents keep happening anyway. Not one or two, but a steady stream in large organisations. Mukkara blames three accelerants. Systems keep getting more distributed and dynamic, with more dependencies. Releases happen all the time, and AI-assisted coding has pushed some teams to tens of releases a day. And agents are now in the loop, which brings a failure shape of its own.

Observability, in his framing, tells you what is happening. It does not tell you what would happen.

## Four things a dashboard never shows

He lists the blind spots plainly:

- **Single points of failure.** A dashboard shows what is instrumented and exercised. An untested dependency stays invisible until it goes.
- **Timeouts and retries that trigger new paths.** The code has been green for months because that branch never ran.
- **Degraded mode.** If the system has never been degraded, nobody knows what degraded looks like on screen.
- **Recovery.** If you never ran a DR test, you have no idea what your dashboards will say during one.

The uncomfortable part is timing. These are precisely the dashboards you need when a single point of failure trips, timeouts pile up and the system drops into degraded mode or DR.

## A retry storm in a path that never carried traffic

His case study is the pattern most on-call engineers will recognise. Everything is green. A third-party API stops responding, and the system fails over to a redundant path that has never carried traffic, so nobody instrumented it. Retries on the new path turn a partial outage into a full one within the next thirty minutes to an hour, and when the full outage lands, the team is debugging blind because nothing captured that hour.

The fix he prescribes is boring in the best way: find that failover path ahead of time, exercise it in a lower environment, and build the dashboards for it before production needs them.

## Agents can report healthy while doing the wrong thing

The new failure shape is the AI agent. A health check can return 200 OK while the model behind it is slow but not down, and Mukkara's point is that a slow model is as bad as a broken one. A tool call can time out silently while the agent keeps answering 200. His suggestion: inject latency between the model endpoint and the agent and check whether your observability reports the agent's real health, or just its HTTP status.

## The four-step loop

The method fits on an index card:

1. Inventory tested versus untested paths. For every "what happens if this network fails", ask whether you have seen it or assumed it.
2. Run controlled experiments with a small blast radius against the untested ones.
3. Add the missing dashboards and metrics the experiments reveal.
4. Repeat it, quarterly or more often.

For a next step he suggests starting with your most critical service, listing every assumption never observed in production, and putting your agentic systems into degraded mode to see if the dashboards tell the truth.

## What the demo shows

The closing demo covers Harness Resilience Testing, which runs chaos experiments, load tests and DR tests from one place. AI-assisted risk scanners read deployment metadata, logs, configuration and runtime events to flag likely risks before you run anything, and a resilience testing agent recommends and creates the experiments to confirm them.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability owners who have ever had to explain a green dashboard in a postmortem. Platform teams adding AI agents to production will get the most from the agent section, which is short but specific.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Boosting System Resilience with Exponential Backoff in Distributed Computing](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Suraj_Modi_system_resilience_backoff_computing) by Suraj Modi (Uber), the antidote to the retry storm in Mukkara's case study.
- [When Clusters Collide: The Misadventures of Disaster Recovery in Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Lev_Andelman_clusters_disaster_kubernetes) by Lev Andelman (TeraSky), on what happens when the DR plan meets reality.
- [Enhancing Hypothesis Development Through Resilience Modeling](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gunnar_Grosch_hypothesis_development_resilience_modeling) by Gunnar Grosch (AWS), on choosing which experiments to run first.

[Watch Uma Mukkara's keynote](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/OORwIuqgKV8).

## From Harness

Harness was the Diamond sponsor of Conf42 Observability 2026. The product shown in the talk is Harness Resilience Testing, part of the Harness platform, covering chaos experiments, load tests and DR tests.
