Title: Conf42 Remix 2026: 52 talks from every corner of the series
Description: Conf42 Remix 2026 roundup: resilience, AI agents in production, Kubernetes GPUs, Go monoliths, security basics and accessible JavaScript in 52 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Remix 2026, on August 20, 2026, is the one event in the series that refuses to pick a topic. It brings together popular talks from across the Conf42 calendar, grouped into tracks named after the series' own conferences, from Rustlang and Golang to Incident Management, DevSecOps and Large Language Models. The 52 talks ranged from Spotify's scaling lessons to monitoring garden plants with IoT sensors, and the whole lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/remix2026).

Here are the threads that ran across the tracks.

## Resilience is a separate goal from uptime

Harness opened with a keynote from [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), Head of Resilience Testing and co-creator of LitmusChaos. His argument: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you come back when a provider fails underneath you, and SREs should push for resilience gates in the pipeline the way they already gate on test coverage. He closed with AI-generated resilience risk reports as a way to win permission for chaos testing.

[Stuart Clark](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Stuart_Clark_scale_fail_spotify) of Spotify told the story of hyper-growth in 2014 creating fragmentation that made onboarding and incident response harder, and the lesson that good abstractions teach complexity rather than hide it. [Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes) of Rootly looked at what LLM-assisted coding does to reliability, including AI-generated tests that mirror the bugs they should catch. [Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Spiros_Economakis_sre_experience_ai) of NOFire AI argued the real AI opportunity in SRE is customer-centred prevention rather than faster RCA, and cloud architect [Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Renato_Losio_mistakes_lessons_scaling) shared five hard lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases.

## AI agents meet production constraints

[Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Samuel_Baruffi_poc_bedrock_agentcore) of AWS addressed why so many agent projects stall at proof of concept, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore covers identity, gateway-based tool access, runtime isolation and memory. [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) of Solo.io focused on the two questions every team running MCP gets asked: how do we observe it, and how do we keep costs down?

Two talks went after the context problem. [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure), co-founder of Anyshift.io, showed infrastructure modelled as a graph so an LLM can follow multi-hop dependencies with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher queries instead of guessing. Lior Schejter asked what happens when an agent that copes well with one repo meets [a distributed system of 200 microservices](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Lior_Schejter_context_agents_reasoning), and how to give it a mental model of the whole. And [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Leo_Visser_governance_apis_control) of OGD ICT-diensten demonstrated API management as the leash that keeps AI usage, budget and risk under control.

## Kubernetes as a platform for everything

[Piotr Zaniewski](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant) of vCluster spun up multi-tenant sandboxes with NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside them to share fractional GPUs between teams. [Christophe Gigax](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Christophe_Gigax_dapr_architectures_cloudnative) of Hager Group made the case for Dapr as an abstraction layer for state, pub/sub and more. [Peng Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Peng_Wang_workloads_oceanbase_powering) of OceanBase showed one database handling RAG, semantic search and log analytics on Kubernetes, and [Alejandro Mercado](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Alejandro_Mercado_observability_kubernetes_ebpf) of Michael Page covered eBPF-powered observability for root cause analysis in clusters.

## Go and Rust, from monoliths to leaderboards

The Golang track had two strong engineering stories. [Victor Lyuboslavsky](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Victor_Lyuboslavsky_modularizing_year_monolith) of Fleet Device Management described modularising a 10-year-old Go monolith whose layers had turned into hidden coupling and unclear ownership, and was candid about the people side as well as the architecture. [Ivan Balashov](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Ivan_Balashov_engineering_high_performance) of SoftSwiss walked through a leaderboard system that suffered daily outages, and the redesign that took its core operation from O(N²) to O(log N). [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_building_secure_pipelines) of SoftNet Technologies used Go to build secure CI/CD automation components. On the Rustlang track, [Tashi Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Tashi_Garg_cloud_ai_rust) of Juniper Networks built dynamic infrastructure UIs in Rust.

## Security fundamentals, explained well

Several talks were good introductions, and said so. [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql) of Microsoft gave a lap around GitHub Dependabot, CodeQL and the other built-in security features. [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep) of MoEngage opened the black box of static analysis using open-source Semgrep. Security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_documentation_artifacts_beginners) set out a minimum viable set of ISO 42001 documents for anyone asked who approved an AI system and on what data, and [Marat Kenzhebulatov](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marat_Kenzhebulatov_vision_computer_imaging) of Booking.com showed how to bring AI agents safely into security-critical backend work like code review and threat modelling.

## The web, data and one garden

[Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Gian_Wild_accessible_easier_than) of AccessibilityOz gave concrete code for accessible forms and JavaScript, reminding everyone that a fifth of the population has a disability. [Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Daniel_Afonso_state_testing_tech) of PagerDuty reviewed a decade of change in JavaScript testing. [Alejandro Duarte](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Alejandro_Duarte_llm_vectors_semantic) of MariaDB covered RAG in production, glue-on-pizza hallucinations included, and [Maximilian Schattauer](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Maximilian_Schattauer_retrievers_documents_ranking) of Perelyn showed LLM-driven pairwise ranking beating semantic retrievers on hard document retrieval.

And for the weekend, [Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics) of Grafana Labs showed how to monitor soil moisture with IoT sensors and Grafana Cloud as a project to do with your kids. The only talk of the day where the alert means water the basil.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), our diamond sponsor, to gold sponsors [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

Every talk is linked from the [Conf42 Remix 2026 page](https://www.conf42.com/remix2026). The next edition, [Conf42 Remix 2027](https://www.conf42.com/remix2027), is set for August 19, 2027.

Title: Reliability keeps your job, resilience gets you promoted
Description: Uma Mukkara of Harness, co-creator of LitmusChaos, at Conf42 Remix 2026 on resilience gates, SLIs in chaos experiments and AI risk reports.
Body:
Your provider will go down eventually; the question is whether you go down with it. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of the CNCF projects LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, made the case that SREs should treat resilience as a separate goal from reliability, test it inside the delivery pipeline, and use AI to make the business case for doing so.

Uma has spent years helping teams practise chaos engineering, and he is candid about why most don't: everyone agrees it matters, but they aren't allowed to run it. Much of this keynote is about getting that permission.

## Reliability and resilience are different goals

Uma's opening distinction: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you behave and how fast you come back when something pushes you over. Your cloud provider, your CDN or a security agent update can all fail on a day when your own code is fine, and no number of nines on their SLA makes that impossible.

Resilience is controlling the blast radius when that happens. Does one region go down, or all of them? Do you have the runbooks, and are people trained on them? Do you understand the dependencies well enough to recover? He also had the line of the session for anyone writing a promotion packet: "If you want to keep your job, focus on reliability. If you want to get yourself promoted, focus on resilience." When a shared provider fails and you stay up while a competitor doesn't, that difference gets noticed.

## Chaos engineering is how you find weaknesses

Uma pushes back on the idea that chaos engineering means breaking things on purpose. The goal is data about weaknesses. A known weakness is already valuable: you can prepare a recovery plan, or tell your most important customer about the risk before it bites, which he argues is often enough to keep that relationship intact.

He describes an experiment as two kinds of boxes. Fault injections are one; checks that the system is still healthy are the other. Real incidents rarely come from one fault, so good experiments chain them: a network path fails over, load shifts, a memory leak starts, and the second provider slows down at the same time.

The SRE's job is defining those health checks. Observability experts know which service level indicators matter in production, and that knowledge rarely makes it back to engineering. Hand over the SLIs and the blast radius map, and pre-production chaos tests start measuring the right things.

## Put resilience gates in the pipeline

Pipelines already gate on test coverage and regressions. Uma asks why they don't gate on resilience: is this release more or less resilient than the last one? If production experiments are off the table, push for chaos tests in staging, then low-intensity game days in production, and escalate if the answer to both is no.

He offers a maturity scale to aim at. In his view most organisations have moved from level one to level two in recent years; the target is level three, where critical services go through chaos testing in lower environments and a few game days run every year. Fully autonomous resilience, he admits, nobody does yet.

## AI writes the risk report for you

The third part is about AI, and it's where the product enters. Uma calls it passive risk detection: feed deployment, incident and service data to an LLM, for example through MCP, and ask for a resilience risk report without running a single experiment. A report that says risk has grown over the last few releases is something you can take to management.

He then describes Harness doing the same from Argo CD or Harness CD data: listing likely incidents and proposing the chaos experiments to run, generated from a prompt. Active testing then confirms what the passive scan suggested.

## Who should watch

SREs who believe in chaos engineering but can't get it approved, and engineering managers deciding where resilience fits in the SDLC. If your team already runs regular game days with SLO-based checks, the AI section is the new material. Uma also gave this keynote at Conf42 SRE 2026.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Chaos Validation Made Easy: Plug & Play with Resilience Probes](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Neelanjan_Manna_Sayan_Mondal_chaos_validation_resilience_probes), the health-check half of an experiment, from the Harness chaos team.
- [Implementing Chaos Engineering in a Risk Averse Culture](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Kyle_Shelton_risk_averse_culture) by Kyle Shelton (Toyota), on the permission problem.
- [Enhancing Hypothesis Development Through Resilience Modeling](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gunnar_Grosch_hypothesis_development_resilience_modeling) by Gunnar Grosch (AWS).

[Watch Uma Mukkara's keynote](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise).

## From Harness

Harness was the diamond sponsor of Conf42 Remix 2026. Uma leads its resilience testing product, which groups chaos, load and disaster recovery testing.

- [Harness](https://www.harness.io/)
- [Harness Resilience Testing](https://www.harness.io/products/resilience-testing)
- [Chaos engineering docs](https://developer.harness.io/docs/chaos-engineering/)

Title: Conf42 LLMs 2026 roundup: context, judges and voice agents
Description: Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 in review, from agent memory and knowledge graphs to verifiers, voice pipelines under 500 ms and regulated AI.
Body:
By June 2026 nobody at [Conf42 Large Language Models 2026](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026) needed convincing that models can write code or answer questions. The 34 talks, streamed online on June 18, 2026, were about everything around the model: what context it sees, who checks its work, how fast it has to answer on a phone call, and how it behaves inside a bank's ledger. Speakers came from Harness, AWS, Revolut, Snowflake, Microsoft, Meta, Walmart, Expedia Group and a good number of startups.

## The bottleneck is context, not capability

The keynote set the tone. [Prateek Mittal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery), Director of Product Management at Harness, argued that the next limit on AI in software delivery is context, and showed a knowledge graph of services, pipelines, deployments and owners that an agent queried to find the pipelines failing most often and why.

Three other talks attacked the same problem from different angles. [Anannya Roy Chowdhury](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Anannya_Roy_Chowdhury_memory_agents_context) (AWS) observed that agents in production rarely fail because they can't reason; they fail because they retrieve the wrong context. The talk's framework splits agent memory into working, retrieval and persistent layers. [Lior Schejter](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Lior_Schejter_context_agents_reasoning) described what happens when an agent meets 200 microservices instead of one repo: it gets lost in the middle. The fix is an AI-maintained architecture hub of APIs, domain models and events written for agents to read. [Varun Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Varun_Joshi_rag_metadata) (AWS) made the data engineer's version of the case: your schema, lineage, query history and dbt models are the context, and most teams haven't wired them into RAG yet.

## Who judges the agent?

[Vsevolod Voropaev](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Vsevolod_Voropaev_verification_agents_production) (Olo din) gave one of the sharper talks of the day: the verifier is the hardest component of an agentic system and usually the last one built. Drawing on a bandit-based verification layer routing across Claude, GPT and Gemini, he argued that verifiers should usually be smarter than the agents they watch. [Liliya Imasheva and Michael Banf](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Liliya_Imasheva_Michael_Banf_validation_summaries_evaluation) (Perelyn) showed a summary-validation pipeline that pairs BERTScore, ROUGE and BLEU with LLM-as-judge scoring on completeness, conciseness, harmlessness, correctness and readability.

Permissions were the other half of trust. [Sohan Maheshwar](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) (AuthZed) pointed out that letting a coding agent decide for itself what is safe is a probabilistic answer to a question that needs a deterministic one, and showed how to add enforceable permission boundaries. [Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_cryptography_compliance_pipelines) (Meta) presented RuntimeGuard-AI, which records tamper-evident, hash-chained evidence across an inference pipeline for EU AI Act compliance, and [Arunkumar Muthuramalingam](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Arunkumar_Muthuramalingam_identity_security_iam) (General Reinsurance) treated IAM as the core of AI security.

## Voice, phones and people who don't want an app

Voice agents got a strong cluster. [Bohdan Snisar](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Bohdan_Snisar_httpsyoutube5XSR13KHev4) (Solea AI) started from the classic STT, LLM, TTS chain, where every stage waits for the last and the whole conversation turn has under 500 milliseconds. He built the pipeline up layer by layer, through realtime audio transport, voice activity detection and turn detection, to show where it hits the wall, then presented an architecture that reasons in parallel while the agent talks. [Pavel Shchekotov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Pavel_Shchekotov_voice_ai_trust) (Denk Solutions) removed the app altogether and put an LLM agent behind an ordinary phone number for people who are sceptical of AI.

The most British title of the event belonged to [Anton Denisov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Anton_Denisov_british_sarcasm) (Dwelly), whose system reads emails and calls for dissatisfaction that customers soften with politeness, understatement or silence. Anyone who has heard a British colleague call a plan 'brave' will appreciate the problem. [Andrii Veremiienko](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Andrii_Veremiienko_shipping_ai_features) (Revolut) brought the mobile view: latency, inference costs, rate limits and UX design around answers that aren't deterministic. [Petras Bazdaras](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Petras_Bazdaras_reading_new_writing) argued that when generating code is cheap, reading it is the skill that matters.

## Shipping it: pipelines, modernisation and serving

[Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Denis_Ermakov_deployment_cicd_automation) (Tehpotok) presented an open-source framework for agent-driven CI/CD with retries, observability and explicit points where humans stay in the loop. [Marco Antonio Silva](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Marco_Antonio_Silva_modernization_specs_cloud) (Microsoft) shared spec-driven modernisation with Spec2Cloud and the GitHub Copilot Modernization CLI, including a large project at a Portuguese financial institution. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Tim_Spann_sql_automation_operations) (Snowflake) showed Cortex Code managing schema changes and deployments from natural language.

On the serving side, [Kosseila Haddalene](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_multimodal_inference_vllm) (Cloudthrill) explained why diffusion transformers, which denoise instead of generating tokens and are compute-bound rather than memory-bound, are awkward to serve next to LLMs, and how vLLM-Omni handles both. [Sergey Speranskiy](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sergey_Speranskiy_kubernetes_infrastructure_llms) covered the Kubernetes assumptions that break first under LLM workloads, [Kandasamy Selvaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Kandasamy_Selvaraj_performance_lag_signatures) (ADP) shifted RAG performance testing left into CI/CD, and [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Leo_Visser_governance_apis_control) (OGD ICT-diensten) put Azure API Management in front of models for content filtering, token-aware throttling and caching. [Andrei Shcherbinin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Andrei_Shcherbinin_moderation_safety_platforms) (Social Discovery Group) walked through a production automoderation stack that mixes lightweight classifiers with multimodal LLMs for grey areas.

## LLMs in regulated systems

A large share of the programme dealt with finance, tax, healthcare and audit. [Abdul Basit Iqbal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Abdul_Basit_Iqbal_compliance_agents_tax) (Amazon) turned changing tax regulations into executable compliance logic, [Karishma Velisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Karishma_Velisetty_governance_audit_assistants) governed AI code assistants in SOX audit analytics, [Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Ravindra_Rajasekhar_Kavuru_privacy_compliance_credit) (Expedia Group) built compliance into co-branded credit card apps, and [Rakesh Jha](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Rakesh_Jha_ledgers_finance_accounting) (DXC Technology) applied LLMs to general ledgers. On the people side, [Lakshmi Priya Gopalsamy](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Lakshmi_Priya_Gopalsamy_latency_reasoning_reliability) made the point that as AI speeds up execution, human decision capacity becomes the constraint, and [Susanta Kumar Sahoo](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Susanta_Kumar_Sahoo_copilots_sre_remediation) looked at LLM copilots for incident response.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) and [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), the diamond sponsors, to the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/) as gold sponsor, to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and to the media partners. The full [Conf42 LLMs 2026 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAbZ-MTonX2gERed7dTODjm) has every talk, and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026) lists them by track.

Next up in the series is [Conf42 Large Language Models 2027](https://www.conf42.com/llms2027).

Title: Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery
Body:
## Shipping with Context: Why Knowledge Graphs Are Becoming the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery

AI is transforming software development at an extraordinary pace. Developers can generate code, write tests, create documentation, and troubleshoot issues faster than ever before.

Yet for most organizations, the real challenge is no longer generating code.

The harder problem is understanding context.

A piece of generated code does not exist in isolation. It interacts with services, infrastructure, security controls, deployment pipelines, compliance requirements, operational processes, and business objectives. Without understanding those relationships, AI systems may be capable of producing outputs, but they struggle to make reliable decisions.

In his session *Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery*, Prateek Mittal explored why context is emerging as the next critical layer of enterprise AI and why knowledge graphs are becoming a foundational component of modern software delivery systems.

### The Next AI Bottleneck Is Not Model Capability

Over the past few years, the conversation around AI has largely focused on model performance.

Organizations compare models, benchmark reasoning capabilities, and evaluate new generations of large language models.

However, many enterprises are discovering that model quality is no longer the primary limitation.

The real bottleneck is access to organizational context.

Most enterprises operate across dozens or hundreds of systems:

- CI/CD platforms
- Security tools
- Cloud infrastructure
- Observability platforms
- Ticketing systems
- Source control repositories
- Incident management platforms
- Cost management tools

Each system contains valuable information.

The challenge is that this information remains fragmented.

An AI assistant may understand how to write code, but it often lacks visibility into which services are affected by that code, which teams own those services, what policies apply to them, and what business risks might be introduced by a deployment.

Without context, intelligence remains limited.

### Why Enterprise AI Struggles With Context

The problem is not simply a lack of data.

Most organizations already have enormous amounts of operational information available.

The challenge is that this information exists inside disconnected systems.

As Mittal explained, enterprise AI initiatives frequently encounter four common obstacles.

#### Data Silos

Critical information is distributed across numerous platforms and tools.

Even when the data exists, it is often inaccessible to AI systems or difficult to connect across domains.

#### Missing Domain Knowledge

General-purpose language models understand public information but typically lack awareness of company-specific terminology, workflows, ownership structures, and operational practices.

This creates a gap between what AI knows and what an organization actually needs.

#### Hallucination Risk

When models lack context, they compensate by making assumptions.

These assumptions can produce inaccurate recommendations, incorrect conclusions, or actions based on incomplete information.

#### Governance and Compliance Concerns

Organizations must carefully control how sensitive information is accessed and shared.

Providing AI systems with unrestricted access to enterprise data can introduce security, compliance, and governance risks.

Together, these challenges limit the ability of AI systems to operate effectively in production environments.

### The Evolution From AI-Assisted DevOps to AI-Operational DevOps

Many teams are already using AI in their software delivery processes.

Most of these implementations fall into what Mittal describes as AI-assisted DevOps.

In this model, AI helps humans perform tasks such as:

- Writing code
- Creating configuration files
- Generating documentation
- Producing runbooks
- Answering operational questions

Humans remain responsible for supplying context, validating outputs, and making final decisions.

This approach delivers productivity gains, but it does not fundamentally change how software delivery operates.

A second model is beginning to emerge.

### What Is AI-Operational DevOps?

AI-operational DevOps shifts AI from being a productivity tool to becoming an active participant in delivery workflows.

Instead of requiring humans to manually provide context, AI systems automatically retrieve information from shared enterprise models.

This allows agents to:

- Evaluate deployment risks
- Analyze dependencies
- Simulate outcomes
- Enforce policies
- Validate compliance requirements
- Recommend corrective actions

In this model, context becomes machine-readable rather than conversational.

The system itself becomes responsible for understanding relationships and applying guardrails before actions occur.

This transition requires a shared understanding of the software delivery ecosystem.

That is where knowledge graphs enter the picture.

### Understanding the Building Blocks of a Knowledge Graph

A knowledge graph is not simply a database or reporting system.

It is a representation of entities and the relationships between them.

Within a software delivery environment, entities may include:

- Services
- Pipelines
- Deployments
- Incidents
- Infrastructure resources
- Cloud costs
- Security findings
- Teams
- Applications

These entities become nodes within the graph.

The relationships between them become edges.

For example:

- A service depends on another service
- A deployment originates from a specific commit
- A pipeline belongs to a particular team
- An incident affects a specific application
- A cloud resource supports a particular workload

Individually, each piece of information has limited value.

Connected together, they create a model that describes how an organization actually operates.

### Context Is More Than Data

One of the key ideas presented during the session is that context is not merely information.

Context is information combined with relationships.

Many organizations already collect deployment events, operational metrics, cloud costs, and security findings.

The challenge is that these data points often remain disconnected.

A knowledge graph introduces a semantic layer that allows systems to understand how information relates across domains.

This transforms isolated records into an interconnected model of software delivery.

Instead of querying a single tool, AI systems can reason across multiple systems simultaneously.

### Building a Knowledge Graph for Software Delivery

Creating a useful knowledge graph requires more than importing data.

Organizations must establish a process for constructing and maintaining relationships.

The process generally includes several stages.

#### Entity Extraction

The first step is identifying important objects within the delivery ecosystem.

These may include applications, services, incidents, deployments, users, cloud resources, or security findings.

#### Metadata Enrichment

Entities become more valuable when supplemented with additional information.

Examples include:

- Ownership details
- Team assignments
- Version information
- Environment data
- Compliance classifications
- Security policies

#### Relationship Mapping

Relationships define how entities interact.

Understanding who owns a service, which deployment modified it, and what infrastructure supports it is often more valuable than understanding any individual component in isolation.

#### Query Exposure

Once the graph exists, APIs and query interfaces allow AI agents to retrieve and reason about context dynamically.

At that point, the graph becomes an operational system rather than simply a data repository.

### Why Knowledge Graph Projects Fail

Knowledge graphs have existed for years, yet many implementations struggle to deliver value.

According to Mittal, the most common failure is not technical.

It is a failure of use case definition.

Organizations sometimes invest heavily in building sophisticated graph models without clearly identifying the problems they intend to solve.

This creates several risks.

#### Over-Modeling

Teams create highly detailed ontologies that are technically impressive but provide little practical value.

The result is significant complexity with limited adoption.

#### Under-Modeling

The opposite problem occurs when relationships are not modeled deeply enough.

Data remains connected only superficially, preventing meaningful reasoning.

#### Stale Context

A graph is only valuable if it reflects reality.

Outdated relationships and stale metadata quickly reduce the usefulness of AI-driven decision-making.

Successful implementations focus on solving specific operational challenges rather than building graphs for their own sake.

### How Knowledge Graphs Enable AI Reasoning

One of the most compelling aspects of knowledge graphs is their ability to support complex reasoning across multiple systems.

During the session, Mittal demonstrated how AI could analyze software delivery pipelines across an organization and identify patterns that would be difficult to discover manually.

Rather than searching individual projects one at a time, the system was able to reason across organizational boundaries.

The AI identified:

- Pipelines with the highest failure rates
- Common failure patterns
- Missing dependencies
- Configuration issues
- Potential remediation actions

The system not only surfaced operational problems but also suggested corrective actions based on the relationships captured inside the graph.

This illustrates a broader shift in how AI interacts with enterprise systems.

Instead of responding only to direct questions, AI can begin to understand operational context and assist with diagnosis, prioritization, and decision-making.

### Shared Context Across Engineering Disciplines

The value of a knowledge graph extends far beyond DevOps.

Modern software delivery requires collaboration across multiple domains.

DevOps teams care about deployments and reliability.

SecOps teams focus on vulnerabilities and compliance.

FinOps teams analyze cloud spending and resource utilization.

Platform engineering teams manage infrastructure and developer experience.

Traditionally, each group operates within its own set of tools and dashboards.

Knowledge graphs provide a shared context layer that connects these perspectives.

When everyone operates against the same model of services, dependencies, ownership, and operational events, decision-making becomes faster and more consistent.

### Governance Becomes a Core AI Requirement

As AI systems gain access to broader organizational context, governance becomes increasingly important.

Enterprise AI cannot operate solely on trust.

Systems require mechanisms for:

- Role-based access control
- Policy enforcement
- Auditability
- Compliance validation
- Permission management

Knowledge graphs provide the contextual foundation that allows these controls to be applied consistently.

Without governance, increased context introduces risk.

With governance, context becomes a strategic advantage.

### The Future of AI-First Software Delivery

The software industry has spent years building increasingly capable AI models.

The next phase of adoption will depend less on model intelligence and more on organizational context.

The most successful AI systems will not necessarily be those with the largest parameter counts.

They will be the systems that understand services, dependencies, ownership, policies, infrastructure, incidents, and business priorities.

Knowledge graphs provide a mechanism for connecting these elements into a unified model.

As AI moves from assisting developers to actively participating in software delivery workflows, shared context will become essential infrastructure.

### Context Is the New Competitive Advantage

Software delivery is becoming increasingly complex.

Organizations operate across dozens of platforms, hundreds of services, and thousands of interconnected components.

AI has the potential to help manage this complexity, but only if it can understand the environment in which it operates.

Knowledge graphs offer a way to transform fragmented organizational knowledge into a connected, queryable system that both humans and AI can reason about.

In an AI-first future, the question will no longer be whether models can generate answers.

The question will be whether they have enough context to generate the right ones.

Title: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026: migrations, operators and AI on call
Description: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 roundup - safe schema migrations, a 30-day Kubernetes operator test, serverless database lessons and AI-assisted tuning.
Body:
Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 ran online on June 4, 2026, with 25 talks about the part of the stack that does not roll back cleanly. The schedule was split into AI, automation, delivery, governance, and scale tracks, but one question ran through all of them: now that AI can write your migrations and tune your queries, which parts of database operations can you safely hand over, and which still need a human with a pager?

Every talk is on the [Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/dbd2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCwmGmMnd2P7QS42DFYdMUU).

## The riskiest deploy you ship

Schema migrations got the most attention, and for good reason. [Ahmed Tariq](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_postgres_mysql_scaling), a Cloud DevOps Engineer, opened his abstract with the line every DBA nods at: application releases can be rolled forward and back, but a migration that locks a 2TB table for an hour, or quietly loses data on rollback, cannot. His field guide covers expand-and-contract, migration tests, approval gates, and post-deploy checks, then adds AI where it earns its keep (drafting forward and rollback DDL, flagging unsafe operations) and is honest about where it breaks, such as hallucinated Postgres flags that are really MySQL flags.

Diamond sponsor Harness showed the pattern end to end. [Stephen Atwell](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Stephen_Atwell_cd_stateful_applications), Director of Product at Harness, had AI write a trigger-based Postgres migration that splits a JSON blob column into real columns, then shipped it through blue-green in staging and canary in production with no downtime, with policy checks, production data cloned to staging, and an AI-written test confirming that both app versions saw the same orders.

[Niraj Katkamwar](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Niraj_Katkamwar_llm_agents_delivery) of Intuit presented independent research on a prompt-driven framework that turns natural-language requirements into microservice and schema changes.

## Can the operator replace the DBA?

[Amarachi Iheanacho](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Amarachi_Iheanacho_postgres_k8s_tuning) of SideroLabs ran the experiment many teams argue about but never run: hand day-to-day operations of a PostgreSQL cluster to the CloudNativePG operator for 30 days, then deliberately inject node failures, pod crashes, storage pressure, replication issues, upgrades, and restores. Some problems were fixed automatically within seconds; others needed a human. The week-by-week walkthrough is the most honest answer to the title you will find.

[Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Renato_Losio_mistakes_lessons_scaling) brought five lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases on AWS. He once drew the New York City skyline with Aurora Serverless v2 capacity at re:Invent, and says fifteen years with AWS does not make him an expert, it just makes him old. Among them: serverless is just an adjective, and storage usually matters more than CPU. His key message: serverless databases remove capacity management, but they don't remove database engineering.

## AI as the junior DBA

Several talks put AI into the tuning loop. [Naga Bellamkonda](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Naga_Bellamkonda_alerts_incident_platform) of Gartner and [Ellavarasan Asokan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ellavarasan_Asokan_monitoring_reliability_platform) of Capital One, both long-time Oracle and Postgres administrators, shared lessons from AI-driven optimisation in production, from predictive tuning towards more autonomous operations. [Sampath Rao Madarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sampath_Rao_Madarapu_azure_cloud_monitoring) of Microsoft showed Copilot in Azure for diagnostics and resource control.

On the AI application side, [Alejandro Duarte](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Alejandro_Duarte_llm_vectors_semantic) of MariaDB covered RAG in production, starting from the infamous glue-on-pizza answers, and [Ankur Aggarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ankur_Aggarwal_llm_inference_models) of Meta tackled a hard gap: how an LLM running in a trusted execution environment can query databases through MCP without exposing sensitive data.

## Same SQL, different answers

The governance track had the talk most data engineers should watch. [Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Muthupalaniappan_Ramanathan_queries_monitoring_sql) of DoorDash showed how identical queries can return different results on Spark, Trino, and Snowflake because of type handling, null semantics, and optimiser behaviour, and proposed a canonical semantic layer with CI-integrated validation to catch the drift.

[Sheena Yap Chan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sheena_Yap_Chan_incident_reliability_platform) argued that the real risk is often not missing data but database signals that never reach the right people in time. [Muthu Saravanan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Muthu_Saravanan_alerts_telemetry_platform) of Mind-Pros and [Dharmendra Ahuja](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Dharmendra_Ahuja_monitoring_analytics_platform) of IBM looked at intentional delivery and ethical validation inside AI-driven data pipelines.

## Always on, at scale

The scale track was heavy on finance. [Priyatham Nagaiya Seenu Naidu](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Priyatham_Nagaiya_Seenu_Naidu_kafka_pipelines_clusters) of Mastercard covered real-time payment networks like FedNow, UPI, PIX, and SEPA Instant, where the database must be up around the clock with sub-second processing. [Ritvik Pandya](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ritvik_Pandya_monitoring_telemetry_reliability) of JPMorgan Chase started from a sudden p99 spike at peak hours and traced it to the ingress layer, fixing it with deterministic routing for cache locality. [Srikanth Uddanti](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Srikanth_Uddanti_distributed_systems_delivery) of Charles Schwab walked through the trade-offs of distributed databases, and [Surya Lankalapalli](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Surya_Lankalapalli_telemetry_analytics_delivery) of Microsoft made the case for active-active, multi-provider DNS, the dependency that quietly delays database failover.

Elsewhere in the lineup: [Jason Lester](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Jason_Lester_productivity_teams_efficiency) of Capgemini on loading cloud API output into a database for analysis the console cannot do, [Sulabh Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sulabh_Jain_kafka_streams_k8s) on modernising insurance core systems, [Sirisha Ayyagari](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sirisha_Ayyagari_telemetry_tracing_platform) of IBM on real-time SAP pricing, [Kamini Murugaboopathy](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Kamini_Murugaboopathy_agents_pipelines_o11y) on real-time marketing analytics, [Bharat Kumar Reddy Karumuri](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Bharat_Kumar_Reddy_Karumuri_models_training_telemetry) of General Motors on operationalising ML and GenAI, [Zeeshan Khan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Zeeshan_Khan_vectors_recruiting_semantic) on hiring as a data infrastructure problem, and [Harsha Vardhani Talluri](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Harsha_Vardhani_Talluri_metrics_telemetry_unified) on multi-vendor DOCSIS deployments.

Thanks to diamond sponsor [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), gold sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

Title: Database DevOps: CD for Stateful Applications
Body:
## Database DevOps: Bringing Continuous Delivery to Stateful Applications

Modern software delivery pipelines are remarkably good at deploying stateless applications. Teams can push application updates multiple times a day, automate testing, validate rollouts, and quickly roll back when something goes wrong.

Databases are often a different story.

While application deployments have embraced continuous delivery, database changes frequently remain manual, infrequent, and high-risk. Many organizations that deploy application code daily still schedule database releases monthly or quarterly because schema changes introduce challenges that traditional CI/CD workflows struggle to address.

In his session *Database DevOps: CD for Stateful Applications*, Stephen Atwell explored how engineering teams can apply modern delivery practices to databases, making stateful systems just as testable, repeatable, and automatable as the applications that depend on them.

### Why Databases Remain a Deployment Bottleneck

The core challenge of database delivery is state.

Stateless applications can be replaced, scaled, or rolled back relatively easily because their state lives elsewhere. Databases contain the data that applications depend on, making every structural change potentially risky.

Simple schema updates can become surprisingly complex when applications remain online throughout the deployment process.

Consider a scenario where a single database column needs to be split into multiple fields. During deployment, both the old and new versions of the application may run simultaneously. If each version reads and writes data differently, inconsistencies can emerge immediately.

This challenge often forces teams into maintenance windows, deployment freezes, or highly manual release processes.

As a result, database changes frequently become the limiting factor in otherwise mature continuous delivery environments.

### Continuous Delivery Requires Backwards Compatibility

Modern deployment patterns such as blue-green and canary releases depend on running multiple versions of an application simultaneously.

This creates a requirement that many database migrations fail to consider: backwards compatibility.

If version A of an application and version B of an application are both serving traffic, the underlying database must support both versions throughout the transition.

Database changes therefore cannot simply focus on the final desired schema. They must also account for the intermediate states that exist while deployments are in progress.

Successful database delivery requires teams to think about migrations as a series of controlled steps rather than a single change.

### The Hidden Complexity of Zero-Downtime Database Migrations

Zero-downtime deployments are relatively common at the application layer. Achieving the same outcome at the database layer is significantly harder.

The challenge becomes particularly apparent when restructuring data.

During the session, Atwell demonstrated a migration that transformed a PostgreSQL table storing serialized JSON data into a properly structured relational schema.

The goal was straightforward: extract fields from a JSON document and store them in dedicated database columns.

The execution, however, required careful planning.

The migration needed to ensure:

- No downtime
- No data loss
- Full backwards compatibility
- Support for old and new application versions
- Safe rollback capabilities

Achieving all of these requirements simultaneously demands more than simply writing migration scripts.

### Using Database Triggers to Maintain Consistency

One of the key techniques demonstrated during the session involved database triggers.

When introducing new columns, the existing application still expects the original data structure. New application versions, meanwhile, expect the updated schema.

Rather than forcing an immediate switch, synchronization mechanisms can keep both representations aligned.

In the demonstrated migration, triggers ensured that updates to the original JSON field automatically updated the new relational columns.

Additional triggers performed the reverse operation, keeping the original structure synchronized whenever the new schema was modified.

This approach allowed both versions of the application to operate simultaneously while observing the same data.

By maintaining consistency in both directions, teams gain the flexibility needed to deploy, test, validate, and roll back safely.

### Large Data Migrations Require More Than Correct SQL

Database migrations often fail not because the migration logic is incorrect, but because operational realities are ignored.

A script that performs well on a development database may behave very differently against production datasets.

Tables may contain millions or billions of rows. Long-running transactions can create lock contention, impact performance, or introduce unexpected downtime.

For this reason, migration strategies must account for scale from the beginning.

Instead of processing entire datasets in a single transaction, modern migration workflows often break work into smaller batches that can execute incrementally and safely.

This reduces risk while allowing migrations to proceed without disrupting production workloads.

### AI-Assisted Database Development

One of the more interesting aspects of the demonstration was the use of generative AI to create migration logic.

Rather than manually writing complex PostgreSQL migration code, the schema transformation was generated through natural language prompts.

The generated migration created new columns, built synchronization triggers, and produced the necessary data migration logic.

While AI-generated code still requires validation, it introduces a new workflow for database teams.

Instead of spending hours building migration scripts manually, engineers can focus on reviewing, validating, and testing generated solutions.

The result is a faster iteration cycle while still maintaining governance and operational controls.

### Governance Matters as Much as Automation

Automation alone does not make database deployments safe.

Every automated process still requires guardrails.

Throughout the deployment workflow demonstrated during the session, database changes passed through governance checks before being applied.

These checks verified that deployments complied with predefined policies and prevented potentially destructive operations from reaching production environments.

Examples include:

- Preventing accidental data loss
- Blocking unsafe schema operations
- Enforcing deployment policies
- Creating rollback checkpoints
- Validating generated SQL before execution

As organizations increase deployment velocity, governance becomes increasingly important because manual review alone cannot scale indefinitely.

### Testing Database Changes Against Production Data

One of the biggest challenges in database testing is reproducing production behavior.

Many database issues only appear when migrations encounter real customer data, realistic workloads, or unusual edge cases.

Traditional testing environments often fail to capture these conditions.

To address this challenge, Atwell demonstrated a workflow that clones production data into staging environments before running migration tests.

This approach allows teams to validate schema changes against realistic datasets while still operating within controlled environments.

When combined with automated testing, production-like data significantly improves confidence in deployment outcomes.

Organizations implementing this strategy must ensure that security controls, access policies, and compliance requirements remain consistent between production and staging environments.

### Verifying Data Consistency During Deployment

Testing database migrations requires more than simply checking whether a deployment completed successfully.

Teams must verify that data remains consistent throughout the transition.

In the demonstrated workflow, automated tests interacted with both the old and new versions of the application.

Actions performed through one version were immediately validated through the other version.

This process confirmed that both applications continued to observe identical data despite significant schema changes occurring underneath them.

These consistency tests become especially valuable when supporting parallel deployments through blue-green or canary release strategies.

Without this validation, subtle synchronization issues can remain hidden until they affect production users.

### Combining Database Migrations with Progressive Delivery

Application delivery practices such as blue-green deployments and canary releases have become common across cloud-native environments.

Database changes can benefit from the same principles.

During the session, schema updates were deployed alongside controlled application rollouts.

In staging environments, blue-green deployments allowed old and new versions to operate simultaneously while automated tests verified compatibility.

In production environments, canary deployments gradually increased traffic to the new version while monitoring system health and behavior.

This progressive approach reduces risk by limiting exposure and creating multiple opportunities to detect issues before they impact all users.

### The Future of Database Delivery

For years, databases have been treated as a special case within software delivery pipelines.

Application teams embraced automation while database changes remained manual, infrequent, and operationally risky.

That distinction is beginning to disappear.

Advances in infrastructure automation, Kubernetes-native workflows, AI-assisted development, automated testing, and database-focused CI/CD tooling are making it possible to manage stateful systems using many of the same practices that transformed application delivery.

The goal is not simply faster deployments.

It is creating a delivery process that is more predictable, more repeatable, easier to test, and safer to operate.

### Bringing Stateful Applications into Modern CI/CD

Database delivery will always require additional care because data cannot simply be redeployed when something goes wrong.

However, that does not mean databases must remain outside modern delivery practices.

By combining backwards-compatible schema changes, automated testing, governance controls, production-like environments, and progressive deployment strategies, organizations can bring databases into the same continuous delivery workflows that already power their applications.

The result is a more unified software delivery process where both application code and data evolve together, safely and repeatedly, without sacrificing reliability or availability.

Title: Conf42 Golang 2026 - Go as the boring backbone under AI and money
Description: Conf42 Golang 2026 in review, 22 talks on MCP servers in Go, monolith surgery at Fleet, O(log N) leaderboards, fallback search at eBay and GPU profiling.
Body:
[Conf42 Golang 2026](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) aired on May 21, 2026 with 22 talks, and the language itself rarely took centre stage. Go showed up the way it does in most companies: as the dependable layer under an MCP server, a leaderboard, a search fallback, a fraud engine or an insurance core. Speakers from eBay, Fleet Device Management, METRO AG, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, General Motors, Ford, Salesforce, Walmart and SoftSwiss showed what that layer has to survive.

## Go as the plumbing for LLMs

The most hands-on AI talk came from [Shadi Elyafi](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Shadi_Elyafi_mcp_b2b_workflow) (METRO AG), who built an MCP server in Go for a real B2B workflow on a platform serving more than 1 million company profiles. It exposes tools for Claude, talks to a GraphQL backend through AWS AppSync, and draws careful read/write boundaries so mutations stay safe. He also covers how TDD with mock GraphQL clients keeps the MCP layer from turning into a fragile demo.

[Swati Kumari](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Swati_Kumari_beyond_chatbots_building) (NucleusTeq) made the case that most chatbots fail because they cannot reach CRM, order management or billing, and showed Go backend integrations that let them act. [Sanjay Basu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sanjay_Basu_building_cognitive_commerce) (TCS) sketched Go-based architectures for LLM-driven grocery and e-commerce platforms, and [Venkat Kamma](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Venkat_Kamma_from_reactive_predictive) (StarGroup Innovations) applied the same idea to Oracle Cloud PPM, catching cost overruns before they happen instead of in the monthly report. [Rejenish Kiran](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Rejenish_Kiran_assisted_test_execution) (Citizens Property Insurance Corporation) positioned AI-assisted test execution as an augmentation layer on top of existing Go test frameworks rather than a replacement.

## Data structures still win the incident

The talk most likely to end up in a team chat was [Ivan Balashov's](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Ivan_Balashov_engineering_high_performance) (SoftSwiss). A production leaderboard was causing daily outages thanks to O(N²) updates, CPU spikes and memory pressure. The fix was an indexed skip list with span counters for O(log N) position queries plus hash-based deduplication, replacing a naive slice-based leaderboard in two days. A good reminder that your outage might be a CS201 exercise wearing a pager.

[Amol Lele](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Amol_Lele_real_time_training) (Hewlett Packard Enterprise) built a multi-layer ML training profiler in Go with 2-5% runtime overhead and walked through the three costliest failure modes he found: data pipeline bottlenecks, communication overhead in distributed training, and straggler workers in heterogeneous clusters. [Akshaya Jayaram](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Akshaya_Jayaram_ammf_attention_based) (Salesforce) presented AMMF, an attention-based fusion model for spotting the same vulnerable function across architectures, a problem Go's easy cross-compilation makes very real.

## Failing gracefully on purpose

[Hima Bindu Yanala](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Hima_Bindu_Yanala_designing_resilient_self) (eBay) treated fallback as a first-class feature of self-service search: a dedicated lightweight fallback index, circuit breakers routing traffic through closed, open and half-open states, and bulkheads protecting fallback capacity. Her point about fan-out amplification, where rare shard outliers become systemic failures, applies well beyond search.

[Yogesh Pugazhendhi Duraisamy Rajamani](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Yogesh_Pugazhendhi_Duraisamy_Rajamani_building_self_healing) (Ford Motor Company) described self-healing streaming pipelines in Go with a reinforcement-learning control plane adjusting ingestion, messaging and compute across Kafka, Pulsar and Flink. [Sudhakar Pallaprolu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sudhakar_Pallaprolu_autonomous_cloud_infrastructure) covered self-healing infrastructure and AIOps from the platform side.

## Evolving the code you already have

[Victor Lyuboslavsky](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Victor_Lyuboslavsky_modularizing_year_monolith) (Fleet Device Management) gave the talk he says the Go community lacks: a real, open source, decade-old Go monolith mid-way to a modular design while still shipping to production. It started as an investigation into slow builds and tests and turned up oversized packages, uncontrolled dependencies and boundaries that no longer matched how engineers thought about the system. The people side gets as much airtime as the architecture.

[Sulabh Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sulabh_Jain_building_cloud_native) took the same question to insurance core systems, where catastrophe-driven claims spikes punish monoliths, and [Sana Fatima](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sana_Fatima_from_code_correctness) (General Motors) argued that code which compiles and passes unit tests can still fail at system level in embedded automotive software, so behaviour validation has to move earlier.

## Compliance and money, engineered in

Regulated platforms got a strong block. [Manasa Uppula](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Manasa_Uppula_designing_defensibility_evidence) (Virtusa) designs financial platforms so that every critical customer interaction produces structured evidence by default: what was shown, how consent was captured, how a decision was made. Audits then become a query, not an archaeology dig. [Sridhar Muthineni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sridhar_Muthineni_driven_fraud_detection) (Capgemini) combined fraud detection and personalisation in Go fintech systems, and [Devi Manoharan](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Devi_Manoharan_building_high_performance) (ASTA CRS) covered AI-driven claims processing on EDI pipelines. [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_building_secure_pipelines) (SoftNet Technologies) showed Go-based automation for secure CI/CD across AWS, Azure and GCP.

The programme also stretched to [DOCSIS networks](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Harsha_Vardhani_Talluri_building_unified_docsis) (Harsha Vardhani Talluri), [3PL warehouse design](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Vivek_Sander_data_driven_warehouse) (Vivek Sander, Sunland Logistics Solution), [digital PMOs in retail](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_George_Job_digital_pmos_retail) (George Job, Walmart) and [design systems for analytics platforms](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sonali_Priya_scalable_design_systems) (Sonali Priya, LB Networks).

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [Virtana](https://www.virtana.com/) at Gold. All 22 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCKzSYaULw7l2nLQKxk2IkS).

Next up for the gophers: [Conf42 Golang 2027](https://www.conf42.com/golang2027).

Title: Conf42 Cloud Native 2026: agents become infrastructure
Description: Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 roundup: 29 talks on running AI agents like services, securing MCP and cloud automation, migrations and EU compliance on AWS.
Body:
Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 ran online on April 23, 2026, with 29 talks under the familiar promise of *everything Cloud Native and Cloud Security*. The thread running through the day: AI agents and MCP servers are turning into ordinary infrastructure, with all the lifecycle, security and cost problems that implies, while the older cloud questions of migration, compliance and observability haven't gone anywhere. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAk91tnHP48BKjDFW9jzf1V).

## Agents need the tooling pods already have

[Andrew Espira](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Andrew_Espira_ai_agents_automation) of Kustode asked the question several other speakers circled: you have `kubectl` for pods, `docker` for containers and `helm` for charts, so what do you use for the agents and MCP servers piling up on your machine and in your cluster? His answer is `agentctl`, a zero-dependency Go CLI that registers, health-checks, starts, stops and discovers them like any other managed service, with a live TUI dashboard on top.

[Elizabeth Fuentes Leone](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_ai_llm_applications) of AWS tackled a cost problem that grows with every tool you add: agents serialise every tool description into the context on every call, then pick the wrong tool anyway. Her semantic tool selection uses vector search to filter tools before they reach the model. [Sandeep Mannapur](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sandeep_Mannapur_ai_agents_workflows) of ServiceNow covered what changes when a single chat interface becomes a distributed system of collaborating agents running real workflows, and [Dhivya Dhayakar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dhivya_Dhayakar_ai_llm_prompts) of Zscaler proposed intent-based orchestration as the fix for enterprises with a dozen isolated copilots and no shared governance.

## The new plumbing is a new attack surface

If agents are infrastructure, so are their connectors. [Aleksandr Pinaev](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandr_Pinaev_security_vulnerabilities_compliance), founder of Swordfish Security, catalogued how cloud MCP servers fail: misplaced trust boundaries, excessive privileges, weak isolation and vulnerable connector logic, plus the defences that work.

Older automation got the same scrutiny. [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Leo_Visser_cloudarchitecture_infra_design) of OGD ICT-diensten asked whether your PowerShell and other cloud automation is quietly creating attack surface of its own. Security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_security_zerotrust_encryption) walked through real Azure attack techniques from Microsoft's Digital Defense Report, from hybrid identity abuse to trusted relationships, with demos. And [Rajasingh Gandhi Ramdas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Rajasingh_Gandhi_Ramdas_distributed_systems_architecture) of IBM looked further out, at moving multi-cloud APIs off RSA and elliptic curve cryptography before quantum computers make that urgent.

## Migrations without the big bang

Harness's keynote came from [Ryan Vila](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Ryan_Vila_feature_flags_migration), who argued that migrations fail because of how they're released, not how they're coded. Flags route traffic gradually from old service to new, and measuring from the point of change makes regressions visible that fleet-wide dashboards would hide. His case study from Split, the company Harness acquired, moved a batch pipeline to streaming behind a flag and cut processing time from 10 hours to 15 minutes.

[Ran Tao](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Ran_Tao_data_analytics_insights) of AWS explained why lift and shift doesn't work for messaging systems moving from on-premises to the cloud. [Devinder Tokas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Devinder_Tokas_cloudarchitecture_backend_systems) of Microsoft made the case for interoperability by design to avoid lock-in across clusters and clouds, and [Purushotham Jinka](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Purushotham_Jinka_ai_llm_optimization) of Citi traced how partitioning and indexing strategies change when databases go cloud-native.

## Compliance as an engineering problem

The most opinionated talk of the day was [Dmytro Hlotenko's](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_distributed_systems_resilience) "Keep Calm and Run on AWS". Dmytro, a senior cloud operations engineer at Sage in Austria, offered a practitioner's defence of running AWS in regulated European environments: what actually needs solving, what is compliance theatre, where Outposts helps and where it quietly fails, and how to keep a stack your team can still operate at 3am. He opened with a disclaimer that he's an engineer, not a lawyer, which is more than most sovereignty debates manage.

[Manasa Uppula](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Manasa_Uppula_data_streaming_realtime) treated digital onboarding in financial services as an architecture problem, where consent boundaries and interaction integrity have to be audit-ready by design. [Karthik Ravva](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Karthik_Ravva_ai_agents_reasoning) of Austin Energy argued that data governance has to be embedded in the lifecycle once AI-powered BI depends on it.

## Operations and real systems in production

[Uudit Misra](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Uudit_Misra_distributed_systems_reliability) of Salesforce asked why dashboards show green while users see failures, and answered with eBPF-based network observability for Kubernetes, deployed as DaemonSets instead of relying on iptables and sidecars. [Sampath Rao Madarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sampath_Rao_Madarapu_distributed_systems_scaling) of Microsoft showed Copilot in Azure as an assistant for diagnostics and resource management.

Two case studies stood out for being about systems that run today. [Anton Solomonov](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Anton_Solomonov_computer_vision_verification) of SIMPLE described a computer vision system that verifies spare parts at warehouse receiving for a manufacturer supplying the mining industry, with confidence thresholds, exception handling and human-in-the-loop checks for parts that look nearly identical. [Gautham Paspala](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Gautham_Paspala_data_warehousing_analytics) of ServiceNow tackled friendly fraud, where a legitimate purchase becomes a fraudulent dispute weeks later, using temporal graph attention and transformers.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), our diamond sponsor, to gold sponsors [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [Virtana](https://www.virtana.com/), and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 29 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026). The series returns with [Conf42 Cloud Native 2027](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2027) on April 8, 2027, by which point your MCP servers will presumably need their own on-call rotation.
