Title: Beyond the Toggle: Feature Flags as Your Cloud-Native Migration Safety Net
Body:
## Beyond the Toggle: Using Feature Flags to De-Risk Cloud-Native Migrations

Cloud migrations, API rewrites, and large-scale architecture transformations rarely fail because engineers cannot build the new system. More often, they fail because organizations attempt to release too much change at once.

A cloud migration often combines infrastructure changes, application updates, data movement, routing changes, and new operational processes. When all of these elements are introduced simultaneously, teams create a single high-risk event where identifying and recovering from problems becomes significantly more difficult.

During his session, *Beyond the Toggle: Feature Flags as Your Cloud-Native Migration Safety Net*, Ryan Vila, Americas Advisory Director at Harness, explored how feature management enables organizations to replace risky cutovers with gradual, observable, and reversible migration strategies.

### Why Cloud Migrations Create So Much Risk

Many migration initiatives begin with good intentions but quickly become coupled to a traditional release mindset.

Teams often build a new service, deploy it, and then switch all traffic to the new system in a single event. This approach creates several common failure modes.

The first is the "big bang" release. Multiple changes are bundled together and activated simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the source of problems when issues emerge.

The second challenge is the lack of a practical rollback path. Organizations frequently discover that moving forward is easy, but moving backward is complex, time-consuming, or impossible without disruption.

The third problem is uncontrolled blast radius. If every user is exposed to a migration immediately, even minor issues can quickly become major incidents.

Successful migrations require teams to treat releases differently. Instead of viewing migration as a single event, they need a framework for introducing change gradually while maintaining the ability to observe, pause, and reverse progress when necessary.

### The Strangler Fig Pattern in Modern Architectures

One of the most widely adopted migration approaches is the Strangler Fig Pattern, originally popularized by Martin Fowler.

Rather than replacing an existing application all at once, teams introduce new services alongside existing systems and progressively redirect traffic toward the new implementation.

This creates a period where both systems operate in parallel.

The value of this approach is not simply technical flexibility. It provides an opportunity to compare old and new behavior in real-world conditions. Teams can evaluate performance, reliability, cost, and user experience before fully committing to the new architecture.

Once confidence has been established, the legacy service can be retired and the technical debt associated with maintaining parallel systems can be eliminated.

Feature flags provide the control layer that makes this gradual transition practical.

### Decoupling Deployment from Release

A key principle of modern feature management is separating deployment from release.

Deployment simply places code into production. Release determines who can actually use it.

By introducing feature flags, engineering teams gain the ability to deploy new functionality without immediately exposing it to every customer.

This enables a progression such as:

- Internal users and engineering teams
- Test accounts and synthetic traffic
- Designated customer groups
- Small production cohorts
- Gradually increasing percentages of traffic
- General availability

Each stage creates an opportunity to validate assumptions before moving forward.

Instead of asking whether the migration succeeds or fails, teams can continuously evaluate whether the migration is producing the desired outcomes.

### Progressive Rollouts Reduce Migration Risk

Canary releases and percentage-based rollouts are often discussed in the context of application features, but they are equally valuable for infrastructure and platform transformations.

A small rollout may mean exposing 1% of traffic to a new service.

For another organization, it could mean routing a specific region, customer segment, or internal department through the new architecture.

The exact definition depends on business requirements and risk tolerance.

The important principle is that every increase in exposure should be accompanied by measurement.

A migration that performs well at 5% traffic may behave very differently at 50% or 100%.

Scaling is itself a test, and each expansion should be treated as a validation step rather than an automatic progression.

### Measuring More Than Deployment Success

Traditional migration programs often focus on a simple question:

**Did the deployment complete successfully?**

Modern engineering teams should evaluate migrations against business and operational outcomes.

#### Performance

Latency, throughput, and response times provide immediate feedback on whether the new implementation delivers improvements over the existing system.

#### Reliability

Error rates and service-level objectives help determine whether stability improves or deteriorates as traffic increases.

#### Cost

Cloud migrations are frequently justified by efficiency gains. Measuring infrastructure consumption and operational expenses throughout the rollout helps validate whether expected savings are actually being realized.

#### Customer Experience

Aggregate metrics can hide problems affecting specific user groups.

Engineering teams should analyze behavior across different cohorts, platforms, regions, and usage patterns to identify issues that may not appear in overall statistics.

A migration that looks healthy at a global level may still introduce significant friction for a specific segment of users.

### Monitoring Versus Measurement

One of the most important distinctions highlighted during the session is the difference between monitoring and measurement.

Most organizations already have dashboards, alerts, and observability platforms.

However, observability alone does not necessarily reveal the impact of a specific change.

In production environments, background noise is constant. Small increases in error rates or latency may be difficult to detect when viewed across the entire system.

Measuring from the point of change creates a different perspective.

Instead of asking how the application is behaving overall, teams can evaluate how the newly introduced migration path is performing relative to the baseline.

This approach makes it easier to identify signals that would otherwise be hidden inside broader operational metrics.

The result is faster detection, clearer attribution, and more informed release decisions.

### A Real-World Migration Example

Ryan Vila shared an example from Split, the feature management and experimentation platform later acquired by Harness.

The company operated a data processing pipeline responsible for handling massive volumes of customer telemetry.

As customer adoption increased, costs grew linearly with traffic volume. Processing times also became a concern, while customers demanded greater visibility into data quality and ingestion reliability.

The engineering team redesigned the pipeline architecture to support more scalable processing patterns.

Feature flags were used to route traffic between the legacy pipeline and the new implementation.

Rather than performing a risky cutover, traffic could be progressively redirected and evaluated throughout the migration.

The results were substantial:

- Approximately 80% reduction in operational costs
- Processing time reduced from roughly 10 hours to 15 minutes
- Migration completed within a single quarter
- No customer-facing disruption during rollout
- Improved visibility and quality controls for customers

The example demonstrates that feature flags are not limited to user-facing features. They can also become a critical mechanism for controlling infrastructure evolution behind the scenes.

### Avoiding Common Feature Flag Pitfalls

Feature flags introduce flexibility, but they also require governance.

#### Stale Flags

Flags created for temporary migrations should not remain indefinitely.

Unused flags increase complexity, create confusion, and may introduce future operational risk.

#### Untested States

Every flag includes multiple potential states, including fallback behaviors.

Teams should validate each possible outcome rather than testing only the primary path.

#### Configuration Drift

Flag definitions must remain consistent across staging, production, and disaster recovery environments.

Differences between environments can create unexpected behavior during critical incidents.

#### Ownership Ambiguity

Every flag should have a clearly defined owner.

When an incident occurs, teams must know who is responsible for evaluating, modifying, or disabling the flag.

Without ownership, response times increase and operational risk grows.

### Building a Safer Migration Strategy

Feature flags are often introduced as a way to control application functionality.

Their broader value lies in helping organizations transform how they manage change.

By decoupling deployment from release, engineering teams gain the ability to:

- Introduce change gradually
- Reduce blast radius
- Validate outcomes continuously
- Roll back safely when needed
- Measure business and technical impact
- Modernize systems without disrupting customers

Cloud migrations will always involve risk. The goal is not to eliminate that risk entirely, but to manage it through controlled experimentation and progressive delivery.

Organizations that treat migrations as a series of measurable steps rather than a single release event are better positioned to deliver successful transformations while maintaining reliability, performance, and customer trust.

Title: Conf42 SRE 2026 roundup: quiet failures, agentic ops, resilience
Description: Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026 in review, from HTTP/2 load balancing traps and in-place pod resize to MCP incident agents and resilience testing.
Body:
The best incident stories at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) were the ones where nothing was technically down. One pod melting while its siblings idled, a security team slowed down by missing signals, a pricing cache that drifted. The event streamed online on March 19, 2026, with 35 talks from Harness, Virtana, Spotify, Rootly, Bloomberg, gridX, Walmart, Oracle, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and others, and it balanced those field stories against a strong thread on letting AI agents into operations.

## Failures that don't show up on the dashboard

[Mariem Sboui](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Mariem_Sboui_kubernetes_default_load) (gridX) told the kind of story that saves other teams a week. After HTTP/2 traffic arrived in their Kubernetes cluster, one backend pod ran hot on CPU and latency while the others sat nearly idle, and node metrics said there was plenty of capacity. The cause: Kubernetes Services and kube-proxy balance at Layer 4, per connection, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection. If you've ever wondered why your gRPC service has a favourite pod, watch this one.

[Abhimanyu Narwal](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Abhimanyu_Narwal_failures_dashboards_reliability) (Bloomberg) presented a case study from security operations where systems stayed up, yet missing signals and reduced clarity slowed people's diagnosis and response without triggering a single alarm. [Stuart Clark](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Stuart_Clark_scale_fail_spotify) (Spotify) went back to Spotify's 2014 hyper-growth, when abstractions oversimplified the system and hurt incident response; the lesson was that a good abstraction teaches complexity instead of hiding it. [Khushboo Nigam](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Khushboo_Nigam_correlation_over_collection) (Oracle) made the same argument for telemetry: SREs have a clarity problem, not a data problem, so organise signals by decision value and make "what changed?" the easy question.

## Agents in the incident channel, with guardrails

Several speakers put LLMs to work on diagnosis. [Makarand Gujarathi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Makarand_Gujarathi_assisted_incident_response) (Walmart) started from a familiar cost: engineers spending two to four hours and writing 15 to 30 SQL queries to correlate logs, metrics and traces across 5 to 10 backend components with skewed timestamps. His approach uses LLMs and MCP to do the correlation. [David McNerney and Daniel Raskin](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems) (Virtana) argued that outages are system problems, not application problems, and demoed agents investigating incidents over an automatically discovered dependency graph spanning services, Kubernetes, network and storage. [Savi Grover](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Savi_Grover_alerts_answers_modern) (Tekskills) and [Rohit Wadhwa](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Rohit_Wadhwa_predictive_workflow_integrity) (Walmart) covered agentic ops and autonomous triage across regions.

The counterweight came from talks about limits. [Ajay Athitya Ramanathan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Ajay_Athitya_Ramanathan_autonomy_guardrails_operating) (FourthSquare) noted that agentic failures in finance and operations rarely look like model errors; they show up as exception backlogs, repeated overrides and escalations. [Suganya Nagarajan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Suganya_Nagarajan_human_governed_automation) (Amazon) described human-governed automation loops for systems where autonomy makes failures spread faster, and [Vishal Shah](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Vishal_Shah_reliable_support_human) (Visa) kept a human in the loop of an agentic RAG system for API support.

[Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes) (Rootly) took the other side of AI in production: code written by assistants, tests that mirror the same flawed logic, hallucinated dependencies, more churn and bigger batches, landing on leaner SRE teams whose developers know their own code less well.

## Resilience you test, not resilience you hope for

[Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), who leads resilience testing at Harness and co-created LitmusChaos, gave the keynote: outages are inevitable, untested resilience accumulates like technical debt, and chaos, load and disaster recovery testing work better as one practice run with every delivery than as three teams' separate projects.

[Bhargavaram Potharaju](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Bhargavaram_Potharaju_national_scale_regulatory) (Wells Fargo) covered HA, DR and audit-ready design for national-scale regulatory reporting, [Rajesh Kumar Balusu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Rajesh_Kumar_Balusu_building_highly_available) (AGAP Technologies) highly available databases, and [Shruthi Sepuri](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Shruthi_Sepuri_testing_reliability_strengthening) (TCS) the gap between functional testing and reliability in regulated systems.

## Platform mechanics: CPU, VMs, caches and queues

[Raman Tehlan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Raman_Tehlan_Shubham_Rai_unlocking_just_time) (Zurich Lab) and Shubham Rai (Truefoundry) combined Kubernetes in-place pod resize with PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics to adjust CPU requests without restarts, aimed at clusters that are over-provisioned and throttled at the same time. [Shruthi Rajashekar](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Shruthi_Rajashekar_reducing_call_pain) (Broadcom) made VMs first-class Kubernetes resources to cut on-call pain on hybrid platforms. [Mukul Kumar Gaur](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Mukul_Kumar_Gaur_ready_shopping_caching) (Accelya) explained how airline NDC shopping platforms cache offers for metasearch traffic without letting prices drift. [Ran Tao](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Ran_Tao_migration_prem_messaging) (AWS) walked through rehosting, replatforming and refactoring messaging systems on the way to the cloud, and [Abhishek Suman](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Abhishek_Suman_compute_sharded_stream) (Microsoft) compute-sharded stream processing for petabyte-scale security analytics.

## SRE outside the server room

The event also showed how far SRE practice now travels. Talks applied it to clinical handoffs ([Abhiram Potharaju](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Abhiram_Potharaju_reliable_clinical_handoffs), Wells Fargo), healthcare utilisation management letters ([Prakash Easwaran](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Prakash_Easwaran_reliable_driven_letters), ZeOmega), bioreactor analytics in biologics labs ([Amogha Tenneti](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Amogha_Tenneti_driven_automation_flex), Eurofins PSS), grocery retail LLMs ([Sanjay Basu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Sanjay_Basu_operationalizing_llms_scale), TCS) and frontend architecture ([Murali Varma](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Murali_Varma_driven_frontend_architecture), Galileo Financial Technologies).

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the diamond sponsor, to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [Virtana](https://www.virtana.com/) as gold sponsors, to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and to the media partners. All talks are on the [Conf42 SRE 2026 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBHJy4EUSvaBe0-wtyjtbaa) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026).

The series continues with [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2027](https://www.conf42.com/sre2027).

Title: Resilience Testing Is Non-Negotiable in the Enterprise SDLC
Description: Outages in distributed systems are inevitable, making resilience testing essential in the SDLC. It must be continuous, covering failures, load, and disasters. Delayed validation creates “resilience debt,” increasing risk. A holistic approach—combining chaos, load, and DR testing—plus cross-team collaboration and AI-driven insights improves reliability and reduces impact.
Body:
### Resilience Testing Is Non-Negotiable in the Enterprise SDLC

Outages in distributed systems are inevitable, making resilience testing essential in the SDLC. It must be continuous, covering failures, load, and disasters. Delayed validation creates “resilience debt,” increasing risk. A holistic approach combining chaos, load, and disaster recovery testing, along with cross-team collaboration and AI-driven insights, improves reliability and reduces impact.

Modern software delivery has dramatically accelerated. AI-assisted development, automated CI/CD pipelines, and cloud-native architectures now enable teams to deploy software dozens of times per day.

But speed alone does not guarantee reliability.

At [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026](https://www.conf42.com), Uma Mukkara, Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of LitmusChaos, delivered a clear message: outages are inevitable. In modern distributed systems, assuming your design will always work is not just optimistic, it is risky.

Failure in distributed systems is a mathematical certainty.

That is why resilience testing must become a core, continuous practice in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

---

### The Reality of Inevitable Outages

Even the most reliable cloud providers experience outages.

Examples of unpredictable failures include:

- Physical disruptions such as drone strikes impacting AWS Middle East data centers  
- Policy or configuration errors triggering cascading outages in platforms like Azure  
- Retry storms and load spikes overwhelming services under unexpected demand  

These incidents highlight a critical reality: failure patterns constantly evolve.

A system validated during design may not be resilient against tomorrow’s failure scenarios. Architecture may remain stable, but surrounding failure conditions change continuously.

Resilience cannot rely on assumptions.

**Hope is not a strategy. Verification is.**

For a broader perspective, explore how [chaos engineering, load testing, and disaster recovery testing](https://developer.harness.io/docs/chaos-engineering/) work together.

---

### What Resilience Really Means

Resilience is often misunderstood as simply keeping systems online.

But uptime alone is not enough.

**Resilience is the grace with which systems handle failure and return to an active state.**

A resilient system must handle three categories of disruption:

#### System Failures
Pod crashes, node failures, infrastructure disruptions, and network faults.

#### Load Conditions
Traffic spikes or sudden demand pushing systems to their limits.

#### Disasters
Regional outages, multi-AZ failures, and infrastructure loss requiring recovery mechanisms.

Testing only one dimension leaves critical risks undiscovered.

True resilience requires validation across all three.

---

### Continuous Verification in the SDLC

Many organizations still treat resilience as a “day-two problem” handled after deployment.

Others assume that once validated during design, resilience is solved.

Both assumptions are flawed.

Resilience must be continuously verified.

As systems evolve with each release, so do their failure modes. Effective teams:

- Test resilience continuously  
- Verify resilience with every delivery  
- Document results across releases  

This shifts resilience testing into the outer loop of the SDLC, alongside functional and performance testing.

Instead of reacting to production incidents, teams proactively identify weaknesses before customers experience them.

---

### Understanding Resilience Debt

Resilience debt is similar to technical debt.

When teams delay resilience validation, they accumulate hidden risks.

Over time, this debt compounds.

When failure inevitably occurs, business impact scales with the amount of unresolved resilience debt.

The solution is consistent expansion of resilience testing coverage.

As testing matures over time, teams gain:

- Better system feedback  
- Earlier risk detection  
- Reduced likelihood of severe outages  

---

### A Holistic Approach to Resilience Testing

Resilience testing should not exist in silos.

Many organizations separate:

- Chaos testing  
- Load testing  
- Disaster recovery validation  

But real-world failures often occur at their intersection.

Examples:

- Resource bottlenecks emerging only under combined load and failure conditions  
- Chaos experiments reused for disaster recovery validation  
- Combined chaos and load testing revealing system limits  

A holistic approach integrates:

- **Chaos Engineering**  
- **Load Testing**  
- **Disaster Recovery (DR) Validation**

Learn more in the [Harness Resilience Testing documentation](https://developer.harness.io/docs/chaos-engineering/).

---

### Collaboration Across Teams

Resilience testing requires cross-functional collaboration.

Key contributors include:

- Developers  
- QA engineers  
- SREs  
- Platform teams  

Many organizations already share infrastructure but run isolated experiments.

By coordinating efforts, teams can:

- Reuse testing environments  
- Share chaos experiments  
- Validate DR workflows more frequently  
- Improve overall efficiency  

Resilience improves significantly when teams share assets instead of operating in silos.

---

### The Role of AI in Resilience Testing

As systems grow more complex, determining what to test and when becomes challenging.

Large organizations may have hundreds of possible experiments.

Agentic AI systems can help prioritize testing by analyzing:

- Incident data  
- CI/CD pipeline history  
- Infrastructure configuration  
- Operational documentation  

AI can recommend:

- Relevant chaos experiments  
- Appropriate load scenarios  
- Timely disaster recovery tests  

This ensures teams run the right tests at the right time without overwhelming engineering capacity.

---

### A Unified Platform for Resilience Testing

Harness has expanded its chaos engineering capabilities into a unified platform: **Harness Resilience Testing**.

This platform enables teams to:

- Design chaos experiments  
- Run load tests  
- Validate disaster recovery workflows  
- Observe system risk patterns  

All within a single environment.

This unified approach provides a **single pane of glass** for identifying and tracking resilience risks across the SDLC.

---

### Resilience Is a Core Practice for Modern SRE Teams

Resilience testing is not optional.

Outages will happen. Infrastructure will fail. Dependencies will break.

What matters is whether systems have been continuously validated against those failures.

As resilience testing coverage increases:

- Feedback improves  
- Risk visibility grows  
- Business impact decreases  

In modern software delivery, resilience is no longer just a reliability practice.

It is a **core discipline of the enterprise SDLC**.

---

### Get Started

Ready to validate your system’s resilience?

- [Book a Demo](https://www.harness.io/demo)

Title: When every dashboard blames someone else, map the dependencies
Description: David McNerney and Daniel Raskin of Virtana at Conf42 SRE 2026 on finding root cause with a live system dependency graph and investigating agents.
Body:
Modern outages are system problems, not application problems. That is the thesis David McNerney, Director of Product Management at Virtana, and Daniel Raskin, Virtana's Chief Marketing Officer, brought to Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026. Their answer to the familiar incident where every tool points at a different culprit is a system dependency graph, discovered automatically and kept current, which both humans and AI agents can use as context while they hunt for root cause.

## The incident where every tool is right and nobody is

Every SRE has been on this call. A service slows down, the dashboards light up, application metrics say one thing and infrastructure metrics say another. Each team's view is accurate for its own layer, and none of them explains the outage, because the cause lives in the interaction between layers.

The examples in the talk are the kind that cost hours. A spike in a storage queue throttles Kubernetes pods, and the pods look like the problem. Network contention shows up as application latency, so the application team starts profiling code. A GPU pipeline stalls, but the real bottleneck is the upstream data feeding it. In each case the symptom appears in one place and the cause in another, and traditional APM, built around services, plus telemetry split across tools, makes the jump between them hard.

## A graph of how the system actually behaves

The approach Virtana presents in the talk is a System Dependency Graph: a continuously updated map of the relationships between services, Kubernetes objects, infrastructure, networks and storage, discovered from production rather than drawn from an architecture diagram. The difference matters. The diagram in your wiki shows how the system was meant to work. A discovered graph shows how it is wired today, including the dependency someone added during last quarter's migration and never documented.

Once you have that map, the question during an incident stops being which dashboard is right. It becomes what this slow service depends on, and which of those dependencies changed. Following edges from symptom to cause is what an experienced SRE does in their head. The graph makes that path explicit and gives everyone on the call the same picture.

## Agents that use the graph as context

The second half of the talk, per the abstract, is a demo of autonomous agents using the dependency graph as operational context: investigating incidents, tracing cascading failures across layers and surfacing root cause faster. This is the same pattern several Conf42 speakers arrived at in 2026. An LLM agent with access to metrics alone tends to produce plausible stories. An agent that can walk a relationship graph has a structure to reason over, so its conclusions can be checked against real dependencies instead of taken on trust.

If you are evaluating any tool in this space, the talk suggests some good questions to ask: how the graph is discovered and how fresh it stays, whether it reaches below Kubernetes into network and storage, and whether the agent's investigation can be traced edge by edge so an engineer can verify it.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who run Kubernetes on shared infrastructure and keep losing the first hour of incidents to blame between layers. It is a vendor talk: the graph and the agents shown are Virtana's. The framing of outages as system behaviour, and the habit of following dependencies rather than dashboards, are useful whatever you run.

[Watch David McNerney and Daniel Raskin's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/z9mjbWbV8eo)).

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery) by Prateek Mittal (Harness), LLMs 2026: the same graph-as-context idea, applied to delivery pipelines.
- [Feature Flags as Incident Evidence: Safer AI-Assisted RCA Workflows](https://www.conf42.com/Feature_Flags_2026_Ishan_Shah_flags_incident_rca) by Ishan Shah (PayPal), Feature Flags 2026.
- [Mastering Observability in Distributed Systems: Tools, Techniques, and Lessons Learned](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Raghavender_Puchhakayala_tools_mastering_techniques) by Raghavender Puchhakayala (JPMorgan Chase), Observability 2025.

## From Virtana

Virtana builds what the talk calls relationship-aware observability; the session shows its System Dependency Graph and agent-driven root cause analysis.

- [virtana.com](https://www.virtana.com/)

Title: Conf42 Machine Learning 2026: shipping models is the hard part
Description: Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 roundup - why models fail after deployment, switchback tests, explainable recommenders, ML security and agents, in 35 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 ran online on February 19, 2026, with 35 talks, and very few of them were about training a better model. The lineup was about everything that happens after the notebook: drift, data skew, failing pipelines, experiments that lie, recommendations nobody can explain, and the identities and compliance rules wrapped around the whole thing. The abstract of a talk by Ancilia Dmello of Ford summed up the mood in six words: shipping ML is harder than training it.

All sessions are on the [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAxRHbUdOPlp1-OnsVso-nC).

## Good models, bad production

[Oleksandr Pyvovar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Oleksandr_Pyvovar_robustness_reliability_models), a machine learning engineer at Meta, opened with the scenario every ML team knows: a model hits 95% accuracy in the lab and six months later barely beats random guessing. His explanation is that good models rarely fail because they were wrong; the world changes after deployment. The talk walks through data drift (train a self-driving car only on sunny days, then send it to a foggy city), concept drift, label drift, feature pipeline degradation, training-serving skew, and feedback loops that amplify bias, followed by a monitoring framework and a remediation playbook.

[Ancilia Dmello](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Ancilia_Dmello_forecasting_inventory_retail) of Ford Motor Company laid out an observable MLOps framework on Google Cloud covering real-time, batch, and streaming inference, drift detection, CI/CD, and retraining. [Srihari Godleti](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Srihari_Godleti_fairness_bias_mitigation) of Roku made the case that slow training is often data skew rather than bad code, with three Apache Spark techniques to fix it. [Kiran Ramanna](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Kiran_Ramanna_retraining_lifecycle_models) of ServiceNow and [Srinivas Talasila](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Srinivas_Talasila_compliance_governance_ai) of SAP covered the organisational and infrastructure halves of the same problem: readiness to stop pilot sprawl, and HA, DR, and zero trust for the platforms models run on.

## Predict the failure before it burns compute

[Pavel Solikov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pavel_Solikov_security_adversarial_attacks) of J.P. Morgan had one of the most practical talks of the day. His team's Prefect flows can run for 30 minutes or two hours and fail at the end. Since Prefect already knows the parameters, environment, and metadata at the start, and the first tasks can cheaply fingerprint data quality, a gradient boosting model can score the risk of failure in the first minute or two and abort, reroute, or warn the developer with a reason.

[Tim Markin](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Tim_Markin_feature_stores_management) of GiftHorse turned the same idea on software delivery: a production ML system that scores pull requests for risk and estimates delivery time before coding starts, using repo metadata, AST features, and CI signals.

## Experiments and recommendations you can trust

[Sergei Nasibian](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sergei_Nasibian_knowledge_graphs_reasoning), a Quantitative Strategist at Rothesay, explained why classic A/B tests break for delivery pricing in food tech: when you change prices, you change courier supply and other users' experience too. Switchback testing, which alternates treatments over time rather than splitting users, is the alternative.

[Lev Fedorov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Lev_Fedorov_optimization_performance_efficiency) of Amazon showed how his team turned a black-box recommender into a traceable ranking system, with per-user recommendation traces and user-facing reasons, such as a productivity video shown because you once liked one about effective planning. The trigger was users reporting irrelevant content and developers unable to say why it appeared. [Rohan Mitra](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Rohan_Mitra_experimentation_reproducibility_science) of PhonePe gave a hands-on tutorial on writing the spec for a recommendation system, and [Murthy Chandrapaty and Chakravarthy Kalva](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Murthy_Chandrapaty_Chakravarthy_Kalva_decisioning_b2c_marketing) of Adobe argued that send-time optimisation should grow from a prediction problem into decisioning.

## ML in money and markets

Finance and marketing filled two tracks. [Avaneendra Kanaparti](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Avaneendra_Kanaparti_experimentation_abtesting_optimization) of American Express covered customer lifetime value models for approvals and credit lines, [Balakumaran Sugumar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Balakumaran_Sugumar_anomaly_detection_signals) of Synchrony mapped where ML sits in payment platforms, and [Vivek Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Vivek_Kumar_responsible_ethics_ai) of Majesco used telemetry to predict performance problems in high-volume transaction systems. [Abhinay Kumar Reddy Seella](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Abhinay_Kumar_Reddy_Seella_satisfaction_prediction_telemetry) of Roku predicted user satisfaction in real time from LLMs and behavioural telemetry instead of waiting for surveys, and [Ashutosh Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Ashutosh_Verma_scalability_architecture_distributed) of Meta connected online and offline journeys for attribution.

## Securing the pipeline, and the people with access to it

The security track treated ML platforms like any other production system. [Reshma Vemula](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Reshma_Vemula_pipelines_orchestration_mlops) of Loma Linda University Health showed how PHI leaks into development environments, and [Neha Asthana](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Neha_Asthana_simulation_synthetic_data) of Abbott argued that ML platforms are only as secure as the identities behind them. [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_documentation_artifacts_beginners) gave a beginner-friendly guide to the minimum ISO 42001 documentation for an AI management system, for the moment someone asks who approved this model and what data it used. [Sagar Sudhir Behere](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sagar_Sudhir_Behere_streaming_realtime_analytics) of Circle and [Sudheer Kumar Aluvala](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sudheer_Kumar_Aluvala_optimization_hyperparameters_tuning) of HCL America applied ML to third-party risk and zero trust compliance.

## Agents arrive, carefully

Agents had their own track, with an emphasis on guardrails. [Sumit Kaul](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sumit_Kaul_architecture_design_patterns) of PayJoy designed incident response agents that propose root causes and mitigations while humans keep decision authority. [Marat Kenzhebulatov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Marat_Kenzhebulatov_vision_computer_imaging) of Booking.com covered AI agents in security-critical backend work, [Rajeshwari Sah](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Rajeshwari_Sah_labeling_annotation_quality) of Apple built a clinical documentation scribe as a LangGraph state machine, and [Sujith Vadakkepati](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sujith_Vadakkepati_deployment_containers_kubernetes) of Oracle combined RAG with ERP data for explainable supplier risk.

Further afield, [Sowmiya Narayanan Govindaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sowmiya_Narayanan_Govindaraj_risk_modeling_assessment) of Motional covered unified perception models for autonomous driving, and [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Mohamed_Najaaf_recommendation_ranking_systems) of AWS showed how to cut the carbon footprint of generative AI workloads. Operations talks from [Anu Arora](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Anu_Arora_personalization_recommendation_platforms) of ServiceNow, [Dinesh Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Dinesh_Garg_evaluation_benchmarks_metrics) of Honeywell, and [Pallab Haldar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pallab_Haldar_orchestration_workflows_ai) of Cognizant covered autonomous IT support, IoT warehouse data, and inventory forecasting.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsors [LLMday](https://llmday.com/) and the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/), the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The next edition, [Conf42 Machine Learning 2027](https://www.conf42.com/ml2027), is set for February 18, 2027. Until then, check your drift dashboards.

Title: Agentic AI, CI/CD Automation, and the Future of DevOps
Description: Explore how AI is redefining DevOps practices across CI/CD, infrastructure, and operations
Body:
# Agentic AI, CI/CD Automation, and the Future of DevOps - Conf42 DevOps 2026

The DevOps landscape is entering a new phase where AI-driven automation, agentic systems, and intelligent CI/CD pipelines are becoming core to software delivery. As organizations scale cloud-native architectures and accelerate release velocity, traditional DevOps approaches struggle to keep pace. Conf42 DevOps 2026 brings together industry experts to explore how AI is redefining DevOps practices across CI/CD, infrastructure, and operations.

This virtual conference is designed for DevOps engineers, platform teams, SREs, and engineering leaders who want practical insights into enterprise-ready DevOps powered by AI. The sessions focus on real-world adoption, architectural patterns, and governance strategies that help teams move from experimentation to production.

## Chinmay Gaikwad Keynote on Agentic AI in CI/CD

The featured keynote at Conf42 DevOps 2026 is delivered by [Chinmay Gaikwad](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chinmay-gaikwad/), Director of Product Marketing at Harness. His session, *(Building Enterprise-ready CI/CD Pipelines using Agentic AI](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai)*, examines how agentic AI transforms modern CI/CD pipelines.

Chinmay explains how AI agents can autonomously reason across pipeline context, detect and remediate failures, enforce security and compliance, and continuously optimize delivery performance. The keynote also addresses enterprise concerns such as scalability, reliability, and governance, making it highly relevant for organizations modernizing their DevOps platforms.

For teams evaluating [AI-powered CI/CD automation](https://www.harness.io/products/continuous-delivery/ai-assisted-deployment-verification), this keynote provides a clear and actionable roadmap.

## DevOps Sessions Featuring AI Agents and Automation

Conf42 DevOps 2026 features multiple sessions that showcase how AI agents are being applied across the DevOps lifecycle.

**Premanand Tiwari** presents a session on autonomous time-series forecasting, demonstrating how AI-driven systems can improve observability and operational decision-making without manual intervention.

**Pallab Haldar**, Technical Architect, shares insights on AI-powered workflow orchestration, focusing on how intelligent automation can dynamically manage complex DevOps pipelines and toolchains.

**Gobu Natarajan**, Manager of Technical Program Management, explores multimodal conversational agents and their role in correlating logs, metrics, and human input to accelerate incident response.

**Praneeth Patil**, Senior Staff Software Engineer, discusses autonomous infrastructure management in cloud environments and how AI agents can improve scalability, resilience, and cost efficiency.

## DevOps Governance and AI at Scale

In addition to automation, Conf42 DevOps 2026 addresses critical topics such as GenAI governance, distributed AI platform design, and operational reliability. These sessions help teams adopt AI responsibly while maintaining control, visibility, and compliance.

## Register for Chinmay Gaikwad’s Keynote

Conf42 DevOps 2026 offers practical, expert-led insights into AI-driven DevOps, agentic automation, and next-generation CI/CD pipelines.

Learn how enterprise teams are applying agentic AI in real-world DevOps environments by attending Chinmay Gaikwad’s keynote:

Title: Conf42 DevOps 2026 - agents joined the pipeline, failover got boring
Description: Conf42 DevOps 2026 in review, 47 talks on agents in CI/CD and on-call, infrastructure as a graph, boring failover, CI-gated SLOs and what green CI misses.
Body:
[Conf42 DevOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) opened the Conf42 year on January 22, 2026 with 47 talks. The loudest question was what happens when AI agents get commit rights, pipeline access and a seat on the on-call rota. The quieter, equally useful one was how to make the old hard things (region failover, migrations, compliance) dull enough that nobody needs a hero. Speakers came from Intuit, Google, Disney, Meta, Microsoft, Cisco, Splunk, Twilio, Workday, Oracle, ASML, Harness and more.

## Agents in CI/CD and on call, with the brakes attached

Diamond sponsor Harness set the frame. [Chinmay Gaikwad](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai) argued that AI made writing code cheap and moved the bottleneck after the commit, then laid out an enterprise-ready pipeline built by agents: a knowledge graph for context, policies enforced outside the prompt, and RBAC that treats the AI as an extension of the user, so if you can't deploy to production, neither can your agent.

[Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) (Meta) proposed GenOps, a governance-first model for letting generative agents act inside CI/CD. [Vladyslav Budichenko](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vladyslav_Budichenko_incidents_agents_security) (Vocaly AI) gave agents in incident response the good, the bad and the ugly treatment, including how to use them safely with MCP. [Neal Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neal_Iyer_guardrails_ai_accountability) (Splunk) brought the same "guardrails first" stance to agents in the security operations centre, keeping human control in the loop. On the infrastructure side, [Praneeth Patil](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Praneeth_Patil_autonomous_infrastructure_cloud) (Equinix) described LLM-driven multi-cloud infrastructure that catches misconfigurations, and [Premanand Tiwari](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Premanand_Tiwari_forecasting_time_autonomy) (Amazon) demoed autonomous time-series forecasting for capacity planning.

## Infrastructure is a graph, so give the model the graph

Context engineering got its own cluster. [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) (Anyshift) explained why LLMs fail at infrastructure: they can't see live dependencies or multi-hop relationships. Her answer is to model infrastructure as a graph, query it with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher, and measure context quality. [Pronnoy Goswami](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pronnoy_Goswami_observability_queries_context) (Workday) used the Model Context Protocol to make telemetry queryable, and [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) (Solo.io) asked the two questions every platform team now hears about agentic and MCP traffic: how do we observe it, and how do we keep the bill sane. [Tina Kanth](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tina_Kanth_finops_streaming_prompts) (Microsoft) showed prompt templates that turn streaming financial events into structured, auditable triage decisions.

## Make failover boring

The most satisfying talks were about removing drama. [Akshay Pratinav](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Akshay_Pratinav_failover_resilience_workloads) (Intuit) described a Kubernetes-native platform where services onboard declaratively to region failover: pre-scale from live traffic, promote standby databases, shift routes through Route53 and Istio. The goal, in his words, is to make failover boring, which is the highest compliment in operations.

[Harris Baskaran](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Harris_Baskaran_kubernetes_modernization_containers) (Google) walked a high-volume ticketing monolith from VMware and Oracle to GCE, then rebuilt it cloud-native on GKE and PostgreSQL, with dependency mapping, replication and multi-region DR lessons along the way. [Kalyan Inturi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Kalyan_Inturi_availability_migration_gateways) (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) used shadow traffic and phased rollouts for a zero-downtime gateway migration. [Nikhil Kokal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikhil_Kokal_apis_scalability_reliability) (The Walt Disney Company) covered architectures for APIs at billions of requests, and [Srinivas Pagadala Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Srinivas_Pagadala_Sekar_gitops_resilience_automation) (Karsun Solutions) built self-healing pipelines with Tekton and Argo CD.

## Observability as a contract, not a nice-to-have

[Sumit Kaul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Sumit_Kaul_slos_instrumentation_observability) (Payjoy) made observability a platform contract: zero-code instrumentation and SLOs gated in CI/CD, so a service cannot ship without traces and metrics. [Mohit Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Mohit_Gupta_gpu_ci_validation) (Intel) applied the same idea to GPU performance, catching compute and memory bottlenecks in the pipeline instead of in production. [Aravind Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Aravind_Sekar_reliability_prevention_ai) (Twilio) and [Raghu Bhupatiraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Raghu_Bhupatiraju_predictive_analytics_outages) (Expeditors) both pushed from firefighting towards prediction, the latter for supply chain systems.

## Green checkmarks are not the whole story

[Tilda Udufo](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tilda_Udufo_cicd_quality_testing) (Outreachy) gave one of the event's sharpest reminders: passing tests don't guarantee quality, as the XZ Utils incident showed, and review practice and culture have to cover what automation misses. [Bhaskar Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Bhaskar_Sawant_security_automation_pipelines) mapped how AI-driven development changes the pipeline attack surface. [Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gian_Wild_accessibility_security_inclusion) (AccessibilityOz) took apart the idea that security and accessibility must trade off against each other. Hands-on security tooling came from [Nikolay Milyaev](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikolay_Milyaev_xdr_security_analytics) (Microsoft) on Defender XDR alert fatigue, [Gareth Emslie](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gareth_Emslie_sentinel_security_automation) (Dynatrace) on extending Microsoft Sentinel, and [Gurdeep Gill](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gurdeep_Gill_firewalls_ai_protection) (Cisco) on NGFWs for AI workloads. [Imran Abdul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Imran_Abdul_sdwan_networking_automation) (Pace University) brought GitOps to the enterprise network, SD-WAN and zero trust included.

## Regulated and physical systems

Compliance and industry talks rounded out the programme: [Pooja Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pooja_Ranjan_compliance_saas_governance) (Oracle) on continuous compliance for SaaS, [Vivek Chittireddy](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vivek_Chittireddy_privacy_regulation_security) (Meta) on privacy by design with differential privacy and anonymisation in the pipeline, [Swapna Chimanchodkar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Swapna_Chimanchodkar_clinical_healthcare_ai) (Cognizant) on deploying real-time sepsis detection, and [Rasmi Ranjan Nayak](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Rasmi_Ranjan_Nayak_embedded_robotics_ai) (ASML) on deterministic embedded AI for robotics.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Gold. All 47 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrB6SG3pv3bmTo7NWFlCGiNx).

The series returns with [Conf42 DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/devops2027).

Title: Shipping faster without losing sleep
Description: This is the practice
Body:
# DevOps, but now it thinks for itself

DevOps has always been about automation.

In 2026, the automation talks back.

Conf42 DevOps 2026 is a very clear signal that agentic AI has moved from experiments to infrastructure. CI/CD pipelines are making decisions. Compliance is running in real time. Incident response is increasingly autonomous. And somehow, it all still needs to be observable, secure, and affordable.

This conference is packed. The agenda spans agents, AI, architecture, compliance, data, FinOps, MLOps, observability, security, SRE, and sustainability. If DevOps touches it, it’s probably here. Often with an AI-powered opinion.

AI agents are everywhere. From enterprise-ready CI/CD pipelines and autonomous cloud engineering to self-healing operations and AI-driven incident response, many talks focus on what happens when systems stop waiting for humans to intervene. There’s excitement, but also a lot of healthy caution.

Compliance and governance get serious attention. Compliance-as-code, continuous regulatory validation, privacy-by-design pipelines, and real-time compliance copilots show how DevOps is adapting to regulated environments like finance, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. This is DevOps where audits are not theoretical.

Data and FinOps show up in force. Medallion data lakes, blockchain-driven BI, read-intensive architectures, streaming financial events, and cost-aware observability all point to a world where DevOps teams are responsible not just for uptime, but for economics and trust.

Observability and SRE round things out. AI-powered observability, predictive reliability, agent traffic monitoring, and multi-workload failover reflect how complex systems have become. The focus shifts from reacting faster to preventing problems before users notice.

If DevOps is your job, your craft, or the thing that quietly connects everything else you do, this one’s for you. In 2026, DevOps isn’t just shipping software anymore. It’s running intelligent systems at scale.

Title: Conf42 IoT 2025: from houseplants to Kafka, edge AI and payments
Description: Conf42 IoT 2025 roundup - Grafana-monitored houseplants, IoT data pipelines and lakehouses, edge AI cameras, supply chain security and device payments.
Body:
Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025 ran online on December 18, 2025, with ten talks that followed sensor data from the moment it is measured to the moment someone pays for it. The data track was the strongest, with four talks on moving and storing device telemetry at scale. Around it sat edge AI, supply chain security, payments, and one talk about keeping houseplants alive that may be the best introduction to observability Conf42 has published.

Every session is on the [Conf42 IoT 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/iot2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAoyYvqm9wESh0loKTsm84Y).

## Observability, explained to an eight-year-old

[Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics), Senior Developer Advocate at Grafana Labs and co-author of Contract Testing in Action, declared 2025 the year of no plant casualties. She teamed up with her eight-year-old daughter on a beginner-friendly project: a soil moisture sensor that reports to Grafana Cloud and tells them when to water.

The project is fun, but the real value is the vocabulary. Marie explains IoT, monitoring, and observability through gardening analogies: each plant gets a little helper in the soil that detects moisture and tells you when it needs water. If you have ever struggled to explain your job at a family dinner, take notes. If you have ever killed a house plant, you are the target audience; Marie asks for a show of hands on exactly that.

## The data track: streams, lakehouses, feature stores

Four talks dealt with what happens after billions of devices start talking.

- [Rehmat Kharal](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Rehmat_Kharal_streaming_scalability_governance) of Conduktor looked at making IoT streams on systems like Kafka reliable, secure, and usable, covering messy pipelines, outages, and governance. The hard part, as the talk frames it, is the move from devices producing data to data producing value.
- [Ketul Dusane](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Ketul_Dusane_messaging_latency_throughput), a Software Development Engineer at AWS, covered messaging at scale with three pillars: low latency, high throughput, and operational resilience, using caching, load balancing, and anomaly detection.
- [Bhanudeepti Chinta](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Bhanudeepti_Chinta_lakehouse_analytics_scalable), an Engineering Manager for data, made the point that organisations rarely fail at IoT because they cannot collect data. They struggle because the cost and complexity of managing it grow faster than the value extracted, which is where lakehouse architectures that unify telemetry, device logs, and analytics come in.
- [Manmohan Alla](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Manmohan_Alla_warehousing_featurestores_optimization) of Apple showed how Snowflake plus a structured feature store turns raw sensor data into ML-ready features, with examples from manufacturing, utilities, energy grids, and smart monitoring.

Watched back to back, these four make a decent reference architecture for device data, from broker to model.

## Edge AI: make the camera think

[Madhu Niranjan Reddy Puduru](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Madhu_Niranjan_Reddy_Puduru_vision_edge_processing), a Software Engineering Manager at Synchronoss Technologies, made the case against cloud-only smart cameras. Streaming raw video costs bandwidth, adds latency that real-time safety alerts cannot afford, raises GDPR and CCPA privacy questions, and gets expensive across hundreds of cameras. Running the model next to the sensor and sending only events like "person detected" fixes all four. The abstract promises neural networks on $10 hardware, which is the kind of constraint that makes edge work interesting.

[Ramakrishna Ambati](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Ramakrishna_Ambati_maintenance_predictive_medical), an Enterprise Solutions Architect at Visby Medical, applied edge computing, machine learning, and zero trust security to medical diagnostic devices, moving maintenance from reacting to failures to predicting them, with results from a real deployment.

## Security: the attack comes in the box

[Gresshma Atluri](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_security_supplychain_defense), a cybersecurity risk analyst, opened with a story from a hospital she consulted for, where a vulnerability planted during manufacturing put patient safety at risk. Supply chain attacks do not break in through the front door; they arrive in trusted updates and embedded components. She also recalled the Mirai botnet built from baby monitors and cameras with default passwords, and a logistics company whose smart scanners were hijacked through compromised firmware. The defences: hardware attestation, network segmentation, and behavioural analytics.

## Money moves at the edge too

Two talks looked at finance. [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payments_microservices_architecture) of GoodLeap, with more than ten years in the payments industry, explained how payment gateways moved from monoliths to microservices to handle transactions initiated by connected devices acting on our behalf. [Swetha Lakkaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Swetha_Lakkaraju_banking_modular_modernization), with more than 18 years in mainframe-based core banking, argued for modular core architectures that let banks decouple from legacy systems without a big-bang rewrite.

## Partners and what's next

Conf42 IoT 2025 was supported by the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners listed on the event page.

For earlier editions of the series, see [Conf42 IoT 2024](https://www.conf42.com/iot2024). And if the data track was your favourite part, the [Conf42 Robotics 2025](https://www.conf42.com/robotics2025) lineup covers similar ground with more moving parts.

Title: From sensors to cities, iot is taking over
Description: Everything is connected
Body:
# Your devices are talking. A lot.

IoT used to be about connecting things.

Now it’s about securing them, scaling them, analyzing them, and explaining why they’re generating so much data at such inconvenient times. Sensors are everywhere, and they’re not shy.

Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025 is a look at what IoT actually looks like once it leaves the lab.

This conference brings together nine talks across two tracks, focused on real-world IoT systems running in production. From smart cameras and medical devices to payment systems and connected supply chains, these sessions are about devices that matter and data that can’t be ignored.

Edge computing plays a big role. You’ll hear about running AI directly on devices, real-time image processing without cloud dependencies, and building IoT architectures that keep working even when connectivity doesn’t. Because sometimes the cloud is far away, and decisions still need to be made.

Security and trust show up everywhere. Talks cover IoT supply chain defense, securing connected ecosystems, and designing edge architectures that can survive cyberattacks without grinding everything to a halt. When devices are deployed at scale, “we’ll patch it later” stops being an option.

Data is the other half of the story. IoT data lakehouses, messaging at scale, low-latency pipelines, and cost-aware analytics all feature prominently. These sessions explore how to turn massive device streams into something useful, reliable, and affordable.

And yes, there’s room for fun too. From monitoring plants with sensors to using Grafana dashboards to keep things alive, IoT still has a playful side, even when the systems get serious.

If your world involves connected devices, edge systems, or figuring out what all that data is trying to tell you, this one’s for you. IoT is messy, powerful, and very much alive.

Title: Secure by Default: Why AI-Driven Delivery Needs a Rethink
Description: Why fast, AI-powered delivery demands secure-by-default pipelines.
Body:
# Secure by Default: Why AI-Driven Delivery Needs a Rethink  
By Dewan Ahmed

Software delivery has been accelerating for more than a decade, and the arrival of AI has pushed us into an entirely new velocity class. Code generation, configuration scaffolding, infrastructure suggestions, remediation hints, and deployment decisions now involve AI. It participates in every stage of the delivery pipeline.

On the surface, this feels like progress. Faster delivery, fewer bottlenecks, happier teams.  
But a closer look reveals something more complicated.

## The Gap Between Speed and Safety

Most modern pipelines were designed for a world where humans made the important decisions, such as writing code, reviewing changes, crafting configurations, and evaluating risks. AI changed that dynamic. It introduced automation that moves faster than traditional security practices can respond to.

The result is a widening gap between the speed at which we can ship and the safety at which we can ship.

Here are a few of the challenges teams are already feeling today.

### 1. AI is amplifying existing weaknesses

If your base images are outdated, your tests barely cover your codebase, or your deployment strategy lacks guardrails, AI does not fix these issues. It accelerates them.

Pipelines automate mistakes with the same enthusiasm they automate features.

### 2. The threat surface has shifted

The most common AI failures today are not the classic vulnerabilities we are used to scanning for.

Instead, organizations are seeing issues such as:

- prompt injection  
- model jailbreaking  
- vulnerable AI-generated code  
- behavior-driven exploits  
- configuration drift caused by AI tools  

These attacks target behavior and reasoning, not code structure.

### 3. Delivery is faster, but security has not kept up

AI-assisted workflows generate code, configurations, and infrastructure definitions at machine speed. Most security models still rely on manual reviews, point-in-time scans, or human approval gates.

This mismatch means misconfigurations are no longer slow, human-scale mistakes. They have become automated hazards.

### 4. Developers are not set up for AI-era security

Most developers have little or no training in AI security or AI threat modeling, yet we expect them to recognize model manipulation, unsafe outputs, and subtle behavioral failures in AI-generated artifacts. The expectations do not match the support we give them.

---

These challenges will define the next era of DevSecOps. If you want to hear about a practical four-pillar framework for secure-by-default AI-driven delivery, [join my keynote at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025).

Title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2025: securing pipelines that AI now writes into
Description: Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 roundup: 26 talks on AI in the delivery pipeline, SBOMs and provenance, safer deployments and security in finance and healthcare.
Body:
Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 ran on December 4, 2025, with 26 talks and one question underneath most of them: what happens to security when AI writes code, generates configuration and makes decisions inside the pipeline? Speakers from Harness, AT&T, Chevron, JPMorganChase, Microsoft, Dropbox, Cisco and others answered from the pipeline, the supply chain and some of the most regulated industries around. Everything is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025), and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCMXkZdQESvj8M_clmevDME).

## AI is in the pipeline, so secure the pipeline

Harness's keynote from [Dewan Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Dewan_Ahmed_secure_ai_delivery), Principal Developer Advocate, set the tone. Pipelines automate whatever you feed them, and AI makes them faster at shipping mistakes as well as good code. His framework for secure-by-default delivery has four pillars: contextual intelligence about what a change means, automatic verification of provenance and drift, behaviour-based anomaly detection, and continuous learning from every deploy and rollback.

Others took the same problem from different angles. [Rajkumar Sukumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Rajkumar_Sukumar_ai_ml_ethics) of AT&T showed how to embed security, privacy-aware training, policy as code and audit-ready steps into machine learning pipelines. [Baradwaj Bandi Sudakara](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Baradwaj_Bandi_Sudakara_ai_ml_secure) of Ascension Health covered AI-driven testing and defect prevention. [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_cloud_mcp_secure) of Zencoder demonstrated MCP workflows that let an LLM trigger CI jobs, query Grafana or debug from Sentry inside the IDE, and the risks to check before plugging that into your stack. [Murali Koney](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Murali_Koney_ai_risk_llm) of Cox Automotive tied LLM adoption to governance, risk and cost, starting from his observation that most enterprise AI projects fail before production.

## Supply chain: know what you ship

[Bhaskar Bharat Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Bhaskar_Bharat_Sawant_supply_chain_ci) of Cornerstone Building Brands gave the most hands-on supply chain session: automated SBOMs, SLSA provenance and attestations, hermetic builds and artifact verification at deploy time, so every release is traceable by default. [Gresshma Atluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_supply_chain_threats) of Chevron built a proactive defence framework from real-world supply chain incidents.

For teams starting closer to the code, [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql) of Microsoft toured GitHub Dependabot, CodeQL and the other built-in security features, and [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep) of MoEngage explained how static analysis actually works using open-source Semgrep. Together they make a good afternoon for anyone whose SAST stage is a box nobody opens.

## Deploying without seeing red

[Rayenn Hamrouni](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Rayenn_Hamrouni_deployments_aws) of Lenstra had the best title of the day, "From Blue to Green Without Seeing Red", and a real case study behind it: implementing blue/green deployment for a web application on AWS using Lambda@Edge, with the trade-offs spelled out. [Meenu Venkataarangam](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Meenu_Venkataarangam_migration_cloud_auto) of Recode Solutions covered automation for enterprise migrations that closes security gaps along the way, and [Nishanth Sirikonda](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nishanth_Sirikonda_risk_secure_system) of First Day Foundation argued for risk-driven DevSecOps with compliance as code. [Raghavendra Reddy Kapu](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghavendra_Reddy_Kapu_resilient_system_secure) brought fault-tolerance patterns and chaos engineering into the security conversation.

## Where the stakes are regulated

Finance had its own track. [Swamy Biru](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_rag_ai) of JPMorganChase covered DevSecOps patterns for RAG and agentic systems in financial operations, [Janardhan Chejarla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Janardhan_Chejarla_trading_cloud_scale) of Calypso Technology secured event-driven order management for high-frequency trading, and [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payment_api_secure) of GoodLeap described keeping PCI compliance while moving a payment gateway to microservices with daily releases.

Healthcare and education followed. [Mahendar Ramidi](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Mahendar_Ramidi_health_cloud_scale) of the Maryland Health Benefits Exchange shared how he built a HIPAA-compliant mobile platform for cancer patients with zero-trust architecture and compliance automation, and [Raghav Sai Cheedalla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghav_Sai_Cheedalla_ai_ethics_edu) of Meta looked at secure, ethical personalisation of learning for students with special needs. [Mallikarjun Bussa](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Mallikarjun_Bussa_data_access_secure) of Dropbox addressed self-service BI that doesn't leak data.

## People are part of the system

Two talks were about the humans who run all of this. [Kuldeep Deshwal](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Kuldeep_Deshwal_culture_teams_secure), Director of Engineering at Proofpoint, unpacked the productivity paradox in DevSecOps culture and how to avoid burning out the people expected to ship securely. [Sanjeevani Bhardwaj](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Sanjeevani_Bhardwaj_health_secure_cloud) of Salesforce proposed a four-dimension technical health index to move teams from reactive to proactive security work. On the infrastructure side, [Nazim Khan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nazim_Khan_ethernet_ai_infra) of Cisco explained how Ethernet with RoCEv2 and Ultra Ethernet standards competes with InfiniBand for AI training networks.

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), our diamond sponsor, to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) as gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 26 talks are linked from the [Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025). The next edition, [Conf42 DevSecOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2026), is set for October 1, 2026. Plenty of time to make the security stage the one that can't be skipped.
