Title: Where code, infrastructure, and risk meet
Description: And nothing ships blind
Body:
# Security at scale is a lifestyle now

DevSecOps used to be about shifting security left.

Now it’s about making sure security doesn’t quietly break everything while AI, automation, and cloud platforms move at full speed. Small difference.

Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 is where those conversations get real.

This conference brings together twenty five talks across eight tracks, covering AI, cloud, data, infrastructure, finance, security, and transformation. The focus is not on adding more scanners, but on building systems that are secure by default, even as pipelines get smarter and faster.

AI is front and center. From AI-driven DevSecOps and autonomous cloud security to embedding security and ethics directly into machine learning pipelines, many sessions explore what happens when intelligence becomes part of the delivery process. There’s a clear theme here: automating insecurity at scale is very easy, and very expensive.

Supply chain security gets serious attention. SBOMs, SLSA, provenance, dependency management, and defending against modern software supply chain attacks show up across multiple talks. These sessions dig into what it actually takes to trust what you’re shipping, and where it came from.

Real industries feature heavily. Finance, healthcare, payments, and enterprise platforms all appear, with talks on securing high-frequency trading systems, payment gateways, clinical platforms, and large-scale migrations. These are environments where “we’ll fix it later” is not an option.

Culture and sustainability round things out. Developer productivity, DevSecOps health frameworks, and avoiding burnout while raising security standards are treated as first-class concerns, not side notes.

If your job sits somewhere between shipping fast and not ending up on the news, this one’s for you. DevSecOps is no longer a phase in the pipeline. It’s the system.

Title: Conf42 Robotics 2025: the software and rules around the robots
Description: Conf42 Robotics 2025 roundup - post-quantum robot networks, DO-178C for electric aircraft, compliance-by-design, and AI in clinics and disaster response.
Body:
Conf42 Robotics 2025 ran online on November 20, 2025, with nine talks, and almost none of them were about motors or grippers. The lineup was about everything that has to be true around a robot before anyone lets it loose: how its network survives quantum computers, how its flight software gets certified, how its decisions are audited, and what data infrastructure feeds it. If you build the systems that robots plug into, this was your kind of robotics conference.

All talks are on the [Conf42 Robotics 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/robotics2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDUt9JKK5BDogRgpbqPK4wc).

## Robots outlive their cryptography

The sharpest framing of the day came from [Nehal Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Nehal_Singh_robotics_quantum_security) of California State University, Long Beach. The robots deployed today in manufacturing, healthcare, defence, and logistics will still be running five, ten, even fifteen years from now. Large quantum computers are not here yet, but a fleet with that lifespan has to assume they will arrive while it is still in service. Robotic systems combine long-lived hardware, sensitive operational data, and real-time autonomy, which makes them an attractive target.

The talk walks through post-quantum cryptography based on the NIST standards, with the constraint robotics engineers care about most: securing the network without breaking real-time performance. A useful one if your hardware refresh cycle is measured in decades rather than sprints.

## Certification is the long pole

[Charles Antony Raj](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Charles_Antony_Raj_avionics_certify_flight), Senior Manager of Systems and Software Engineering at Collins Aerospace, brought about two decades of aerospace experience to a problem most software engineers never meet: certifying flight software under DO-178C when it runs on multicore processors. Multicore chips are what electric aircraft programmes want for performance, and they are also what makes interference between cores hard to bound and hard to prove safe.

The talk covers the certification paths and strategies for cutting the delays they cause. It is a rare look at what "shipping" means when the regulator, not the CI pipeline, is the final gate.

## Compliance as an architecture choice

Two talks treated regulation as a design input rather than paperwork bolted on at the end.

[Sneha Nallapu](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Sneha_Nallapu_compliance_design_finance) of J.B. Hunt Transport Services made the case for compliance-by-design in automated financial systems. The patterns are ones backend engineers will recognise: event sourcing, bi-temporal data so you can answer what you knew and when, graph lineage, CQRS, and adaptive workflows. Audit trails stop being a report someone generates and become a property of the system.

[Vinaya Nadig](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Vinaya_Nadig_governance_banking_robots), a Principal Engineer at Amazon, opened with the 2008 financial crisis: algorithms making decisions with opaque logic and incomplete data, long before generative AI. Today AI approves loans, flags fraud, and advises on investments in real time. The argument is that a unified AI data governance framework is what keeps banking automation from repeating that history at machine speed.

## AI and robotics where the stakes are human

[Srinivasa SKN Ambati](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Srinivasa_SKN_Ambati_healthcare_analytics_ai), an Engineer Lead at Anthem, looked at how advanced analytics and AI are changing clinical robotics, with an emphasis on building systems that are scalable and compliant enough for patient care.

[Vivek Karnam](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Vivek_Karnam_cloud_response_robots) of Surge Technology Solutions started from the shortcomings of traditional emergency response and showed how cloud computing, robotics, and predictive analytics can combine into faster, smarter disaster response frameworks.

## The infrastructure underneath

The remaining talks went one layer down, to the data and even the walls that robotic systems depend on.

- [Adithya Sirimalla](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Adithya_Sirimalla_oracle_azure_cloud) of Enliven Technologies gave a practical framework for tuning Oracle and SQL Server on AWS and Azure, on the premise that in automation every millisecond of database latency can shape a real-time decision.
- [Ankita Saxena](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Ankita_Saxena_ai_insights_industry), a Senior Product Manager at Amazon, traced recommendation systems from a "you may also like" widget to strategic infrastructure, including in robotics-enabled marketplaces.
- [Rahul Pingale](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Rahul_Pingale_iot_materials_smart), Technical Director at Wallquest, gave the most unexpected talk of the day: PVC-free non-woven wall surfaces with embedded sensors and connectivity, turning something as ordinary as a wall into part of a smart environment. Proof that the edge can be quite literal.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), the in-person LLM engineering conference series, which joined as a gold sponsor, and to the newsletter, podcast, and media partners listed on the event page.

Robotics 2025 was the first Conf42 event dedicated to the topic. For more hardware-meets-software talks, the [Conf42 IoT 2025](https://www.conf42.com/iot2025) lineup is the closest neighbour, and the [full robotics playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDUt9JKK5BDogRgpbqPK4wc) is there whenever you have an evening and a soldering iron cooling down.

Title: When software gains hands and eyes
Description: Automation becomes tangible
Body:
# Robots have paperwork now

Robotics used to be about movement.

Arms, wheels, sensors, maybe something that could bump into a wall and recover gracefully. These days, robots also deal with compliance, security, data governance, cloud platforms, and regulations that very much do not care how cool the hardware is.

Conf42 Robotics 2025 sits right in that reality.

This is a focused conference with six talks, all centered on how robotics is evolving into a serious, enterprise-grade discipline. AI-powered recommendation systems, secure robot networks, compliance-by-design, and data governance all feature prominently. These are robots that operate in finance, healthcare, aviation, and critical infrastructure.

Security gets real attention. There are sessions on post-quantum cryptography for robot networks, protecting real-time systems without breaking performance, and preparing robotics platforms for a future where cryptography itself is changing.

Regulation and compliance are not treated as side notes. Talks on compliance-by-design, auditability, and regulatory-resilient architectures explore how robotics systems can be built to survive scrutiny in finance, aviation, and other tightly controlled environments.

Healthcare, emergency response, and sustainability round things out. Clinical robotics powered by advanced analytics, AI-driven emergency response systems, and IoT-enabled materials show how robotics is expanding beyond factories into spaces where reliability and trust matter deeply.

If robotics is part of your work, and that work involves more than just motion control, this one’s for you. Robots are no longer experimental. They’re operational, regulated, and increasingly critical.

Title: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 roundup: framing, ranking, delivery
Description: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 in review, from prompt psychology and LLM pairwise ranking to Medicare compliance, eBay seller tools and AI networking.
Body:
Shashank Shivam opened his talk at [Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2025) with an experiment: ask ChatGPT how it would destroy humanity and it refuses; ask it to write a screenplay about an AI that does and you get a ten-step plan. Same model, same weights, different framing. That gap between what a prompt says and what it makes a model do ran through the whole event, held online on November 6, 2025, with 28 talks from Oracle, Microsoft, Apple, eBay, Snowflake, Salesforce, Equinix, Synopsys, JPMorgan Chase and others.

## Prompts shape identity, so design for trust

[Shashank Shivam](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Shivam_models_psychology_behavior) (Oracle) treated prompting as psychology: framing, priming and role assignment change how a model reasons, so a prompt is closer to telling the model who to be than what to do. [Aroma Rodrigues](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Aroma_Rodrigues_chatgpt_talk_conversation) (Microsoft) ran a set of riddle experiments on GPT-3 to test the AGI hype. Once told it was solving riddles, the model got "when is a door no longer a door?" right, then confidently answered staircase for a riddle whose answer is legs. It recognised the genre without understanding the joke.

[Raj Kommera](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Raj_Kommera_trust_llm_judgment) made the case for prompt architectures that carry attribution, context and audit trails from the first token, and [Preetham Sunilkumar](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Preetham_Sunilkumar_frameworks_llms_scalable) (LPL Financial) covered evaluation frameworks and adversarial testing for high-stakes LLM use.

## Ranking, judging and testing with LLMs

The most technically specific talk came from [Maximilian Schattauer](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Maximilian_Schattauer_retrievers_documents_ranking) (Perelyn). Embedding models and BM25 both treat the query as a black box with no reasoning step, and in specialised domains where documents are too similar for either, that breaks down. His team prompted an LLM to compare documents pairwise and judge which better answers the question, then reordered results accordingly, and saw recall@k improve in those special cases. Worth watching if your search results are all plausible and none of them are right.

[Yash Panjari](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Yash_Panjari_testing_conversational_automation) (Apple) applied LLM-as-judge and generated test data to the hard problem of testing voice and chat systems, where human dialogue never follows the script. [Balraj Govindaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Balraj_Govindaraj_testing_automation_agile) (MVP Plus Consulting) showed manual testers moving to automation through codeless tools and prompts, and [Swamy Biru](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_efficiency_agents) (JPMorgan Chase) presented RAG-backed agents for financial operations.

## Prompts in the delivery and data pipeline

[Bandanawaz Mulla](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Bandanawaz_Mulla_healthcare_cloud_solutions) (Health Care Service Corporation) had a deadline-shaped story: a 2024 CMS mandate for Medicare Advantage supplemental benefit reporting meant consolidating 102 benefit types from more than ten systems for two million members. LLMs were used across the development lifecycle, including rapid prototyping of the ETL logic. [Janak Bhalla](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Janak_Bhalla_code_developers_scale) (Microsoft) covered LLM tooling for code migrations and fixing compile errors at scale.

On the data side, [Jimish Kadakia](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Jimish_Kadakia_data_cloud_access) (Snowflake) showed natural-language interfaces for querying data and triggering pipelines, [Siva Kumar Raju Bhupathiraju](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Siva_Kumar_Raju_Bhupathiraju_sql_infrastructure_hybrid) (Paycor) prepared SQL backends with Azure SQL Managed Instance for LLM workloads, [Annapurneswar Putrevu](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Annapurneswar_Putrevu_pipelines_learning_systems) (Bloom Energy) combined prompts with reinforcement learning for self-healing pipelines, and [Richa Solanki](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Richa_Solanki_data_lakehouse_enterprise) (Ally Bank) covered lakehouse architecture. [Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Bhavana_Reddy_Chadagonda_science_testing_experimentation) argued that experimentation skills remain a data scientist's edge in AI-heavy roles.

## The infrastructure under the prompt

A cluster of talks went below the API. [Praneeth Patil](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Praneeth_Patil_agents_infrastructure_multicloud) (Equinix) looked at LLMs moving from writing infrastructure snippets to acting as multi-cloud agents, with hallucinations, misconfigurations and cost as the risks to design around. [Rahul Thakur](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Rahul_Thakur_infrastructure_resilience_scale) (Salesforce) sharded AI services across zones for resilience. [Rajesh Arsid](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Rajesh_Arsid_ethernet_performance_scaling) (Synopsys) explained how Ultra Ethernet and UALink affect inference throughput and latency across distributed systems, a reminder that prompt engineering at scale is also a networking problem. [Vamsi Gadireddy](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Vamsi_Gadireddy_network_protocols_reliability) (Microsoft Azure) covered AI in network engineering itself.

## Industry case studies

The remaining talks applied prompt engineering domain by domain: seller tools at eBay ([Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Sureshkumar_Karuppuchamy_ecommerce_tools_ai)), insurance claims triage and underwriting ([Chetan Prakash Ratnawat](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Chetan_Prakash_Ratnawat_insurance_transformation_workflows), Capgemini), Power BI supply chain analytics at Kellogg's ([Victor Gabriel](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Victor_Gabriel_supplychain_savings_bi), GEP Worldwide), multi-agent ERP design ([Kasee Palaniappan](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Kasee_Palaniappan_enterprise_erp_intelligence), SAP Ariba), fleet telematics ([Preeti Sali](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Preeti_Sali_fleet_management_telematics), Ford), supply chain automation ([Kunal Dixit](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Kunal_Dixit_supplychain_automation_resilience), Zensar), Security Copilot for Conditional Access and Zero Trust ([Cynthia Akiotu](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Cynthia_Akiotu_security_defense_cyber)), agile delivery ([Hema Yalamancheli](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Hema_Yalamancheli_agile_delivery_prompt), Tyler Technologies) and enterprise migrations ([Meenu Venkataarangam](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Meenu_Venkataarangam_migrations_automation_innovation), Recode Solutions).

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [LLMday](https://llmday.com/) and the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrC9ZgozU8V1FhRF147_HDjp) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2025).

The series continued with [Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2026).

Title: Small changes in phrasing, massive shifts in results
Description: Design the prompt
Body:
# So yes, prompts are infrastructure now

There was a brief moment when prompt engineering felt like a party trick.

You typed a clever sentence, the model did something impressive, everyone nodded, and we moved on. That moment is very much over.

Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 is about what happens when prompts stop being experiments and start running real systems.

This conference brings together twenty four talks across seven tracks, covering prompting, data, infrastructure, testing, finance, culture, and commerce. The focus is not on clever phrasing, but on building prompt-driven systems that are secure, scalable, and actually useful.

Security shows up early and often. From prompt injection and zero trust enforcement to using prompts as part of cyber defense workflows, several sessions explore what it means to protect systems where words can trigger actions. When prompts touch infrastructure, governance stops being optional.

Enterprise use cases take center stage. Insurance workflows, healthcare compliance, supply chain automation, ERP systems, finance platforms, and e-commerce tooling all appear, powered by prompt-driven AI. These talks are about scale, regulation, and measurable impact, not demos that only work once.

Agents are everywhere. Multi-agent systems, autonomous workflows, RAG pipelines, and prompt-driven orchestration show how LLMs are moving beyond responses and into coordinated action. Alongside that comes a lot of discussion about trust, transparency, and keeping humans in the loop when systems start making decisions.

Testing and evaluation round things out. LLM-as-judge, automated QA, prompt psychology, and performance optimization all show up, because once prompts become part of production systems, “it feels right” is no longer a valid test strategy.

If prompt engineering is part of your job now, whether you planned it or not, this one’s for you. Prompts aren’t just instructions anymore. They’re becoming the interface between humans, machines, and the systems we rely on.

Title: Conf42 JavaScript 2025 - give the main thread a break, give the AI the docs
Description: Conf42 JavaScript 2025 in review, 25 talks on scheduler.yield(), testing pain, accessible JS, web games, docs-as-context for AI and privacy in the browser.
Body:
[Conf42 JavaScript 2025](https://www.conf42.com/js2025) streamed on October 30, 2025 with 25 talks, and the programme split neatly in two. Half was about the browser itself: a main thread that needs to breathe, tests that still hurt, forms that still lock people out. The other half was about JavaScript as the glue around AI, from docs wired into the IDE to NLP running client-side. Speakers came from PagerDuty, Cloudinary, Playtech, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, Nike, ADP, UBS and the game studio Hology.

## The main thread is a shared resource

[Aleksandr Tkachenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Aleksandr_Tkachenko_let_browser_take) (Playtech) gave the most immediately useful talk of the day on `scheduler.yield()`, part of the new Prioritized Task Scheduling API. You call it inside a long task and the browser gets to handle the clicks and keystrokes that piled up, then resumes your code where it left off, which helps Interaction to Next Paint. He is upfront that the API is experimental and not in every browser yet, and spends time on the imperfect alternatives you can use in the meantime. Think of it as a polite `await` for the main thread.

[Deepika Annam](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Deepika_Annam_revolutionizing_performance_intelligent) (Nike) covered optimisation techniques across Node.js backends and React frontends, and [Lakshmi Bhargavi Mullapudi](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Lakshmi_Bhargavi_Mullapudi_real_time_engineering) (Techstar Group) looked at the architectures behind real-time systems for fraud detection and personalisation.

## Testing still hurts, and the survey says where

[Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Daniel_Afonso_state_testing_tech) (PagerDuty) built his state of JavaScript testing around the State of JS survey. Mocking came out as the number one pain point, ahead of configuration, performance, the ESM versus CommonJS mess, excessive complexity and flakiness, and satisfaction with testing sat at 2.5 out of 4. From there he traced a decade of change in test runners, testing libraries, mocking and production practices, and where AI-based tools fit. Come for the history, stay for the honest scorecard.

## Accessibility is a JavaScript problem with JavaScript fixes

Two talks argued that accessible front ends are mostly a matter of knowing the rules. [Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Gian_Wild_accessible_easier_than) (AccessibilityOz) gave concrete code examples, the three types of JavaScript functionality, and ten principles for accessible JavaScript and forms, starting from the fact that around twenty percent of people have a disability. [Anisat Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Anisat_Ahmed_introduction_aria_guide) delivered a good first talk on ARIA, cutting a confusing set of attributes down to how to use them well.

## Docs are the context your AI is missing

[Sharon Yelenik](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Sharon_Yelenik_ai_docs_accuracy) (Cloudinary) worked on turning Cloudinary's APIs into MCP servers and came away convinced that the thing holding AI back in the IDE is the context it gets as much as its accuracy. Her talk shows what happens when documentation is connected directly to the LLM client in the editor, with examples across Cloudinary, Auth0 and Firebase. It is one of the more grounded takes on agentic coding from the docs side of the house.

Agents showed up elsewhere too. [Jyoti Kunal Shah](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Jyoti_Kunal_Shah_agentic_autonomous_micro) (ADP) proposed an agentic framework that co-evolves React micro-frontends with the microservices behind them, [Ajitha Buvanachandran](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Ajitha_Buvanachandran_agentic_search_multi) built multi-agent search that decomposes queries, and [Linga Annela](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Linga_Annela_micro_frontends_fast) used Module Federation micro frontends to ship AI features without touching the monolith. [Ujjwala Modepalli](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Ujjwala_Modepalli_client_side_nlp) (Wells Fargo) kept the text analytics in the browser with Natural.js and TensorFlow.js, no backend required.

## Securing the stack from npm to the VM

[Srinivasa Rao Gunda](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Srinivasa_Rao_Gunda_securing_framework_frontend) (UBS) laid out a vulnerability management framework for full-stack JavaScript, from npm dependencies to DOM-based attacks. [Vivekananda Chittireddy](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Vivekananda_Chittireddy_privacy_design_building) (Meta) brought privacy by design to JavaScript data systems with differential privacy, anonymisation and encryption. [Rehana Sultana Khan](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Rehana_Sultana_Khan_rate_limiting_cost) (Versa Networks) built adaptive, AI-driven API rate limiting, and [Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Priyadarshni_Shanmugavadivelu_scaling_trust_security) (Microsoft) went below the runtime to confidential computing, Trusted Launch and zero trust for VMs.

## And yes, games

[Annie Tsai and Adam Ringhede](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Annie_Tsai_Adam_Ringhede_level_why_typescript) (Hology) made the case for TypeScript and JavaScript as game development languages. Web game platforms such as Poki reach players in over 100 countries, Discord activities put games where people already hang out, and the genre range has stretched from puzzle and cozy games to racing and FPS. A long way from playing Flash games and hiding the browser from your parents.

## Where to watch

All 25 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/js2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCSMU1ZoGrRWPFA6oD7KG3X). Start with Tkachenko if your INP is red and with Afonso if your mocks are.
Author: Conf42

Title: Written in moments of optimism and caffeine
Description: Still shipping the modern web
Body:
# JavaScript is still running the internet

JavaScript has been “overused” for at least a decade now.

And yet, here it is. Powering browsers, servers, APIs, data pipelines, AI workflows, accessibility tooling, and entire businesses that would quietly fall apart without it. Funny how that works.

Conf42 JavaScript 2025 is a snapshot of what JavaScript looks like today. Big. Mature. Everywhere.

This conference brings together twenty talks across five tracks, covering foundations, integrations, intelligence, security, and systems. From core browser APIs and performance tuning to JavaScript running serious workloads in healthcare, finance, and enterprise platforms, the focus is firmly on real-world use.

AI is woven throughout the program. Generative AI for claims and fraud, agentic search, client-side NLP, AI-assisted documentation, and micro frontends designed to integrate intelligence directly into web apps all make an appearance. These sessions focus less on demos and more on how JavaScript fits into AI systems that actually ship.

Accessibility and performance get proper attention too. Talks cover ARIA, inclusive JavaScript patterns, testing practices, browser scheduling, and keeping applications responsive as they grow more complex. Because fast and accessible still matters, even when everything else is getting smarter.

Security is not an afterthought. Rate limiting, API security, vulnerability management, privacy by design, zero trust architectures, and protecting both frontend and Node.js systems show up across the schedule. JavaScript may be flexible, but production systems still need guardrails.

If JavaScript is part of your stack, your job, or your long-running love-hate relationship, this one’s for you. The language keeps evolving, and somehow, it keeps ending up right in the middle of everything.

Title: Conf42 Kube Native 2025: GPUs, fewer clusters and regulated AI
Description: Conf42 Kube Native 2025 roundup - GPU sharing with vCluster, fewer environments, Dapr and eBPF, defence in depth, and AI in regulated industries on Kubernetes.
Body:
Conf42 Kube Native 2025 ran online on October 16, 2025, with 53 talks, which makes it one of the larger events in the series. Two conversations ran side by side. One was about Kubernetes itself: sharing GPUs, cutting environment sprawl, observing clusters with eBPF, and securing them in depth. The other was about what enterprises now run on it, above all AI workloads in banks, insurers, and hospitals, where compliance is part of the architecture.

Every session is on the [Conf42 Kube Native 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBfaAPyif8OXN3e1XcXeO2A).

## GPUs are the new scarce resource

[Piotr Zaniewski](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant), Head of Engineering Enablement at vCluster, had the most hands-on pitch of the day: in 30 minutes, spin up vCluster sandboxes, drop NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside, and use fractional GPUs to share expensive hardware across tenants without deadlocks or a cluster per team. Multi-tenant, multi-scheduler, with the YAML to copy.

[Deepika Annam](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Deepika_Annam_optimization_reinforcement_performance) of Nike went further up the stack, applying deep reinforcement learning to pod scheduling, autoscaling, and resource management. [Jyotirmoy Sundi](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Jyotirmoy_Sundi_reinforcement_learning_distributed), co-founder and CTO of Votal.ai, covered scaling reinforcement learning with human feedback across distributed cloud systems.

## How many clusters do you really need?

[Arsh Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Arsh_Sharma_kubernetes_environments_scalability), Senior DevRel Engineer at MetalBear, asked the question in the title that every platform team should ask: one environment for production, one for staging, one for CI, one per developer so nobody blocks staging. Do you need them all? The talk shows how to reuse existing environments for development and CI, lowering cloud costs and cluster sprawl.

Platform developers also got two takes on simplifying the code itself. [Christophe Gigax](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Christophe_Gigax_dapr_architectures_cloudnative), Cloud Solution Architect at Hager Group, showed how Dapr exposes state management, pub/sub, and other building blocks as standard APIs, so microservices stop reimplementing them. [Anupama Pathirage](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Anupama_Pathirage_ballerina_integration_opensource), Head of Engineering for integration at WSO2, presented Ballerina, an open-source language with cloud deployment constructs built into the code.

## Resilience patterns that hold up

The architecture track was strong on concrete patterns. [Rahul Singh Thakur](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Rahul_Singh_Thakur_sharding_uptime_architecture) of Salesforce gave a practical guide to multi-zone sharded microservices with intelligent request routing. [Karthik Reddy Beereddy](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Karthik_Reddy_Beereddy_streaming_redis_selfhealing) of LexisNexis Risk Solutions covered self-healing streaming with Redis Streams and Azure Event Hubs, and [Shalini Katyayani Koney](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Shalini_Katyayani_Koney_kafka_streaming_scalable) of Walmart scaled Kafka on Kubernetes with StatefulSet tuning, autoscaling, and GitOps. [Ashif Anwar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Ashif_Anwar_azure_eventdriven_patterns) of Wolters Kluwer and [Dhruvesh Talati](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Dhruvesh_Talati_resilience_design_recovery) of Ally added event-driven patterns on AKS and architectures for crisis response.

On the observability side, [Alejandro Mercado](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Alejandro_Mercado_observability_kubernetes_ebpf), DevOps Lead at Michael Page, made the case for eBPF-powered observability for incident detection and root cause analysis, and [Srinivas Pagadala Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Srinivas_Pagadala_Sekar_observability_llms_paas) of Karsun Solutions looked at LLM-assisted diagnostics to cut MTTR and alert noise.

## Defence in depth, and the post-quantum clock

[Karthikeyan Thirumalaisamy](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Karthikeyan_Thirumalaisamy_security_missioncritical_kubernetes), a Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, laid out a defence-in-depth blueprint for mission-critical services on AKS, EKS, and GKE, covering insider threats, supply chain attacks, and runtime exploits. [Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Derek_Asir_Muthurajan_Caleb_quantum_security_infrastructure) of Broadcom looked further ahead, at moving Kubernetes clusters and service-to-service traffic to quantum-resistant cryptography. [Vivek Koodakkara Shanmughan](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Vivek_Koodakkara_Shanmughan_identity_keycloak_deployment) of Aryaka Networks described a regional hub model for running Keycloak identity across a global SASE deployment, and [Satya Purella](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Satya_Purella_integration_fintech_platforms) of Fifth Third Bank covered secure integration platforms for fintech.

## AI in regulated industries

The biggest cluster of talks was about running AI on Kubernetes where regulators are watching. In finance, [Ashish Dibouliya](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Ashish_Dibouliya_banking_compliance_governance) of Webster Bank presented a Kubernetes-ready AI data governance framework with drift detection, [Jaydeep Taralkar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Jaydeep_Taralkar_finance_ml_orchestration) of UBS focused on responsible ML at scale, [Kiran Purushotham](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Kiran_Purushotham_trading_llm_insight) of JPMorgan Chase showed swarms of LLM agents for market insight, and [Manoj Kalakoti](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manoj_Kalakoti_finops_costgovernance_autonomous) of Apple embedded FinOps cost governance into the delivery pipeline. [Manisha Sengupta](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manisha_Sengupta_finance_risks_modernization) of Brown Brothers Harriman covered the attack vectors that come with AI in finance.

In healthcare, [Tharun Nallamothu](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Tharun_Nallamothu_copilot_clinical_workflows) of Microsoft presented Dragon Copilot, an AI clinical assistant built around ambient recording for documentation. [Manikesh Iruku](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manikesh_Iruku_ehr_pipelines_accuracy) of Amazon built LLM auditing for EHR pipelines, [Amala Umakanth](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Amala_Umakanth_genai_healthcare_fraud) of McKinsey applied GenAI to claims processing and fraud, and [Venus Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Venus_Garg_ethical_ai_trust) of Boston University asked whether Kube-native stacks are ready for the bias, privacy, and trust questions healthcare AI raises.

## The rest of the lineup

Data engineering got its own track, including [Sruthi Erra Hareram](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_etl_airflow_optimization) of TELUS Digital on tuning PySpark and Airflow on Kubernetes and [Vamsi Pulusu](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Vamsi_Pulusu_datapipeline_streaming_modern) of Ford on moving from legacy ETL to streaming and lakehouses. [Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Bhavana_Reddy_Chadagonda_abtesting_experimentation_careers) of Intuit offered career advice through A/B testing techniques like CUPED. And for something different, [Chandan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Chandan_Kumar_lighting_immersion_responsive) of Google explained pre-computed surround lighting that reacts in under 100ms, while [Preeti Sali](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Preeti_Sali_ev_charging_infrastructure) of Ford covered cloud-native EV charging infrastructure.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

For earlier editions, start with [Conf42 Kube Native 2024](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2024). Then go and count your clusters.

Now it’s where streaming platforms live. Where AI runs. Where healthcare systems process claims. Where finance does fraud detection. Where compliance, security, data, and automation all collide. No pressure.

Architecture and scalability are front and center. From scaling Kafka to hundreds of thousands of messages per second, to event-driven patterns, multi-zone sharding, API gateways, and self-healing streaming platforms, this is Kubernetes pushed hard in real environments.

Title: Conf42 Incident Management 2025: work the incident, not the tools
Description: Conf42 Incident Management 2025 roundup: Twilio on incident comms, AI for detection and RCA, incidents under HIPAA and GDPR, and the platforms underneath.
Body:
Conf42 Incident Management 2025 took place on October 2, 2025, with 22 talks about the moment something breaks and everything that decides how badly it goes. AI showed up in most of them, as a summariser, a detector, a root cause assistant and a tester, but the talk that stuck was about something older: telling people what is going on. The lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/im2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBU25vUS7hZWANfG6r4D4oK).

## Communication is the incident customers see

[Gandhi Mathi Nathan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Gandhi_Mathi_Nathan_Kumar_ai_automation_resilience), Principal Incident Commander at Twilio, chose incident communications because, as he put it, there is plenty of content on detection and resiliency and very little on how responders keep everyone informed. He walked through the tool stack a single Twilio incident touches: FireHydrant to declare and run it, PagerDuty to page, Zoom for the bridge, Slack for the asynchronous work where most incidents actually happen, Datadog, Atlassian Statuspage, Google Docs for retrospectives, Confluence and Slack canvases for action items.

His warning applies to any shop with that many tabs open: the trouble starts when "You end up working the tools instead of working the incident". From the customer's side, the status page is still green, nobody has told them anything, and support tickets start to flood in. He then demoed how AI can take on the updates and bring late joiners up to speed so the incident commander can keep the room focused on mitigation.

Two more talks looked at the screens responders stare at. [Priyanshi Deshwal](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Priyanshi_Deshwal_visual_interfaces_intelligence) of Mode argued for AI-powered visual interfaces that replace static dashboards with real-time insight, and [Sujit Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sujit_Kumar_contactcenters_automation_scale), VP of Technology at Copart, covered contact centres built to stay calm and coordinated when incidents push call volume up.

## AI for detection and root cause, with receipts

[Mallikarjun Ramasani](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Mallikarjun_Ramasani_intelligence_cloud_future) of Barclays surveyed ML-driven detection, root cause analysis and auto-remediation in cloud operations. [Vasanth Mudavatu](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vasanth_Mudavatu_transparency_algorithms_ai) of Dell Technologies asked the question every on-call engineer should ask of these tools: can you trust your AI during a breach? His answer was algorithmic transparency, so responders can see why the model flagged something before they act on it.

[Pushap Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Pushap_Goyal_graph_spanner_security) of Google showed Spanner Graph tracing security incidents across distributed systems, turning scattered events into a connected attack story. [Mahmood Nawaz](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Mahmood_Nawaz_knowledge_cloud_resilience) of LTIMindtree focused on knowledge systems that turn each incident into something the next responder can find, which is the part of the postmortem that usually goes missing.

## When the regulator is on the other line

[Nisheedh Raveendran](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Nisheedh_Raveendran_compliance_hipaa_gdpr), Senior Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, opened with three short sentences every compliance-adjacent engineer will recognise: system down, regulators calling, patients waiting. His talk covered why normal incident response fails when HIPAA, GDPR or the EU's Digital Markets Act are in play, and the playbooks that work instead.

[Nirup Baer](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Nirup_Baer_finance_modernization_resilience) of Wells Fargo looked at how financial firms embed compliance into cloud architecture so resilience and speed don't trade off against each other. In healthcare, [Sreenivasul Reddy Meegada](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sreenivasul_Reddy_Meegada_healthcare_biometrics_security) drew on deployments of NICE and Omilia voice biometrics to tighten security without slowing patient workflows.

## The platforms underneath the incident

A good chunk of the day was about systems that shouldn't need an incident commander in the first place. [Sruthi Erra Hareram](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_databricks_analytics_reliability) presented a cross-cloud analytics pipeline on Azure Databricks and AWS built with incident-aware orchestration. [Adithya Sirimalla](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Adithya_Sirimalla_multicloud_databases_resilience) of Enliven Technologies covered running Oracle and SQL Server across AWS, Azure and OCI with automation, monitoring and disaster recovery. [Vijaykumar Pasunoori](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vijaykumar_Pasunoori_apigateways_microservices_serverless) of Valet Living made API gateways part of detection and recovery, and [Rehana Sultana Khan](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Rehana_Sultana_Khan_ratelimiting_api_protection) of Versa Networks showed AI-driven rate limiting that adapts to malicious traffic instead of relying on fixed thresholds.

## Preventing the next one

Prevention got its own track of sorts. [Vijay Kumar Kola](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vijay_Kumar_Kola_sap_salesforce_testing) of Intuitive used AI-powered testing to catch SAP and Salesforce failures before production, [Gobinath Kasimayan](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Gobinath_Kasimayan_sap_governance_agility) of Deloitte Consulting treated SAP master data governance as an incident prevention tool, and [Krishna Chaitanya Yarlagadda](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Krishna_Chaitanya_Yarlagadda_supplychain_automation_prevention) of Mercury Financial applied anomaly detection to supply chain disruptions that cascade into incidents within hours.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), our gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 22 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Incident Management 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/im2025). Next in the series is [Conf42 Kube Native 2025](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2025) on October 16, and the reliability conversation picks up again at [Conf42 SRE 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) on March 19, 2026. Meanwhile, check whether your status page knows about your last incident.

Title: Conf42 MLOps 2025 roundup: where the lab meets production
Description: Conf42 MLOps 2025 in review, from warehouse robots and vendor lockouts to trillion-parameter training, AgentCore, zero trust pipelines and fintech ML.
Body:
Two days before Elementor launched its AI Site Planner, OpenAI locked the company's account. Dennis Nerush told that story at [Conf42 MLOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025), and the punchline was that it barely mattered, because the team had built for exactly that failure. The 37 talks at the event, streamed online on September 18, 2025, kept coming back to the same gap: models that work in the lab, in the notebook or in the demo, and what it takes to keep them working once real traffic, real dust and real vendors get involved. Speakers came from Meta, Amazon, AWS, Mastercard, Oracle, Intuit, JPMorgan Chase, Barclays, SiriusXM and many more.

## The real world is messier than the lab

[Shubham Beldar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Shubham_Beldar_when_ai_automation) (Symbotic) brought the most physical failures of the event. Picking robots that look flawless in the lab meet transparent shrink wrap, irregular products and dust on their vision sensors, and accuracy drops from the mid-nineties to the low sixties. His diagnosis is an MLOps one: training data missing the messy cases, and validation done in the lab instead of on the warehouse floor.

[Dennis Nerush](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Dennis_Nerush_scaling_ai_fault) (Elementor) covered the vendor version of the same lesson. His team's infrastructure integrates several AI vendors and can switch between them, which is why an account lockout two days before launch turned into a manageable incident instead of a war room. [Madhavi Bhairavabhatla](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Madhavi_Bhairavabhatla_fail_fast_recover) (Mastercard) went one level down to timeouts: set too generously, they hold resources, delay failure detection and let one slow service drag down the rest, so the talk lays out cascading timeouts across system layers.

Several talks addressed the lab-to-production pipeline directly, including [Jimmy Katiyar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Jimmy_Katiyar_model_production_building) (SiriusXM), [Srikanth Vissarapu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Srikanth_Vissarapu_lab_production_building) (Meta), [Bharath Reddy Baddam](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Bharath_Reddy_Baddam_bridging_mlops_gap) (New York Life) and [Naveen Edapurath Vijayan](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naveen_Edapurath_Vijayan_mlops_scale) (AWS), who covered CI/CD for ML, monitoring and governance.

## Scale at the largest platforms

[Anjan Dash](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Anjan_Dash_mlops_trillion_parameter) (Meta) talked about operating training pipelines for trillion-parameter LLMs, where failure recovery and cost are daily concerns. [Prabhakar Singh](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Prabhakar_Singh_production_mlops_spam) (Meta) covered real-time, multimodal spam detection at billion-user scale, including sampling strategies that cut labelling cost and privacy-preserving ML. [Mohan Singh](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Mohan_Singh_building_autonomous_mlops) (Amazon) presented self-healing ML infrastructure that predicts failures and scales itself.

On agents, [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_poc_bedrock_agentcore) (AWS) addressed why so many agent projects stall at proof of concept: production needs identity, governed tool access and a runtime, which is what Amazon Bedrock AgentCore packages as managed services. [Nishanth Joseph Paulraj](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Nishanth_Joseph_Paulraj_deploying_ai_literature) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) deployed literature agents for biomedical research, and [Brian Irish](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Brian_Irish_embracing_sky_computing) (Ditto) made the case for sky computing across clouds.

## Humans, governance and security in the loop

[Tejasvi Nuthalapati](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Tejasvi_Nuthalapati_human_loop_mlops) (Amazon) argued for production patterns that keep humans in the loop to improve models rather than replace people. [Bhanu Maryala](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Bhanu_Maryala_automating_ai_ethics) (Informatica) automated data governance inside generative AI pipelines so compliance doesn't slow deployments. [Sudheer Obbu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sudheer_Obbu_zero_trust_mlops) (JPMorgan Chase) applied Zero Trust to ML pipelines from development to production, and [Arfi Siddik Mollashaik](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Arfi_Siddik_Mollashaik_ai_driven_cybersecurity) (Securiti) looked at threat detection and privacy with post-quantum defences in mind. Healthcare got its own governance angle from [Nikitha Edulakanti](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Nikitha_Edulakanti_mlops_scale_designing) (Fresenius Medical Care) and [Aishwarya Pai](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Aishwarya_Pai_mlops_healthcare_scaling) (Deloitte).

## Finance was the busiest track

No other domain came close. [Naresh Karri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naresh_Karri_production_mlops_finance) (Intuit) covered keeping fraud models alive under extreme load and drift, [Mallikarjun Ramasani](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Mallikarjun_Ramasani_operationalizing_ai_finance) (Barclays) ML-powered BI and real-time analytics, [Narasimha Rao Vanaparthi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Narasimha_Rao_Vanaparthi_mlops_fintech_architecting) (State Street) responsible AI in regulated environments, and [Dileep Kumar Kanimetta](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Dileep_Kumar_Kanimetta_mlops_scale_operationalizing) (Microsoft) drift detection and automated governance for risk models. [Parul Purwar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Parul_Purwar_scaling_ai_finance) (IMC Trading), [Pushpalika Chatterjee](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Pushpalika_Chatterjee_generative_ai_fintech) (Huntington National Bank) and [Naganarendar Chitturi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naganarendar_Chitturi_paperwork_pipeline_building) (Newrez), who built MLOps for autonomous mortgage processing, rounded it out. Insurance came via [Sameer Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sameer_Joshi_ai_driven_insurance) (Cognizant) and [Sreelatha Pasuparthi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sreelatha_Pasuparthi_intelligent_error_response) (Liberty Mutual), whose ML-driven Slack integration predicts which errors matter across 17 enterprise systems.

## MLOps at the edges

Some of the most interesting constraints came from outside big tech. [Lalitha Potharalanka](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Lalitha_Potharalanka_scaling_educational_ai) (FDA) took educational AI to rural schools with poor connectivity through low-code platforms and edge inference, and [Anoosha Cherukuri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Anoosha_Cherukuri_low_code_meets) (State of Tennessee) brought low-code automation to public sector systems. [Krishna Munnaluru](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Krishna_Munnaluru_production_ready_mlops) (Oracle) built a VoIP monitoring pipeline on Kafka, Kubeflow and MLflow, [Manoj Kumar Vunnava](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Manoj_Kumar_Vunnava_scaling_conversational_ai) (GoDaddy) scaled conversational AI in contact centres, [Muruga Angamuthu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Muruga_Angamuthu_transforming_manufacturing_ai) (Techtronic Industries) covered predictive maintenance in manufacturing, and [Rajeev Chevuri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Rajeev_Chevuri_scaling_mlops_self) (Freddie Mac) built self-service ML platforms.

## Partners and where to watch

Thanks to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners who supported the event. Every talk is on the [Conf42 MLOps 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCyZXSIA8uy6Fq0cdcNfl4f) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025).

The series continues with [Conf42 MLOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2026).

Title: Turning fragile models into dependable systems
Description: Machine learning, sustained
Body:
# MLOps: where models meet reality

Training a model is the easy part.

Getting it into production, keeping it running, making sure it behaves, scales, stays secure, and doesn’t quietly ruin someone’s day at 3 AM? That’s the real job.

Conf42 MLOps 2025 is all about that gap between “it works on my notebook” and “this powers a real system”.

This conference digs into MLOps at scale. Trillion-parameter models, governed pipelines, self-healing infrastructure, automated deployments, and AI systems that need to run reliably across cloud, enterprise, and regulated environments. From healthcare and finance to telecom, manufacturing, and public sector platforms, these talks focus on production, not demos.

There’s a strong emphasis on automation and resilience. Cascading timeouts, failure recovery, self-service MLOps platforms, AI-driven code evolution, and pipelines that can survive real traffic and real users. Several sessions look at what happens when automation goes wrong, and what teams learned the hard way.

LLMs and generative AI are everywhere, of course. Training pipelines, inference platforms, agent-based systems, RAG architectures, and scaling conversational AI all make an appearance. Alongside that comes governance, ethics, security, and making sure models don’t leak data, drift silently, or surprise regulators.

Finance and healthcare get plenty of attention, with talks on fraud detection, risk modeling, clinical workflows, and responsible AI in highly regulated environments. These sessions show what MLOps looks like when the cost of failure is measured in more than just uptime.

If you’re responsible for turning machine learning into something stable, repeatable, and trustworthy, this one’s for you. MLOps is no longer optional. It’s the difference between promising models and systems people can actually rely on.

Title: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 - paved roads, self-healing and sane thresholds
Description: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 in review, 83 talks on developer platforms, SCM at 50K engineers, ML inference, self-healing infra, zero trust and thresholds.
Body:
[Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/platform2025) ran on September 4, 2025 with 83 talks, one of the biggest line-ups of the Conf42 year. The common thread: a platform is a product with internal customers, and its job is to remove decisions developers shouldn't have to make, whether that is which Git permissions to request, where an ML model gets served, or what the alert threshold should be. Engineers from Meta, Google, Microsoft, Qualcomm, eBay, Roku, Starbucks, Intuit, Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, JPMorgan Chase, Fidelity and AWS showed their versions.

## The platform is a product, and DevEx is the metric

[Vasdev Gullapalli](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Vasdev_Gullapalli_scm_git_policies) (Qualcomm) gave the clearest example of platform thinking applied to something most companies treat as plumbing: source control. Managing GitHub, GitLab and Gerrit for more than 50K engineers, his team treats SCM as a platform with governance built in. Licence activation, deactivation and reactivation are all self-serve and automated, because a developer waiting on a licence is a developer not writing code, and an unused licence is opex nobody wants.

[Anil Kumar Veldurthi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Anil_Kumar_Veldurthi_internal_ops_impact) (US Bank) covered how to build internal developer platforms that move delivery speed, and [Michel Murabito](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Michel_Murabito_practical_elevate_strategies) (Mia-Platform) focused on using AI in platform tooling to cut developer cognitive load. [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_developer_gitlab_level) (AWS) demoed GitLab with Amazon Q Developer for modernising legacy Java and generating merge requests and reviews. [Rajani Jayantha](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Rajani_Jayantha_monolith_microservices_decision) (Wayfair) offered a decision framework for the eternal microservices versus monolith argument, and [Jayant Tyagi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Jayant_Tyagi_development_ides_performance) (Salesforce) looked at cloud IDEs as a platform concern, security and performance included.

The most unexpected platform: design. [Pallav Laskar](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Pallav_Laskar_design_tokens_multi) (Zscaler) treats design tokens as infrastructure, run through GitOps workflows, with automated theming across platforms.

## Thresholds are maths, not vibes

[Emmanuel Bakare](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Emmanuel_Bakare_math_exploring_thresholds) (Twilio) gave the most quietly nerdy talk of the day. Static thresholds are easy to estimate and diagnose but noisy, single-variable and blind to organic growth. Dynamic ones adapt and produce fewer false positives, but need more data and a model of the system up front. He walks the numerical process for static thresholds step by step: filter outliers with IQR or z-scores, choose an aggregate, then reduce the error. If your alert thresholds were picked because a round number felt right, this one is for you.

## Self-healing is the new uptime

A whole cluster of talks tried to take humans out of the 3am loop. [Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Sureshkumar_Karuppuchamy_defense_dashboard_large) (eBay) went beyond dashboards to adaptive rate limiting, auto-rollbacks, circuit breakers and closed-loop pipelines for a high-scale listing platform. [Shailin Saraiya](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Shailin_Saraiya_cache_millions_latency) (Roku) described self-healing cache infrastructure built to scale with a fast-growing user base. [Konstantin Berezin](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Konstantin_Berezin_context_agents) (Rapyd) used AI agents to tag anomalies in logs and traces so engineers are paged only for the outliers that matter, and [Lakshmi Srinivasarao Kothamasu](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Lakshmi_Srinivasarao_Kothamasu_firefighting_manual_pipelines) (Fidelity Investments) applied the same thinking to self-healing data pipelines. [Ajay Averineni](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Ajay_Averineni_observability_healing_intelligent) (IBM) tied AI-driven observability to automated remediation.

## Platforms for ML, data and money

ML infrastructure is now a platform team's job. [Gangadharan Venkataraman](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Gangadharan_Venkataraman_inference_orchestration_kubernetes) (Starbucks) shared patterns for Kubernetes-native ML inference platforms that keep data scientists productive, drawing on production systems at Starbucks and eBay. [Bhaskar Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_container_paradise_chaos) (Google) went from container chaos to production-ready AI platforms, and [Peng Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Peng_Wang_workloads_oceanbase_powering) (OceanBase) ran many workloads, AI included, on one database on Kubernetes. [Srinivas Chennupati](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Chennupati_knowledge_rag_strategies) (Fannie Mae) treated production RAG as enterprise knowledge infrastructure.

Financial systems got a strong showing. [Tapan Vijay](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Tapan_Vijay_card_planet_resilience) (Meta) covered the distributed systems and zero-downtime strategies behind planet-scale card processing, [Karthickram Vailraj](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Karthickram_Vailraj_sharding_replication_database) (Charles Schwab) went into database sharding and replication for fintech, and [Tarun Chataraju](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Tarun_Chataraju_modernizing_fixed_index) (JPMorgan Chase) modernised fixed-income index systems cloud-native.

## Security and the network underneath

[Naveen Kumar Birru](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Naveen_Kumar_Birru_perimeters_zero_trust) (Palo Alto Networks) laid out zero trust at enterprise scale, [Naresh Yelkoti](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Naresh_Yelkoti_transforms_code_bulletproof) (U.S. Bank) made the case for security as code in the pipeline, and [Anjan Kaleru](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Anjan_Kaleru_governance_identity_secure) (Sony Interactive Entertainment) used data to drive identity governance.

Then there was the network trivia question you didn't know you had. [Srinivas Shamkura](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Shamkura_ditched_multicast_challenge) (SADA) explained why the big clouds don't offer native multicast: forwarding-state explosion in software-defined networks, a protocol designed for one administrative domain colliding with multi-tenancy, dynamic routing that is hard to automate, and packet processing costs in virtual environments that can eat the bandwidth savings. The radio-station analogy alone is worth the click.

## Where to watch

All 83 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/platform2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBMHyARfX-JY_7WHoF5qmDh). The series returns with [Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/platform2026).

Title: When developer experience becomes an engineering problem
Description: Platforms evolve
Body:
# Platforms: because glue code became a career

Platform engineering usually starts with good intentions.

“We’ll make this easier for teams.”  
“We’ll standardize things.”  
“We’ll reduce cognitive load.”

Next thing you know, you’re running dozens of services, managing policies across clouds, supporting AI workloads, and explaining to developers why the platform exists in the first place.

Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 is all about that reality.

This is a big conference. Seventy plus talks across architecture, APIs, automation, developer experience, security, reliability, AI, compliance, and transformation. If your job involves building internal platforms that other teams depend on, this one speaks directly to you.

AI is deeply woven into the program. Agentic platforms, self-healing infrastructure, anomaly detection, AI-driven CI/CD, and ML platforms at scale all show up. There are sessions on building AI platforms that actually deliver value, and others on keeping them reliable, observable, and secure once they hit production.

The use cases are very real. Financial systems processing massive volumes with low latency. Healthcare platforms operating under strict regulation. Smart cities, subscription payments, fraud detection, industrial IoT, and enterprise data platforms that move hundreds of terabytes a month. These are not toy examples.

Developer experience gets serious attention too. Talks cover internal developer platforms, cloud IDEs, unified Git policies, design systems as platform infrastructure, and using automation to reduce friction instead of adding more dashboards.

Security, compliance, and resilience are baked throughout. Zero trust, identity governance, multi-tenant platforms, regulated environments, and building systems that stay upright even as usage and complexity grow. Because platforms are only useful if people trust them.

If you’re building the foundations that everyone else stands on, this one’s for you. Platform engineering is hard, invisible work. At least here, you’ll be among people who get it.

Title: Conf42 Rustlang 2025: Rust leaves the systems niche
Description: Conf42 Rustlang 2025 roundup - Rust in data lakes, AWS Lambda, networks, 5G, factory vision, security pipelines and carbon-aware Kubernetes, in 27 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Rustlang 2025 ran online on August 21, 2025, with 27 talks, and the striking thing was who gave them. Very few speakers were compiler hackers or crate maintainers; most were data engineers, network engineers, security engineers, and architects at banks, carmakers, telcos, and retailers, explaining why Rust ended up in their production stack. The borrow checker has clearly left the systems programming niche and found a job in the enterprise.

All sessions are on the [Conf42 Rustlang 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBMebMWQQ03iUNjed9luMsp).

## Rust under the data stack

Data infrastructure was the most convincing track. [Rahul Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Rahul_Joshi_memory_rust_tech), a Distinguished Data Engineer at Capital One, walked through three eras of enterprise data: on-prem Hadoop with its JVM garbage collection and memory overheads, cloud warehouses like Snowflake and Redshift, and today's lakehouses built on open formats with storage separated from compute. His argument is that Rust, through projects like Apache Arrow and DataFusion, has become a critical piece of that third era because it offers memory safety without a garbage collector.

[Venkata Appalapuram](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Venkata_Appalapuram_systems_architecture_ai) of Ritepros gave the most transferable talk for library authors. Starting from a Spark JMS connector built at Capital One to read from ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, and Amazon SQS, he mapped JVM library patterns to Rust crate design: provider interfaces become traits, exception handling becomes `Result`, plus testing and documentation strategies that work across both ecosystems.

[Narendra Reddy Mudiyala](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Narendra_Reddy_Mudiyala_memory_safety_systems) of Accenture applied Rust to data mesh, and [Ritesh Kumar Sinha](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Ritesh_Kumar_Sinha_memory_safety_zero) of Kotak Mahindra Bank to large-scale pipelines for climate data.

## Rust in the cloud

[Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_aws_cloud_scale), a Software Development Engineer at Amazon, gave a practical tour of the AWS SDK for Rust. His comparison is a fair one: Go is strong on Lambda but carries a bigger runtime, Java has the ecosystem but pays for cold starts and memory, Python wins at prototyping but slows at scale. Rust's small binaries mean faster Lambda cold starts, and with Tokio you can run thousands of async calls to AWS services.

[Bandhavi Sakhamuri](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Bandhavi_Sakhamuri_cloud_ai_rust), a Senior SRE at SolarWinds, built a carbon-aware Kubernetes scheduler in Rust. Default schedulers weigh performance and availability but not where the electricity comes from; the framework adds that signal, whether you run on EKS, AKS, or GKE. [Uday Kiran Yedluri](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Uday_Kiran_Yedluri_cloud_security_rust) covered Rust across multi-cloud enterprise environments, and [Karthik Mohan Muralidharan](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Karthik_Mohan_Muralidharan_edge_cloud_divide) of Walmart Global Tech looked at orchestration patterns between the edge and the cloud.

## Packets, radios and robots

Rust's home turf, low-latency systems, still had a strong showing. [Rahul Tavva](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Rahul_Tavva_memory_code_zero) of Kairos Technologies covered zero-copy packet processing and async routing, [Prasanth Kosaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prasanth_Kosaraju_memory_safety_systems) of Dataquest applied Rust to network infrastructure in educational and industrial settings, and [Riddhi Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Riddhi_Patel_memory_safety_zero) of DRC System explored how the ownership model fits ultra-low-latency 5G systems. [Venu Madhav Nadella](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Venu_Madhav_Nadella_memory_safety_zero) of Spectrum moved telecom operations from reactive to predictive.

On the factory floor, [Sankar Subramanian](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sankar_Subramanian_memory_safety_zero), a Staff Engineer at Lucid Motors with over 20 years in control and automation, showed zero-copy machine vision pipelines for spotting battery defects in EV manufacturing. [Anushree Nagvekar](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_edge_memory_safety) of AEye looked at edge AI for autonomous vehicles, where zero-cost abstractions and memory safety both matter.

## When a crash is not an option

Several talks made the safety argument where it hits hardest. [Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Lakshmi_Vara_Prasad_Adusumilli_memory_safety_systems) of Conduent started from a blunt premise, that when 911 systems crash, people die, and showed compile-time guarantees in emergency response systems. [Raphael Shobi Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Raphael_Shobi_Thomas_memory_safety_code) covered a healthcare and travel safety platform for seniors, and [Prabhakar Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prabhakar_Singh_memory_safety_systems) of Meta built real-time fraud prevention for gig platforms.

Security engineers had their say too. [Naresh Yelkoti](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Naresh_Yelkoti_memory_security_cloud) of U.S. Bank built security scanning pipelines in Rust, [Sachin Kapoor](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sachin_Kapoor_memory_security_safety) walked through zero trust fundamentals implemented in Rust, and [Ketankumar Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Ketankumar_Patel_memory_safety_zero) of Wind River proposed a framework for ethical AI in Rust.

## Agents, dashboards and business systems

Rust for AI agents appeared too. [Sidhanta Panigrahy](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sidhanta_Panigrahy_memory_safety_zero) of Okta built a Tokio-based multi-agent system, and [Sarat Piridi](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sarat_Piridi_agents_zero_systems) of Hanwha Qcells covered Rust-powered process automation across industries. Dashboards got two takes: [Tashi Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Tashi_Garg_cloud_ai_rust) of Juniper Networks on dynamic UIs for cloud infrastructure, and [Shahzeb Akhtar](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Shahzeb_Akhtar_memory_security_rust) of UnitedLex on business intelligence.

The business-systems corner rounded it out: [Swetha Priya Sathiyam](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Swetha_Priya_Sathiyam_systems_memory_code) of ADP on HR tech, [Nageswara Rao Nelloru](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Nageswara_Rao_Nelloru_memory_ai_zero) on claims management APIs, and [Shikha Duttyal](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Shikha_Duttyal_ml_ai_rust) of Meta on digital twins for supply chains.

## Partners and what's next

Conf42 Rustlang 2025 was supported by the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners listed on the event page.

For more, the earlier editions are still online, starting with [Conf42 Rustlang 2024](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2024). Fair warning: you may come out wanting to rewrite something.
