Title: Low-level control, high-level guarantees
Description: Rust changes expectations
Body:
# Rust: safe, fast, and somehow everywhere

Rust has a reputation.

Memory safety. Performance. Fearless concurrency. A compiler that cares deeply about your life choices. Naturally, it’s now being used to build some of the most intense systems out there.

Conf42 Rustlang 2025 is a showcase of exactly that.

This conference goes all in on real-world Rust. Ultra-low latency 5G systems, high-performance cloud platforms, data lakes, data meshes, financial APIs, and mission-critical emergency response systems all show up. If it needs to be fast, correct, and not crash at the worst possible moment, Rust is probably involved.

Cloud, data, and infrastructure get plenty of attention. From Rust on AWS and multi-cloud environments to edge cloud orchestration and distributed systems, the talks focus on how Rust is being used to replace bottlenecks and simplify complexity without sacrificing performance.

AI is everywhere too. Rust-powered machine vision, edge AI, predictive telecom systems, fraud prevention, multi-agent AI platforms, and ethical AI frameworks all make an appearance. It’s less about hype and more about building systems that need to run fast, safely, and continuously.

Security and regulation are a big theme. Zero trust architectures, DevSecOps pipelines, secure networking, regulatory environments, and memory-safe security tooling all feature heavily. Rust’s guarantees are put to work where mistakes are expensive and downtime is not an option.

You’ll also find plenty of Rust fundamentals in action. Concurrency patterns, cross-language libraries, zero-copy networking, performance tuning, and designing systems that stay maintainable as they scale.

If you like building serious systems and sleeping slightly better because the compiler has your back, this one’s for you. Rust isn’t just a language choice anymore. It’s an architectural one.

Title: Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: hybrid sidecars, cloud QPUs and PQC
Description: Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 roundup: 19 talks on preparing architecture and cryptography, cloud quantum services, hybrid sidecars and finance use cases.
Body:
Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 ran on June 19, 2025, with 19 talks and a useful tension between them. Some speakers treated quantum advantage as a business plan for this year; the most practical ones treated it as an engineering problem: wrap a small, noisy quantum core in classical systems you already run, and get your architecture and cryptography ready before the hardware forces the issue. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/quantum2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDLJsZ2QLy2_0A5YjP6CaRq).

## Get ready before the hardware is

[Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Laxmikanth_Mukund_Sethu_Kumar_classical_quantum_enterprise), Executive Director at JPMorgan Chase, gave the most grounded framing of the day. Quantum isn't production-ready for every enterprise use case, he said, but architects can lay groundwork now with patterns they already know: event-driven design, hybrid orchestration and API-driven interfaces that a quantum service could slot into later. He drew on platforms he has designed for banks, airlines and government systems, and kept the quantum mechanics to a minimum.

The cryptography side got its own warning. [Pavan Nutalapati](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pavan_Nutalapati_quantum_cloud_security) laid out how quantum computing threatens today's encryption in the cloud, the emerging standards, and how to build a quantum-safe strategy. [Sarah Choudhary](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Sarah_Choudhary_quantum_algorithms_problem) covered the algorithms behind the cryptography and optimisation headlines for anyone who wants to know what the machines would actually run.

## Quantum arrives as a cloud service

Most engineers will meet quantum hardware through an API. [Naga Murali Krishna Koneru](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Naga_Murali_Krishna_Koneru_cloud_aws) of Hexaware Technologies walked through Amazon Braket and hybrid quantum-classical workflows on AWS. [Srinivas Sriram Mantrala](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Srinivas_Sriram_Mantrala_quantum_cloudops_devops) explored what quantum-enhanced DevOps and hybrid cloud integration could look like, and [Srikar Kompella](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Srikar_Kompella_quantum_saas_architecture) of Twilio looked at multi-tenant SaaS architecture where quantum and edge processing meet.

Then [Denish Tomar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Denish_Tomar_quantum_cloud_qum) of Qumulus asked the question nobody else did: who is going to understand the bill? He opened with a founder whose usual monthly cloud spend jumped several times over because an autoscaling setting sent a cluster to 50 servers instead of five, for three days instead of two hours. If we can't predict classical cloud costs, he argued, usage-based pricing for quantum will be worse, and bundled, predictable resource models are the way out. The only quantum talk of the year where the scariest number was on an invoice.

## Hybrid sidecars and research tooling

Two talks showed what a sensible first step looks like. [Pradeep Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pradeep_Karanam_plm_teamcenter) of Facebook described a small sidecar for Siemens Teamcenter, the product lifecycle management system, that sends only the hardest part of a "what if" question about product options or purchase plans to a cloud quantum computer. Everyone's daily workflow stays the same, and the classical system does everything else. He also explained why today's noisy machines are always wrapped in classical code.

[Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_low_code_experimentation) of Amazon tackled the research side with a schema-driven approach: one JSON schema, stored versioned and immutable, generates a React control panel, a serverless Step Functions workflow that runs and post-processes circuits, and a lineage tracker that tags every run. Researchers edit a manifest instead of copying notebooks, and the audit trail comes for free.

## Finance wants to go first

Financial services supplied the most use cases, and the most optimism. [Nikhil Kassetty](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Nikhil_Kassetty_quantum_payments_latency) of Intuit looked at how quantum could affect real-time payments, fraud detection and settlement, based on emerging pilots and experiments. [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_finance_optimization) of JPMorganChase covered data engineering for quantum-enhanced personalisation, and [Siva Prakash](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Siva_Prakash_quantum_data_streaming) and [Ganesh Marimuthu](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Ganesh_Marimuthu_quantum_trading_systems) took on streaming feature stores and trading systems. [Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Sai_Kaushik_Ponnekanti_quantum_business_value) of Meta argued that business value is available in the NISQ era already, with today's noisy machines.

## Edge and IoT

Two speakers pushed quantum toward the edge. [Anushree Nagvekar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_quantum_edge_ai) of AEye presented a hybrid quantum-classical architecture for embedded edge AI, and [Gayathri Jeganmohan](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Gayathri_Jeganmohan_quantum_iot_security) of Microsoft looked at what quantum means for IoT security and optimisation as device counts keep climbing.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), our gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 19 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/quantum2025). Next on the Conf42 calendar is [Conf42 Rustlang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2025) on August 21, a good place to rewrite your classical half in something memory-safe while the qubits settle down.

Title: Where bits become possibilities
Description: And math bends reality
Body:
# Quantum computing, but make it real

Quantum computing has a reputation.

It’s mysterious. It’s powerful. It’s either “the future of everything” or “not ready yet”, depending on who you ask and how much coffee they’ve had.

Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 lives right in that tension.

This conference brings quantum out of the abstract and into real systems. There are talks on quantum algorithms, hybrid quantum classical architectures, and what it actually means to run quantum workloads alongside the cloud platforms we already depend on.

AI and data play a big role. You’ll hear about quantum-enhanced edge AI, personalization in finance, real-time data engineering, and how quantum techniques could reshape optimization, machine learning, and decision-making at scale. Not someday. Actively being explored now.

Security and infrastructure show up early and often. Quantum-safe cryptography, cloud security, DevOps for quantum systems, and preparing enterprise architectures for a post-quantum world are all on the agenda. Because when encryption changes, everything else has to change with it.

The use cases are surprisingly practical. Finance, supply chains, IoT, SaaS platforms, storage systems, and enterprise data architectures all make appearances. From shaving microseconds off payments to rethinking how data moves and is protected, these sessions focus on where quantum could deliver real advantage first.

If quantum computing has ever felt too distant, too theoretical, or too confusing to engage with, this one’s for you. No hype. No hand-waving. Just a clear look at how quantum is starting to plug into the systems we already build and run.

Title: Conf42 Observability 2025 roundup: instrument, tame OTel, cut costs
Description: Conf42 Observability 2025 in review, from config-driven instrumentation and eBPF to honest OpenTelemetry lessons, smaller bills, Kafka signals and identity.
Body:
Auto-instrumentation gets you about 80% of the way; the last 20% is manual work, and at Wave, Jean-Mark Wright estimated it at roughly ten years of it. That is where his talk title, "Instrumenting at 10 years per second", comes from, and it set up the main tension of [Conf42 Observability 2025](https://www.conf42.com/obs2025): teams want deeper telemetry, and they want to spend less effort and less money getting it. With 61 talks streamed online on June 5, 2025, it was one of the largest Conf42 events of the year, with speakers from Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Meta, Salesforce, Confluent, Adobe, WSO2, Palo Alto Networks, AT&T and Telstra.

## Better instrumentation for less effort

[Jean-Mark Wright](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_JeanMark_Wright_instrumenting_second_months) (Wave) opened with an on-call story: the system was quietly giving a premium feature, bank transaction import, to customers who hadn't paid for it, and only detailed manual instrumentation made the cause findable. His team's answer is Config-Accelerated Custom Instrumentation, which captures telemetry from function inputs through configuration instead of hand-written spans.

[Isala Piyarisi and Nilushan Costa](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Isala_Piyarisi_Nilushan_Costa_fluent_opensearch_zero) (WSO2) went further and rebuilt their platform's observability on Fluent Bit, OpenSearch and Prometheus with zero-instrumentation telemetry via eBPF, reporting log latency under five seconds and large cost savings. If you want to write the eBPF yourself, [Sooter Saalu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sooter_Saalu_writing_programs_ebpf) (Draft.dev) covered custom programs for tracing syscalls and profiling latency. [Divya Darshana](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Divya_Darshana_clarity_gofr_grpc) showed how the open source Go framework GoFr builds tracing, logging and metrics into gRPC services, and [Dharmendra Ahuja](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Dharmendra_Ahuja_fluent_eks_aws) walked through Fluent Bit on EKS.

## OpenTelemetry, with the caveats left in

Two talks gave OpenTelemetry an honest review. [Narendra Reddy Sanikommu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Narendra_Reddy_Sanikommu_opentelemetry_messy_problems) (NVIDIA) credited it with removing vendor lock-in and unifying OpenTracing and OpenCensus into one standard across languages, then spent the rest of the talk on the new problems it creates and how to tame them. [Meletius Mgbeodichimma Igbokwe](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Meletius_Mgbeodichimma_Igbokwe_lessons_field_bullet) collected field lessons from teams that tried to make it work in production. Between them you get a realistic adoption plan, not a brochure. [Vignesh Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vignesh_Iyer_lightweight_teams_system) (NVIDIA) added an open source pipeline for lean teams, and [Neel Shah](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Neel_Shah_logs_metrics_traces) (Middleware) looked at what comes after the three pillars.

## The bill is an observability signal too

Cost had its own track in all but name. [Aritra Ghosh](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Aritra_Ghosh_shrinking_kubernetes_cost) (Microsoft) shared techniques to cut Kubernetes monitoring spend without losing visibility, and [Venkata Madhu Prateek Reddy Kambala](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Venkata_Madhu_Prateek_Reddy_Kambala_logging_cost_cutting) (Synapsis) traced rising logging bills to their root causes. [Yury Nino](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Yury_Nino_series_cost_anomalies) (Google) turned the problem around, running time series analysis on logs to catch billing anomalies before the invoice does. [Denish Tomar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Denish_Tomar_dashboards_clouds_fun) (Qumulus) argued for fixed-cost infrastructure so dashboards stop being a monthly surprise, and [Ganeshkumar Palanisamy](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ganeshkumar_Palanisamy_platforms_scale_finops) (Reltio) combined AIOps with FinOps on multi-cloud data platforms.

## Find the signals that matter in your system

The most reusable talks picked one kind of system and asked which signals actually matter. [Abhishek Walia](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Abhishek_Walia_kafka_visibility_scale) (Confluent) pointed out that Kafka doesn't fail cleanly; it stalls and lags, so you need the few signals that catch that early. [Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_aws_serverless_workflows) (Amazon) tackled Step Functions fan-outs that launch thousands of Lambdas, streaming telemetry into a graph neural network to spot hot branches. [Sudeep Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sudeep_Kumar_traces_user_synthetic) (Salesforce) aggregated synthetic traces into critical user journeys, and [Palak Bhawsar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Palak_Bhawsar_synthetic_monitoring_outage) (Telstra) made the case for synthetic monitoring that catches the outage while you sleep.

Data and frontend teams got their turn. [Chaitanya Reddy Krishnama](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Chaitanya_Reddy_Krishnama_dashboards_qa_nightmares) (MoneyGram) described dashboards that looked great until they started lying because of silent pipeline failures and schema drift. [Vadim Tsaregorodtsev](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vadim_Tsaregorodtsev_passport_frontend_navigating) (ETG) gave every frontend project an Observability Passport linking its logs, Sentry and security tools. [Alexandru Hang](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Alexandru_Hang_logs_behaviour_experience) (ING Tech Romania) used activity logs to predict what users will do next and prefetch assets. [Ashwin Das Gururaja and Devang Gaur](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ashwin_Das_Gururaja_Devang_Gaur_dashboard_payment_commerce) (Adobe) covered end-to-end observability for checkout and payments.

## Identity and security belong in the telemetry

[Cynthia Akiotu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Cynthia_Akiotu_identity_access_breach) (Tesco Bank) argued that most observability ignores who is doing what, and that privilege misuse and insider threats only show up when identity is part of the picture. [Srikanth Potla](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Srikanth_Potla_modeling_insight_spots) (SoFi) threat-modelled the observability stack itself, since logs, metrics and traces leak too. [Krishna Ganeriwal](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Krishna_Ganeriwal_privacy_infrastructure) (Meta) looked at observability for privacy infrastructure, [Chintan Udeshi](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Chintan_Udeshi_edge_realtime_security) (Palo Alto Networks) at edge security monitoring, and [Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Onyebuchi_Mark_Irozuru_signatures_observability_federated) (Botanixlabs) at monitoring federated multisig node operators with Grafana Alloy.

## Further afield

Observability ideas also travelled: AI-assisted pipelines to reduce noise and MTTR at Informatica ([Kirti Ranjan Parida and Sarav Jagadeesan](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Kirti_Ranjan_Parida_Sarav_Jagadeesan_mttr_pipelines_reduce)), generative models on Amazon Bedrock ([Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Hazel_Andrea_Saenz_Giron_serverless_bedrock_generative), Caylent), aircraft digital twins ([Divakar Duraiyan](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Divakar_Duraiyan_aircraft_digital_twins), TCS), and event-driven collaboration between electronic and mechanical hardware design teams ([Pradeep Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Pradeep_Karanam_ecad_mcad)). For something different, [Anastasiia Zvenigorodskaia](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Anastasiia_Zvenigorodskaia_opensource_profitable_making) (Epicmax) talked about making open source profitable.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Observability 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDEJMKwPJN2wRgGdf8sIpnn) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/obs2025).

The series continued with [Conf42 Observability 2026](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026).

Title: When metrics, logs, and traces tell a story
Description: Insight follows
Body:
# You can’t fix what you can’t see (and sometimes you still can’t)

Observability always sounds straightforward.

Collect some logs. Add a few metrics. Throw in traces. Build a dashboard. Feel accomplished.

And then production happens.

Conf42 Observability 2025 is for everyone who has stared at a perfectly green dashboard while users were very clearly not having a good time.

This conference goes deep into what observability actually looks like in modern systems. Distributed architectures, serverless workflows, event-driven platforms, cloud-native everything, and systems that span multiple clouds, regions, and teams. There are talks on logs, metrics, traces, telemetry, and what to do when all of them still leave blind spots.

AI shows up everywhere. AI-powered anomaly detection, cost analysis, AIOps, predictive monitoring, and observability for ML systems themselves. Some sessions focus on catching issues earlier. Others focus on reducing noise, cutting observability bills, and figuring out which signals actually matter at 3 AM.

Identity, security, and trust are big themes too. From observable identity systems and threat modeling to monitoring access patterns and preventing breaches before they happen, observability is treated as a security concern, not just an ops one.

The use cases go wide. Finance, healthcare, telecom, retail, public sector, e-commerce, and high-frequency systems all make an appearance. You’ll hear about Kafka at scale, OpenTelemetry in the real world, synthetic monitoring, edge observability, and what happens when your monitoring strategy grows faster than your infrastructure.

If you’ve ever asked “why didn’t we see this sooner” or “why is this alert firing again”, this one’s for you. Observability isn’t about having more data. It’s about finally understanding what your systems are trying to tell you.

Title: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 - when "don't" means nothing to your embeddings
Description: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 in review, 136 talks on embedding blind spots, LLM evaluation, tiny models, agents, guardrails and ML in finance and health.
Body:
[Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) went out on May 8, 2025 with 136 talks, enough to fill a long weekend of viewing. Under the volume sat a sensible mood: less awe at what models can do, more scrutiny of where they quietly fail and what it takes to run them somewhere real. Speakers came from Google DeepMind, Microsoft, Meta, AWS, NVIDIA, Dropbox, Samsung Research, Expedia Group, Palo Alto Networks, Walmart, JPMorgan Chase and many more.

## Your model is more confident than it should be

The talk most likely to change how you build RAG came from [Ritesh Modi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Ritesh_Modi_embedding_models_language) (Microsoft). In *Hallucination by Design* he shows test results where embedding models treat "take medication" and "don't take medication" as the same thing, then walks through the patterns that cause it and how to make GenAI systems more reliable anyway. Negation, it turns out, is a rounding error in vector space.

[Alok Ranjan and Saurabh Suman](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alok_Ranjan_Saurabh_Suman_modern_approaches_bleu) (Dropbox, San José State University) argued that BLEU and ROUGE can't measure what modern LLMs do, and moved through benchmarks like MMLU and TruthfulQA to real-world and human-in-the-loop evaluation. [Andrei Stroganov and Andrei Visochan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_Andrei_Visochan_estimation_regression_confidence) (Samsung Research) took the mathematical route: fast, real-time confidence estimation for classification and regression models using C++ compile-time numerical integration. [Gaurav Bansal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Gaurav_Bansal_evaluation_enterprise_language) covered scalable evaluation and QA for enterprise LLMs.

## Small models, tight budgets

Not every model gets an H100. [Max Navrotsky and Oleksandr Gordieiev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Max_Navrotsky_Oleksandr_Gordieiev_llms_optimization_devices) (VGS, Lutsk National Technical University) shrank GPT-2 for very weak hardware with pruning, quantisation and fine-tuning. [Hitesh Saai Mananchery](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Hitesh_Saai_Mananchery_compression_pixel_video) (Expedia Group) presented R2S, an ML approach to video compression that removes frame redundancy by tracking pixel shifts. At the other end of the scale, [Praneel Madabushini](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Praneel_Madabushini_tesla_openai) (NVIDIA) looked at how Kubernetes handles resource-hungry AI and ML workloads, with lessons drawn from Tesla and OpenAI, and [Bhaskar Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_enterprise_cloud_patterns) (Google) covered architectural patterns for cloud-native AI at scale.

## Agents, with and without guardrails

[Naman Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Naman_Goyal_generation_text_agentic) (Google DeepMind) traced the move from passive text generators to agents that make decisions and act on their environment. [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_code_agents_coding) (Zencoder) got practical about AI coding agents and how to build them, and [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_chatbots_bedrock_enterprise) (AWS) showed Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrating enterprise workflows with access to business data and APIs. [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_guardrails_responsible_bedrock) (AWS) followed with the brakes: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for responsible AI. [Laly Bar-Ilan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Laly_BarIlan_language_components_understand) (Bit) proposed composable components as the shared language between developers, non-technical teams and AI, so an agent can build features from product intent while humans stay in the loop.

For anyone still fuzzy on the basics, [Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector) (AWS) gave a good first talk on vector embeddings and RAG, and [Sergey Polyashov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sergey_Polyashov_recommendation_search_scalable) (Microsoft) did the same for search and recommendation systems, trade-offs and pitfalls included.

## ML where mistakes have consequences

Trust and safety got serious treatment. [Georgina Tryfou](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Georgina_Tryfou_moderation_scalable_safety) (Gcore) described an AI system for detecting and moderating harmful content such as CSAM in near real time, with privacy built into the design. [Lianne Potter](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Lianne_Potter_bias_builders_history) (Compromising Positions) went back to the early builders of AI to show how their choices about bias and power still shape what we build. [Arun Vivek Supramanian](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_privacy_engineering_ethical) (Amazon) covered privacy, bias and fairness from the data engineering side.

Finance and healthcare filled whole tracks. Highlights include [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_fraud_detection_db_graph) (JPMorganChase) on graph databases for fraud detection, [Surendra Lakkaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Surendra_Lakkaraju_ecommerce_fraud) (Amazon) on real-time e-commerce fraud detection, [Sandeep Gourneni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sandeep_Gourneni_banking_optimization) (Hitachi Digital Services) on LLM-assisted legacy banking code transformation, and [Sachin Telalwar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sachin_Telalwar_compliance_healthcare) (Zocdoc) on secure distributed healthcare systems.

## ML out in the world

Some of the most memorable talks left the data centre. [Aroma Rodrigues](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Aroma_Rodrigues_imagination_source_journey) (Microsoft) told the story of an open source journey that began in 2016 with a shoe for visually impaired people, built from an Arduino, an Android phone and an unreasonable amount of optimism. [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Dmytro_Hlotenko_photography_community_serverless) (APA-IT) processed 8,000 event photos in real time on AWS AI and serverless at Community Day DACH 2024, sorting them and delivering them back to the community. [Avraam Tolmidis](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Avraam_Tolmidis_traffic_smart_systems) (Meta) applied multi-agent systems and predictive optimisation to urban traffic, and [Karthikeyan Rajamani](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Karthikeyan_Rajamani_iot_accoustic_analysis) (Thomson Reuters) listened to machines, literally, with IoT acoustic analysis for predictive maintenance.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) at Gold and [APA Tech](https://apa.at/about/apa-tech/) at Silver. All 136 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbH1VBaoA60lLAAVqmiLPe). Start with Modi's embedding tests; you will look at your retrieval results differently afterwards.

The series returns with [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026).

Title: Teaching machines to recognize the unseen
Description: Prediction in motion
Body:
# Machine learning is doing… a lot

Machine learning used to be a niche.

Now it’s everywhere. Finance, healthcare, retail, cloud, security, HR, supply chains, marketing, manufacturing, smart cities, and probably something involving your fridge. Subtle.

Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 leans fully into that scale.

This is a big conference. One hundred plus talks across twenty tracks, covering everything from core ML concepts to full-blown AI systems running in production. You’ll find sessions on agents, generative AI, analytics, architecture, cloud, data engineering, security, testing, and the slightly terrifying joy of putting models where real decisions are made.

There’s a strong focus on real-world ML. Fraud detection at scale, healthcare platforms, financial risk modeling, recommendation systems, supply chain forecasting, and enterprise data pipelines all show up. Less “look what the model can do” and more “here’s how we made this work without breaking everything”.

Generative AI and LLMs are everywhere, of course. Evaluation, hallucinations, embeddings, RAG, agents, optimization, and running models on everything from massive clusters to very small devices. Several talks focus on keeping things safe, explainable, and compliant once the hype wears off.

The program also makes room for the human side of ML. Ethics, bias, accessibility, trust, governance, and what happens when AI systems start influencing people, products, and policies at scale. There are talks that zoom out, and others that go deep into very specific problems.

If machine learning is part of your job, your roadmap, or your long-term existential questions, this one’s for you. It’s broad, practical, and very honest about the fact that ML is no longer optional or simple.

Welcome to the mess.

Title: Conf42 SRE 2025: postmortems, pit stops and SLOs over alerts
Description: Conf42 SRE 2025 roundup - postmortem lessons from reality TV and Formula 1, SLOs against alert fatigue, databases without DBAs, and AI in incident response.
Body:
Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025 ran online on April 17, 2025, with 107 talks, one of the largest lineups Conf42 has run. With that many sessions, the tracks covered almost everything that can page you: observability, SLOs, resilience, databases, cloud, fintech, healthcare, and a growing pile of AI. The talks worth starting with, though, were the ones about people: how teams review incidents, decide what deserves an alert, and stay curious about their systems.

Every session is on the [Conf42 SRE 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCu4WV3_Ve7-ChGVhr_-DbU). Below is a guided path through it.

## Incident reviews, from unexpected teachers

[Paige Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Paige_Cruz_what_real_housewives), Principal Developer Advocate at Chronosphere, gave the most quotable title of the event: what The Real Housewives taught her about postmortem meetings. Bringing "receipts" and holding "the meeting before the meeting" turn out to be useful habits for structured, blame-aware incident reviews. It is funnier than most postmortems and more useful than most postmortem templates.

[Ricardo Castro](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Ricardo_Castro_what_can_we), Principal Engineer and SRE at FanDuel, found his teacher in Formula 1: the race where Red Bull Racing repaired Max Verstappen's car in Hungary and turned a potential disaster into a podium finish. The talk pulls out the incident management lessons that apply when your outage has no pit wall.

[Saurabh Phaltane](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Saurabh_Phaltane_curious_sre_cultivating), a Senior SRE at Google, argued for curiosity as the core SRE skill, balancing breadth and depth and thinking about the system as a whole. [Shaalmali Raychaudhury](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Shaalmali_Raychaudhury_navigating_sre_incident) of PayPal and [Pradeep Gaddamidi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_deployments_downtime_unexpected) added practitioner stories about incident management and deploy-day fires.

## Alert on what users feel

[Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue), DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, took on alert fatigue with SLOs: metrics centred on the user experience give teams a focus, and give them permission to disable alerts that contribute nothing to customer happiness. [Siddharth Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Siddharth_Joshi_reliability_excellence_slo) of Nagarro covered the tooling side of SLO management, and [Gaurav Mittal](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Gaurav_Mittal_slos_failute_prediction) of Nordstrom went beyond SLOs to anomaly detection, finding the signals hidden in your data before they become outages.

[Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Veliswa_Boya_application_resilience_whose), Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, asked whose job application resilience is anyway, and how resilience and innovation can coexist through both culture and technical choices. [Sai Sahiti Nemalikanti](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_Sahiti_Nemalikanti_designing_failure_using) of AWS followed with patterns for designing for failure.

## Observability you can actually use

[Alok Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Alok_Ranjan_fragmented_logs_unified), an Engineering Manager at Dropbox, told the story of unifying fragmented container logs with open-source tools, along with what it taught him about DevOps culture. [Swapnil Kulkarni](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Swapnil_Kulkarni_observe_or_not) of Kloudfuse reframed the debate: whether to observe is not the question; whether observability solves the right use cases is. [Sai KR Pentaparthi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_KR_Pentaparthi_xray_ebpf_o11y) showed eBPF for network-level visibility in cloud-native systems, and [Mohit Menghnani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mohit_Menghnani_unlocking_observability_react) of Twilio brought observability to React and Node.js applications.

## Databases without a DBA

[Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Renato_Losio_things_fall_apart), Principal Cloud Architect at Funambol, shared a decade of running managed production databases without DBA expertise, from crashing managed instances to storage costs that grew far faster than planned, plus a warning about trusting benchmarks. [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_amazon_aurora_dsql), Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, introduced Amazon Aurora DSQL, a serverless distributed SQL database with active-active availability. [Andrei Manakov](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Andrei_Manakov_tradeoffs_distributed_nosql) of ShareChat walked through the real-world CAP trade-offs in distributed NoSQL design.

## Real-time systems with no second chances

Some talks dealt with systems where reliability is not abstract. [Vlad Onetiu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Vlad_Onetiu_serverless_confluent_kafka) of DataIceberg built a real-time earthquake alert system with Lambda functions and Confluent Kafka that checks for event changes every second and sends SMS and email notifications. [Bhushan Gopala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Bhushan_Gopala_Reddy_resilient_health_monitoring) of Aruba Networks engineered Bluetooth Low Energy health monitoring for disaster zones. [Srihari Pakalapati](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Srihari_Pakalapati_ransomware_readiness_backup) of Trader Interactive covered ransomware readiness with immutable backups and automated recovery, and [Payal Godhani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Payal_Godhani_zero_downtime_ml) of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure applied SRE techniques to zero-downtime ML deployments.

## AI on call

AI was everywhere, and the most practical uses were small. [David Asamu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_David_Asamu_ai_sre_prometheus_nl), who leads the SRE team at Nomba, started from a wish every on-call engineer has had: "What if you could chat with your monitoring metrics?" The talk shows asking Prometheus questions in natural language instead of writing queries mid-incident. [Smita Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Smita_Verma_alerts_action_building) of Adobe built AI-powered autonomous incident response at scale, and [Rahul Amte](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Rahul_Amte_smarter_failure_testing) of Nivid Technologies combined AI with chaos engineering for smarter failure testing. [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Peter_De_Tender_azure_load_testing) of Microsoft kept it grounded with a hands-on tour of Azure Load Testing.

Beyond these, the lineup ran deep into fintech, healthcare, insurance, and manufacturing reliability, with dozens more case studies on the event page.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), gold sponsor [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continued with [Conf42 SRE 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) and returns as [Conf42 SRE 2027](https://www.conf42.com/sre2027) on March 4, 2027.
Author: Conf42

Title: When availability becomes a feature
Description: SRE makes it measurable
Body:
# Reliability is everyone’s job (but somehow also yours)

Site Reliability Engineering sounds calm and responsible.

In practice, it’s alerts at odd hours, dashboards you don’t fully trust, postmortems that could have been emails, and a deep, personal relationship with latency. Still, someone has to keep the lights on.

Conf42 SRE 2025 is for the people doing exactly that.

This is a big one. One hundred talks across reliability, observability, incidents, automation, architecture, security, cloud, data, AI, healthcare, fintech, hardware, and just about every place where failure is not an option. If a system needs to stay up, it probably shows up here.

AI plays a starring role. From self-healing infrastructure and anomaly detection to AI-assisted monitoring, chaos engineering, and SRE practices for ML systems, the program digs into how automation is changing reliability work. Sometimes for the better. Sometimes with new things to worry about.

But SRE isn’t just about tools. There are talks on culture, postmortems, ownership, accessibility, inclusion, and the very human side of running complex systems. You’ll hear about quiet engineers, impostor syndrome, and what reliability looks like across different organizations and industries.

The real-world use cases go deep. Healthcare platforms, financial systems, gaming infrastructure, supply chains, cloud migrations, legacy modernization, and systems operating at global scale all make an appearance. From sub-50ms architectures to multi-cloud resilience, this is SRE in production, not theory.

If your job involves preventing outages, responding to incidents, or explaining why five nines is harder than it sounds, this one’s for you. Reliability is a moving target. At least here, you don’t have to chase it alone.

Title: Conf42 Golang 2025: real dependencies in tests, hidden ones in go.mod
Description: Conf42 Golang 2025 roundup: 64 talks on testing Go services, dependency hygiene, Wasm and eBPF, confidential computing and Go in banking and fintech.
Body:
Conf42 Golang 2025 ran on April 3, 2025, with 64 talks, the biggest lineup of any Conf42 Golang so far, under the usual greeting to the gophers from outer space. Two ideas kept coming back: test against real dependencies instead of mocks, and know exactly which dependencies you're carrying. Around them, Go showed up at the edge, in the kernel, inside secure enclaves and in a lot of banks. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbxTLhVidTfS-6lJeAH6m-).

## Test against the real thing

Two talks made the same argument from different directions. [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed a talk-rating service tested against real Postgres, Redis and Redpanda containers, plus an AWS Lambda running inside LocalStack. He then broke the average calculation on purpose and watched the test catch it in seconds. His tour of wait strategies is a good reason never to write `time.Sleep` in a test again.

[Nikolay Kuznetsov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Nikolay_Kuznetsov_testing_go_services) of Zalando gave the companion piece: a practical guide to testing a Go service layer by layer. He leans on the testing trophy over the classic pyramid, since integration tests are now cheap enough to run more of them, and tests the repository layer against a real database rather than a mock. His toolkit covers Testcontainers, mocks generated with mockery, `httptest` for handlers, testify and go-cmp for comparing whole structs, and randomised test data. [Sridhar Dachepelly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sridhar_Dachepelly_testing_erp_orchestration) of Dell Technologies applied Go to test orchestration in large ERP systems.

## Know what's in your binary

[Andrii Raikov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Andrii_Raikov_dependencies_code_management), Principal Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, asked the audience to name the indirect dependencies of their current project, then showed why most can't. Importing `fmt` silently pulls in `io`, `os`, `reflect` and more, and a few lines using the AWS SDK make a binary several times bigger. The second half covered patterns he has seen at Delivery Hero: a v2 client library that broke its v1 interfaces and stranded teams on the old version, and a `helpers` package that drifts into circular dependencies. His most practical advice: don't skip the import block in code review.

On the framework side, [Divya Darshana](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Divya_Darshana_http_communication_apis), an open source contributor to GoFr, showed circuit breakers, authentication and health monitoring for inter-service HTTP calls using the GoFr framework. And [Namkat Cedrick](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Namkat_Cedrick_career_experience_journey) of Iknite Studio gave the most personal talk of the day, "How Golang Changed My Life", revisiting old programming fears with a new mindset.

## Go beyond the server

[Alex Casalboni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly), Developer Advocate at Edgee, explained why WebAssembly suits edge computing, where logic in the request path has a budget of a few milliseconds. He traced Go's Wasm support from the `wasm` target in Go 1.11 to WASI preview 1 in Go 1.21, pointed to TinyGo for the component model, and showed how Edgee runs analytics SDKs as Wasm components at the edge.

[Pranshu Srivastava](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking) of Cloudera spoke to people starting with eBPF who don't want to write their user space code in Rust, sharing his experience with Cilium, why he chose it and which mistakes to avoid. [Brian Loomis](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Brian_Loomis_cloud_platforms_resilience), Director of Architecture at Progress, covered a distributed job runner designed to survive an unreliable network. [Utham Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Utham_Kumar_v2x_communication_vehicles) of Nanyang Technological University took Go into vehicle-to-everything networks for connected cars.

## Security in Go services

[Srinivas Vallabhaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential) of Walmart showed how Go fits confidential computing, keeping sensitive data inside secure enclaves in distributed systems without giving up performance. [Aditi Mallesh](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Aditi_Mallesh_identity_security_microservices) of Microsoft built identity orchestration as high-performance Go microservices across clouds, and [Santosh Bompally](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Santosh_Bompally_security_iac_threat) of Humana combined infrastructure as code with AI-driven threat detection. [Sudeep Shanubhog](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sudeep_Shanubhog_security_cloud_adaptive) of Tential Solutions covered adaptive, real-time security for Microsoft cloud services written in Go.

## Go where the money moves

Finance had a strong showing. [Srinivas Allam](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Allam_banking_modernization_fintech) of Core ITS described Go modernising a tier-1 bank's legacy IBM iSeries infrastructure with zero-downtime migrations. [Deepu Komati](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Deepu_Komati_fintech_cloud_infrastructure) of PenFed Credit Union built financial decision systems in Go, and [Srinivas Reddy Mosali](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Reddy_Mosali_fintech_infrastructure_scaling) of Visa made the case for fintech infrastructure that never blinks. Beyond banking, [Ankita Kamat](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Ankita_Kamat_notification_latency_scaling) of Microsoft used Go's concurrency model for notification systems that handle millions of messages while keeping millisecond latency, [Hardik R Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Hardik_R_Patel_data_pipelines_analytics) of PayPal designed multi-hop data pipelines for real-time analytics, and [Srikar Kompella](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srikar_Kompella_serverless_migration_aws) of Prime Video used Go for a serverless SaaS migration on AWS.

Silver sponsors [Edgee](https://www.edgee.cloud/), [Tential](http://www.tential.com/), [Delivery Hero](https://careers.deliveryhero.com/deliveryhero-jobs) and [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) all joined in, each with a speaker on the lineup. Thanks also to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter.

Title: Put the database in the test, not in the CI config
Description: Manuel de la Pena of Docker, maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, at Conf42 Golang 2025 on integration tests against Postgres, Redis, Redpanda and LocalStack.
Body:
If reproducing one failing integration test means starting the whole application, the test setup is in the wrong place. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed how to move databases, brokers and even AWS Lambda out of the CI configuration and into the Go test that needs them.

The talk is mostly live code: one small service, four real dependencies, four test files, and timings on screen. It shows Docker's open source library, and it is about as practical as Go testing talks get.

## The CI server is a bad place for dependencies

Manuel starts with the setup many teams still run. A CI server, Jenkins or GitLab runners or GitHub Actions, is configured by you or a platform team to start every database, queue and cloud emulator your tests need. Those dependencies must match production versions and configuration, and the workers must be big enough to run all of them next to the tests.

Every dependency upgrade becomes a CI change, often in a system developers don't own. Each new service adds load to shared runners. And when a test fails, there's no easy way to run just that test on your laptop.

## Containers as test fixtures

Testcontainers for Go gives your test code programmatic access to the Docker engine: create, start, stop and terminate containers right where they're used. Testing the persistence layer means starting one Postgres container in that test, not the whole stack.

Each container's well-known port (5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL) is mapped to a random host port, so many containers can run in parallel. Manuel lists three benefits: consistency, because dependencies run in containers instead of on your host; test data isolation, because each container has its own data; and build speed. Onboarding shrinks to installing Docker and running the tests, which the project calls the clone and run experience.

## One service, four dependencies

The demo app rates conference talks in real time. It stores ratings in PostgreSQL through `pgx`, caches in Redis, streams events through Redpanda with the `franz-go` Kafka client, and calls an AWS Lambda to compute statistics.

Each repository takes a connection string, which is what makes it testable. The Postgres test uses the Postgres module with an init SQL script, database name and credentials, waits until a log line appears twice, and hands the connection string to the repository. On the Postgres 15 Alpine image it passes in about 10 seconds. Redis needs no customisation and passes in about seven. Redpanda, with topic auto-creation on, takes 14 seconds on the first run because it pulls the image, and five on the next.

The Lambda test is the clever one. A Makefile builds and zips the function. The test starts LocalStack, copies the zip into the container, and runs the create-function command inside it once the container is up. It then reads the function URL and swaps in the randomly mapped port. Then Manuel breaks the average calculation on purpose, reruns, and the test catches it in seconds: total count correct, average wrong. A Lambda tested end to end on a laptop, with no AWS account involved.

## The parts of the API worth knowing

The second half tours the building blocks behind the modules:

- **ContainerRequest** defines image, exposed ports, network and readiness conditions.
- **Lifecycle hooks** run your code before and after create, start, readiness, stop and terminate.
- **Files** are copied in after the container is created but before it starts, so a database can boot with a known state.
- **Ryuk**, the extra container you may have spotted in `docker ps`, cleans up containers, networks, volumes and images when tests finish.
- **Wait strategies** replace `time.Sleep`: wait for an exec result, an exit, a file, a health check, a listening port, an HTTP response with a given status or header, a log line or regex, a SQL query, or all of them together.

Testcontainers can also build an image from a Dockerfile and run it, which is handy when the dependency is your own service.

## Who should watch

Go developers whose integration tests either live only in CI or don't exist, and platform teams tired of maintaining test databases on shared runners. If you already use Testcontainers, the LocalStack Lambda pattern and the wait strategies list are the parts to steal.

- [Cloud Testing Without the Wait](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anita_Ihuman_kubernetes_development_testing) by Anita Ihuman (MetalBear), on testing against real Kubernetes from your machine.

Title: Designed for servers, services, and scale
Description: Go runs quietly
Body:
# Go is calm. The systems are not.

Go has a reputation.

Simple. Clean. Predictable. The language you pick when you want fewer surprises and fewer late-night debugging sessions. Naturally, it ends up powering some of the most intense systems out there.

Conf42 Golang 2025 is all about that contrast.

This conference goes deep into building fast, reliable, very serious systems with Go. High-performance microservices, identity orchestration, notification systems handling millions of messages, and cloud-native platforms that really care about latency. If it needs to be fast and not fall over, Go is probably involved.

Security and resilience show up everywhere. From telemedicine platforms with military-grade protection to secure multi-cloud microservices and confidential computing, there’s a strong focus on building systems that can be trusted at scale. Not just in theory. In production.

AI is very much in the picture too. Go powering AI-driven ETL pipelines, edge computing, TinyML, OCR, and intelligent automation across finance, healthcare, IoT, and public sector platforms. It’s less “AI magic” and more “how do we ship this safely and make it fast”.

You’ll also find plenty of practical Go topics. Concurrency patterns, inter-service communication, dependency management, testing strategies, API design, and the occasional reminder that simplicity is a feature, not a limitation.

If Go is your language of choice, or you’re curious why so many critical systems quietly rely on it, this one’s for you. Solid engineering, real-world problems, and just enough chaos to keep things interesting.

Title: Why WebAssembly fits the edge, and where Go stands with it
Description: Alex Casalboni of Edgee at Conf42 Golang 2025 on how CDNs became compute platforms, why Wasm suits the edge, and Go's WASI support.
Body:
Code that runs before and after every HTTP request gets a budget of a few milliseconds, and that rules out most of the compute models we're used to. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Alex Casalboni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly), Developer Advocate at Edgee and previously six years at AWS, explained why WebAssembly is the runtime that fits that budget, how far Go's support has come, and how Edgee builds its edge platform on it.

It's a sponsor talk with a clear structure: history and fundamentals first, then Edgee's own architecture. The first part works as a solid primer on server-side Wasm even if you never touch Edgee.

## CDNs quietly became clouds

Alex's history lesson runs in two parallel tracks. On the cloud side: AWS from 2006, then virtual machines, then containers and Kubernetes, then serverless functions around 2014 and 2015. On the CDN side: companies as old as Akamai built for caching and DDoS protection, with limited custom logic through things like the Varnish Configuration Language.

Then, roughly between 2016 and 2019, the tracks crossed. Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions and Fastly Compute put code on hundreds of points of presence. Key-value stores, databases, queues and object storage followed. His conclusion is that many CDN providers have become cloud providers, and the line between edge and cloud keeps blurring.

## Why Wasm and the edge match

WebAssembly was announced in 2015, shipped in 2017 and became a W3C recommendation in 2019. Alex focuses on the server side, where WASI, the WebAssembly System Interface, gives modules controlled access to files, sockets, clocks and HTTP. He also mentions the well-known remark from Docker's founder that Wasm plus WASI would have made Docker unnecessary.

The edge brings hard constraints. You get less memory and CPU than a VM or container, and because the logic sits in the path of every request, it needs to finish in single-digit milliseconds. Alex puts the target at five to ten. Containers that take seconds to start and serverless functions with hundreds of milliseconds of cold start don't fit.

Wasm's properties line up with that: near-native performance, small binaries with fast initialisation, and sandboxing by default. A module can't make an HTTP call or touch the filesystem unless the host grants it. That last one matters most if you're a platform running other people's untrusted code.

## Go and WebAssembly, version by version

For Gophers, this is the most useful section. Go has had a `wasm` target since Go 1.11 in 2018, with JavaScript glue for browser use. WASI preview 1 support arrived as experimental in Go 1.21 in 2023. For WASI preview 2 and the component model, Alex points to TinyGo plus `wit-bindgen-go`, which generates Go bindings from WIT, the interface definition language for components. Edgee defines its own WIT interfaces so developers can write components against them.

He also flags Go 1.24's expanded support for exporting Go functions to a Wasm host, and Google Cloud's announcement in the same post that its Application Load Balancer accepts service extensions written in Wasm, custom logic right in the request path. For runtimes, he recommends Wasmtime from the Bytecode Alliance rather than reinventing the host.

## What Edgee built

Edgee's first product is data collection and web analytics. The idea is to take heavy client-side SDKs, he names Google Analytics, Segment and Amplitude, and run them as Wasm components at the edge before the page reaches the browser. The proxy runs on Fastly today, with other CDNs such as Cloudflare planned, and talks to backend services, currently on AWS Lambda, for work that can't happen at the edge yet.

Around that sits a component registry for publishing and sharing public or private Wasm components, and an Edgee CLI that scaffolds, builds, tests and pushes components in Go, Rust, Python, C# and TypeScript. The proxy, the CLI and the components are open source. A/B testing, feature flags and AI inference were on the roadmap he described.

## Who should watch

Go developers curious about WebAssembly outside the browser, and platform engineers deciding what belongs at the edge versus in a region. If you already ship Wasm in production, skip to the Go version notes and the Edgee architecture. If you don't, the first half explains the "why" better than most docs.

- [Go Containerless on Kubernetes with WebAssembly and Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Deepu_K_Sasidharan_kubernetes_containerless_webassembly) by Deepu K Sasidharan (Auth0).

Title: Read the import block, because that's where Go tech debt starts
Description: Andrii Raikov of Delivery Hero at Conf42 Golang 2025 on hidden Go dependencies, breaking v2 libraries and the helpers package that ate a codebase.
Body:
Can you name the indirect dependencies of the Go service you work on, and say why each one is there? At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Andrii Raikov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Andrii_Raikov_dependencies_code_management), Principal Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, opened with that question and spent the rest of the talk showing why most of us can't, and how small package decisions turn into years of tech debt.

Delivery Hero runs a lot of Go, and Andrii's examples come from its own code base, good and bad. The talk has two halves: a set of binary-size experiments that make hidden dependencies visible, and three patterns from production that he has watched go wrong more than once.

## Your binary knows what you imported

Andrii starts with a hello world that prints with the built-in print function, then swaps in `fmt` and recompiles. The binary grows noticeably. Then he adds `os` to read a name from the arguments, and the size barely moves. The reason is in `fmt` itself: it already pulls in `io`, `os`, `reflect`, `strconv`, `sync` and `unicode`, so by the time you ask for `os` you already have it. Moving the code into an external module on GitHub changes almost nothing either.

The bigger experiment uses the AWS SDK to list S3 buckets in a few lines of code, and the binary jumps several times over. Andrii then had ChatGPT write the same call by hand, signing the request against the S3 API using only the standard library. That version is about six megabytes smaller, but still around eight. Commenting out imports one by one, he finds `crypto` and `encoding` barely matter on their own. A tiny program that only calls a URL with `net/http` already lands at about five megabytes.

He is explicit that the lesson isn't "rewrite net/http". The lesson is that nobody looks. You add one small library and have no idea what it drags in, or what its dependencies drag in.

## A v2 that breaks v1 can trap a team for years

The second half is about culture, and the first story will be familiar to anyone in a large company. A platform team owns a global service-to-service token service and ships client libraries in several languages, Go included. Version one works. Then version two changes the interfaces without a new module path.

Service teams look at the migration cost, decide "if it works, don't touch it", and stay on v1. The platform team has no capacity to support both and deprecates v1, so no more fixes or security updates. Then a different team builds a new shared library on top of v2. Any service still on v1 that tries to use it gets a conflict: two implementations under the same name. Andrii says he has seen this happen several times, and it takes a year or two to build up, by which point untangling it can cost more than a greenfield rewrite.

The fix he points to is the one the Go ecosystem already expects: a breaking change gets a separate major-version path with its own `go.mod`, so v1 and v2 can live side by side.

## The helpers package is a dependency magnet

The other two patterns are about DRY applied without thought. A `helpers` package grows a function that prints details of a `Gopher` type, so helpers now depends on the gopher package. The day the gopher package needs a helper, you have a cycle, and the usual workaround is a second helpers package, which brings back the duplication you were trying to remove. His fix is plain: that function should be a method on the type, with private fields if you like.

Scale the same habit across services and you get his worst case: the same helper code living in a service's own package, in a newly extracted shared library and again in a third dependency, with three slowly diverging implementations and three sets of vulnerabilities.

## What to do on Monday

Andrii's closing list is short: write a dependency policy and actually follow it, audit dependencies and update versions regularly, scan for vulnerabilities in transitive packages too, and work with product to prioritise the debt. His most practical tip: don't skip the import block during PR review. Several of his horror stories would have been caught there.

## Who should watch

Go developers in teams with more than a handful of services, and anyone maintaining a shared internal library. It's a good talk for mid-level engineers who haven't yet been burned by a breaking minor version. Seniors may know the theory, but the binary-size experiments are worth a look before your next `go get`.

- [Supply Chain Attacks: Focused on NPM attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks), for what an unnoticed transitive dependency can do.
- [Compelling Code Reuse in the Enterprise](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Travis_Gosselin_compelling_codecreuse_enterprise) by Travis Gosselin (SPS Commerce), on sharing code without the helpers trap.

Title: Conf42 LLMs 2025 roundup: evals, attacks and agents in production
Description: Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 in review, from evals and AI testing AI to BadGPT and prompt injection, hierarchical agents and fine-tuning economics.
Body:
In March 2025 the question at [Conf42 Large Language Models 2025](https://www.conf42.com/llms2025) was no longer whether to build on LLMs but how to know the thing you built works, and how someone might break it. The 39 talks, streamed online on March 20, 2025, split roughly into three camps: people measuring model behaviour, people attacking it, and people wiring models into agents and products. Speakers came from Arato.ai, Kusho, Palisade, Microsoft, AWS, PayPal, IBM, Lime, Warner Bros. Discovery and others.

## You can't ship what you can't measure

[Hilik Paz](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) (Arato.ai) laid out why testing changes with LLMs: well-defined outputs and errors give way to unpredictable ones, identical inputs can produce different answers, and pass or fail turns into scoring across several dimensions. Good evals, in his framing, are measurable, repeatable and actionable, and the talk covers building the test dataset that gets a prompt all the way to production.

[Sourabh Gawande](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_applications_practices_tradeoffs) (Kusho) brought the engineering view from 18 months of building Kusho's API-testing agent: retries and timeouts from day one, schema validation with Pydantic, Server-Sent Events for streaming, Redis-backed task queues for long jobs, and promptfoo evals in CI, which he called unit testing for prompts. [Robin Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Robin_Gupta_test_systems_process) (Testzeus) used AI to test AI, combining rule-based and model-based checks for bias, hallucinations and inconsistencies with open source tools, and [Ankush Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Ankush_Sharma_observability_models_predictions) applied SRE practices to observability for LLM systems.

## Attacks are cheaper than you think

The security track was the event's most sobering. [Dmitriy Volkov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_hacking_underrated_security) (Palisade) presented BadGPT, a fine-tuning poisoning attack that strips safety measures from a model without hurting its performance or adding token overhead. His title, "LLM hacking is underrated", was the thesis. [Jorrik Kiijnsma](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Jorrik_Kiijnsma_attacks_risks_security) (Sopra Steria) live-coded prompt injection attacks against LLM-powered web apps and the defences against them, the best kind of talk to send a frontend team.

[Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Kartheek_Medhavi_Penagamuri_Shriram_threats_risks_defenses) (Microsoft) walked through the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, [Jose Manuel Ortega](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Jose_Manuel_Ortega_security_auditing_tools) surveyed security and auditing tools, and [Balaji Thadagam Kandavel](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Balaji_Thadagam_Kandavel_code_data_security) (Cox Automotive) made the case for deploying and fine-tuning in-house so your code and IP don't feed someone else's next model.

## Agents, RAG and the build-or-tune question

[Aleksandr Khramogin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Aleksandr_Khramogin_sequential_agents_hierarchical) (LogicBoost) moved past sequential agent chains to hierarchical planning, with specialised agents that decompose complex tasks, built in Python with LangChain, CrewAI and OpenAI's API. [Sandeep Kumar P](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sandeep_Kumar_P_data_insights_amazon) (AntStack) set out to show that RAG, vector databases and multi-stage flows only seem complex because they're explained badly, using Amazon Bedrock. [Manish Ballal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Manish_Ballal_automation_process_operations) (AWS) looked at agentic automation in business process operations.

[Muddassar Sharif](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_fine_tuning_business) (Virtuans.ai) asked the question every team eventually faces: is fine-tuning worth the data, compute and people it needs, or is RAG the better fit? [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Peter_De_Tender_azure_models_management) (Microsoft) showed Azure AI Foundry hosting models from several vendors, [Graziano Casto](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Graziano_Casto_workloads_cloud_environments) (Mia-Platform) the gaps in running AI workloads on Kubernetes, and [Shoeb Bustani](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Shoeb_Bustani_aws_reviews_architecture) (AWS) generative AI speeding up Well-Architected reviews.

## LLMs inside real products

Some of the most concrete talks were product case studies. [Rustam Musin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Rustam_Musin_automated_content_localization) built automated podcast localisation in Kotlin, chaining Whisper for transcription, GPT-4 for refinement and translation, and LLM-powered speech synthesis. Title: Teaching machines to work with meaning
Description: The next platform layer
Body:
# LLMs are no longer a side quest

There was a time when large language models felt like a fun experiment.

You tried a prompt, laughed at the output, maybe used it to rewrite an email, and moved on. That time is very much over.

Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 is all about what happens when LLMs move into production, decision-making, business workflows, and places where “oops” is not an acceptable outcome.

This conference covers the full LLM lifecycle. From how models are trained and evaluated, to fine-tuning, retrieval, agents, orchestration, and getting things safely into production. There are talks on evals, testing AI with AI, prompt injection, observability for LLMs, and what it actually takes to trust model output beyond demos.

Agents are a big theme. Hierarchical agents, agentic automation, task decomposition, and systems where models don’t just respond, but act. Some sessions focus on building these systems. Others focus on keeping them from doing something creative in all the wrong ways.

LLMs show up across real industries too. Finance, healthcare, payments, insurance, retail, media, and enterprise platforms all make an appearance. You’ll hear about fraud detection, compliance, customer experience, product management, and how businesses are trying to extract value without accidentally leaking data, IP, or sanity.

Security gets plenty of attention. LLM hacking, data leaks, auditing, threat models, and defending against prompt injection are all on the agenda. Because once LLMs touch real systems, they inherit all the same risks, plus a few new ones we’re still naming.

If LLMs are part of your stack, your roadmap, or your long-term anxiety, this one’s worth your time. The hype phase is fading. The real work has already started.

Title: Building LLM apps means retries, streaming, queues and evals
Description: Sourabh Gawande of Kusho AI at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on the plumbing every LLM app needs, from retries and schema checks to background jobs and evals.
Body:
Treat an LLM API like any other API and your app will break in production. That is the opening claim from Sourabh Gawande, co-founder and CTO of Kusho AI, at Conf42 Large Language Models 2025. Drawing on 18 months of building Kusho's AI agent for API testing, he walked through the unglamorous engineering that sits between a working prompt and a working product: retries, schema validation, streaming, background jobs and evals, with the specific libraries his team runs in production.

## Plan for the model to be wrong a few percent of the time

The root cause is simple: "LLMs are inherently non-deterministic." A stable REST API might fail around 0.1% of the time in his experience; even the most mature LLMs come in at roughly one to five percent depending on the task. Chain calls, feeding one response into the next prompt, and the error rate compounds. Sourabh's point is that this won't be fixed by waiting for better models. It's the application's job.

So retries and timeouts go in on day one, not after the first incident. In Python his team uses tenacity: a decorator on the function, with stop conditions (three attempts, ten seconds), fixed or random waits, and timeout decorators in the same package. LangChain users get a retry output parser that resends the prompt along with the failed output so the model knows what went wrong.

## Validate structure, then fix the prompt

Structured output is where most failures show up: extra fields, missing fields, a lost bracket. The fix is a schema library rather than hand-rolled checks. Pydantic on Python, Yup on JavaScript, with failed validation triggering a retry. Usually one or two retries clear it.

The useful nuance is cost in time. A call that should take five seconds can take 15 to 20 after retries, and users notice. If the same mistake keeps coming back (single quotes in JSON, say), put that rule in the prompt so the first answer is right. He also mentioned OpenAI's structured output mode, but prefers validation in the app: rely on one vendor's feature and switching to Claude or another provider gets harder.

## Stream short tasks, queue long ones

Users drop off well before ten seconds, and many LLM calls take five to ten. Streaming tokens as they arrive hides most of that. WebSockets work but mean a rewrite and possibly a different language; Server-Sent Events reuse your existing HTTP stack, and in Flask or FastAPI amount to a generator and a couple of headers. His recommendation: SSE, unless you truly need two-way traffic.

Streaming stops making sense when a task takes minutes. His example is an essay generator fed a hundred topics: do it in the request path and you tie up the backend for everyone else. Store the task, process it in the background, and notify the user by email or Slack, because they've left the tab. Start with a cron job polling the database. When you need more workers, move to a task queue. Kusho uses RQ (Redis Queue), which he says takes about 15 minutes to set up; they found Celery more than they needed.

## Evals are unit tests for prompts

The evals section is short and practical. Think of it, in his words, as "unit testing for your prompts": take a prompt template, run it against many inputs and several models, assert on the outputs, and compare cost. Hook it into CI so every build checks the prompts still behave. His team's pick is promptfoo, configured in YAML and available as open source or hosted.

## A provider tour with a timestamp on it

The talk closes with a quick tour of model APIs as they stood in early 2025: OpenAI as the versatile, reliable default; Anthropic's Claude for coding; Groq's custom chips for low latency; AWS Bedrock for keeping sensitive data inside AWS; Azure OpenAI, which was slightly faster in their tests but gated behind forms; and DeepSeek's open weights. The specific models have moved on since. The way of choosing (task fit, latency, data residency, reliability) still applies.

## Who should watch

Developers shipping their first LLM feature into an existing product, especially in Python. Experienced backend engineers will recognise every pattern; the value is in seeing which ones matter more with LLMs, and which libraries a small team found good enough. It is a talk by a vendor's CTO, but it's about engineering practice, not Kusho's product.

[Watch Sourabh Gawande's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_applications_practices_tradeoffs) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/aZo37Cyaprk)).
