Title: Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 - follow the packet, rotate the secret, read the bill
Description: Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 in review, 81 talks on EKS networking, dynamic secrets, edge APIs, Wasm on Kubernetes, microservices, cloud costs and databases.
Body:
[Conf42 Cloud Native 2025](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2025) ran on March 6, 2025 with 81 talks, and the best of them were refreshingly unglamorous. How does a packet actually reach a pod in EKS? How do you rotate a secret every two weeks without restarting the app? Why is the database still the one tier that doesn't scale? Speakers from AWS, HashiCorp, Microsoft, Meta, Mirantis, Fermyon, Comcast, Expedia Group, Booking.com, Salesforce and a strong group of sponsors answered with demos rather than diagrams.

## Know your plumbing

[Dumlu Timuralp](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Dumlu_Timuralp_networking_performance_optimization) (AWS) took the packet's-eye view of Amazon EKS, from the internet through Route53, the ALB and the VPC to the pod, pitched as the Magic School Bus for cloud networking. The point is practical: stop being stuck between teams during an outage because nobody can trace the path. [Roman Rastiehaiev](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Roman_Rastiehaiev_api_gateways_comparison) (HiBob) compared open source API gateways such as Kong, Traefik and Envoy, and [Akim Mamedov](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Akim_Mamedov_p2p_networks_decentralization) explained the principles behind P2P networks like BitTorrent and IPFS.

Sponsor Zuplo added the global angle. [Adrian Machado](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Adrian_Machado_api_network_distribution) argued for running auth, validation, rate limiting and caching at the edge while keeping data-bound services near the database, then debugged his own 1.3-second demo live. Sponsor Dimensigon's [Daniel Moya](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Daniel_Moya_automation_decentralization_orchestration) showed open source, decentralised automation that moves commands and files between networks that can't see each other, through a bridge node.

## Secrets, segments and the supply of trust

[Rosemary Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Rosemary_Wang_secrets_handling_security) (HashiCorp) started from a requirement every security team writes and every app team dreads: rotate the secrets applications use every two weeks without manual restarts. Her answer is automation, comparing application-agnostic and application-aware ways to inject secrets. [Venkata Nedunoori](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Venkata_Nedunoori_security_segmentation_optimization) (dentsu international) covered micro-segmentation in cloud environments, and [FNU Parshant](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_FNU_Parshant_securing_hardware) (Arm) went down to the silicon with dual-state models for hardware security.

## The developer loop and the runtime

[Anita Ihuman](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anita_Ihuman_kubernetes_development_testing) (MetalBear) made the case for "remocal" development: test against a realistic cloud environment from your laptop and cut the inner loop from hours to seconds. [Eti Ijeoma](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Eti_Ijeoma_docker_cache_efficiency) (Manufactured) gave a tidy talk on Docker build caching with layer ordering, bind mounts and cache mounts. [Mikkel Mork Hegnhoj](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Mikkel_Mork_Hegnhoj_kubernetes_architecture_extensions) (Fermyon) introduced Spin and SpinKube for running WebAssembly apps on Kubernetes, with an honest comparison against containers. [Bharath Nallapeta](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Bharath_Nallapeta_cluster_provisioning_scale) (Mirantis) presented k0rdent, which hides the hundreds of lines of YAML Cluster API normally demands, and [Siri Varma Vegiraju](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Siri_Varma_Vegiraju_workflow_dapr_failure) (Microsoft) used Dapr workflows so one failed step doesn't force a restart of a long-running process.

## Microservices, defended and questioned

[Chad Green](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Chad_Green_microservices_architecture_defense) (Jasper Engines & Transmissions) delivered "In Defense of Microservices", taking the complexity critiques head on with real implementations. [Asher Sterkin](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Asher_Sterkin_cloud_flexibility_ports__adapters) argued for applying Ports and Adapters systematically so today's cloud choices don't lock out tomorrow's. [Praful Konduru](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Praful_Konduru_resilience_scalability_faulttolerance) (Meta) covered fault-tolerant cloud-native design, and [Prithvi Raj](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Prithvi_Raj_community_tales_future) (Mirantis), former community manager of LitmusChaos, told the story of growing the chaos engineering community as the project became CNCF incubating.

## Every cloud has a bill

Cost came up from every direction. [Maksymilian Kalek](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Maksymilian_Kalek_aws_cost_efficiency) (Perelyn) built an ultra-budget AWS backend with Lambda and Powertools, self-hosted PostgreSQL on a cheap EC2 instance, and React on S3 and CloudFront. [Seshendranath Balla Venkata](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Seshendranath_Balla_Venkata_cost_cloud_efficiency) (Comcast) shared how his team optimised AWS EMR and Databricks workloads, and [Shinu Pushpan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shinu_Pushpan_saas_multitenancy_security) (Expedia Group) balanced performance, security and cost in multi-tenant SaaS. [Brian Loomis](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Brian_Loomis_observability_insights_telemetry) (Progress) used OpenTelemetry for something other than debugging: consumption-based pricing and showing customers what they use.

Gold sponsor Rapydo took on the most expensive tier. [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Matan_Nataf_rapydo_databases_broken) argued that developers own the queries while CloudOps owns the consequences, then demoed blocking, throttling and caching runaway queries across a fleet of MySQL and PostgreSQL instances.

## People and AI

Not everything was infrastructure. Sponsor Buildly's [Gregory Lind](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gregory_Lind_teams_collaboration_efficiency) made the case for radical transparency in software teams, from one shared backlog to committing code on day one. On the AI side, [Shivay Lamba](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shivay_Lamba_container_ecosystem_automation) (Couchbase) tackled AI projects whose datasets, models and weights live in separate places, using ModelKits to package them, and [Anant Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anant_Kumar_apache_spark_clusters) (Salesforce) built resilient Apache Spark clusters on Kubernetes for AI workloads.

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Platinum, [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) at Gold, and [APA Tech](https://apa.at/about/apa-tech/), [Buildly](https://www.buildly.io/), [Dimensigon](https://www.dimensigon.com/), [Jozu](https://jozu.com/) and [Zuplo](https://zuplo.com/) at Silver. All 81 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDi1jv-thhvcy4pJ3sBeUJr).

The series returns with [Conf42 Cloud Native 2026](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026).

Title: Commit on day one - radical transparency for software teams
Description: Gregory Lind of Buildly at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on radical transparency, one shared backlog, open decisions, admitted mistakes and fewer silos.
Body:
New developers at Buildly are expected to commit code on their first day, into their own branch, and get feedback on it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Gregory Lind](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gregory_Lind_teams_collaboration_efficiency), CEO and founder of Buildly, used that ritual as the entry point to "radical therapy for software teams": a set of practices built on radical transparency, drawn from a book of the same name he co-wrote.

This is a culture talk, not a technical one, and it comes from a founder whose product (Buildly's AI-assisted product management, with humans in the loop) is built around the same ideas. No code on screen, a lot of hard-won management advice.

## Radical as in fundamental, therapy as in what managers end up doing

Lind defines his terms up front. Radical means a fundamental, far-reaching change, not the surfing kind. Therapy is a nod to what anyone who has managed a team already knows: a lot of the job is helping people through struggles and rebuilding trust and accountability. He is clear he is not a licensed therapist, he just plays one in product management.

## Four principles of transparency

The framework rests on open communication inside the team and with the wider organisation, data-driven decision making, continuous feedback from the team and later from customers, and inclusivity and diversity of perspectives. The practical move that ties them together is merging the product backlog with the developer backlog, so there is one process everyone can see. The payoff he claims: fewer silos, faster decisions, shorter conflicts (data settles arguments faster than seniority), and people who stay because they feel heard.

He points to Atlassian and to Google's habit of sharing engineers across cross-functional teams as examples, and to IBM's AI Fairness 360 and Netflix's responsible AI work as models for ethics tooling.

## Show your reasoning, not just your result

Transparency, in Lind's version, goes further than most teams are comfortable with:

- Share how a decision was made, not only what was decided, by opening the backlog to the team and even to customers.
- Ask for criticism, and keep it constructive inside the team.
- Make performance and compensation policies transparent, since that is where a lot of unhappiness actually comes from, along with reporting lines.
- Test AI features in production, not just the model that built them, and embed ethical checks in the process so nothing quietly skews what customers are shown.

## Run your product like a startup, and your startup like an open source project

The most memorable line in the talk is his summary of the method: run a product like a lean startup, and run a startup like an open source project. Share work openly, ask for feedback early, and build communities that contribute. He also defends building the better mousetrap: an existing tool that doesn't fit your needs is a reason to build in the open, not a reason to stop.

His counter-example is Theranos, built behind closed doors with fake-it-till-you-make-it secrecy and too much control in one person's hands. Transparency from the start, he argues, would have changed the story.

## Where Agile and Scrum fall short

Lind's critique of Scrum is that it separates roles (the pigs and chickens) when a cloud-native, multi-repo product needs everyone pulling together. His radical process brings development, product, marketing and design cycles into one, treats developers as stakeholders alongside management and marketing, and favours demo days and surveys over documentation for its own sake.

Two rules stand out. When you ship a bug that breaks part of the application, say so before users find it. And keep the CEO from going straight to individual developers; route questions through shared, consistently updated channels so nobody gets yanked out of focus.

He is also realistic about morale. The goal is not to be a cheerleader, but to build trust and safety, run daily check-ins people actually read, celebrate the occasional win, and notice who is struggling, including whether they are buried in too many tools.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, product managers and founders of small teams who suspect their process has more walls than it needs. Engineers looking for technical content can skip it.

- [The Future of Work: Engaged Leaders and Empowered Teams](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Leslie_Martinich_future_work_teams) by Leslie Martinich (Competitive Focus) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.
- [Principles of Team Topologies Applied to Platform Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Cansu_Kavili_Ornek_Val_Yonchev_topologies_principles_engineering) by Cansu Kavili Ornek and Val Yonchev (Red Hat) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

[Watch Gregory Lind's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gregory_Lind_teams_collaboration_efficiency) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/OSrSVhj5knQ).

## From Buildly

Buildly was a Silver sponsor of Conf42 Cloud Native 2025. Lind describes it as a software architecture as a service company with open source products and Buildly Labs, AI-assisted product management with human oversight that now carries insights from the Radical Therapy book. He also runs OpenBuild, a mentorship programme for developers moving from junior to senior and from senior to CTO.

Title: Where software expects failure and keeps running
Description: Cloud native thinking
Body:
# Cloud native, but make it… manageable

Cloud native started as a promise.

You know the one. Faster deployments. Infinite scale. Fewer problems. More sleep.

Somewhere along the way, it turned into Kubernetes YAML, surprise cloud bills, fifteen dashboards, and a deep emotional relationship with latency. Growth.

Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 is here for everyone living that reality.

This is a big one. Seventy plus talks across Kubernetes, microservices, APIs, data, observability, security, AI, scaling, and all the tools that somehow became “essential”. From cloud testing without the wait to running ultra budget workloads for pennies, this conference covers the whole spectrum from scrappy to enterprise-grade.

AI is everywhere, naturally. Cloud-native LLMs, predictive analytics, AI-powered fraud detection, recommendation systems, digital twins, and AI-driven operations show up across industries like healthcare, finance, insurance, retail, manufacturing, and entertainment. There’s plenty of “this is cool”, and also a healthy dose of “here’s how this breaks in production”.

Kubernetes gets a lot of love. Real-world stories about running clusters at scale, improving uptime, reducing costs, simplifying connectivity, and making microservices behave. There are also talks questioning assumptions, defending simpler architectures, and reminding us that not every problem needs twelve services and a service mesh.

Security, resilience, and observability are baked throughout the program. Secrets management, zero trust, multi-cloud monitoring, chaos engineering, disaster recovery, and cost optimization all make an appearance. Because cloud native is not just about shipping faster, it’s about surviving success.

If your job involves containers, clouds, APIs, data pipelines, or explaining to someone why the architecture diagram looks like that, this one’s for you. Cloud native is powerful, messy, and still very much evolving.

Bring curiosity. And maybe your favorite kubectl alias.

Title: Put the API gateway at the edge and keep the data near the database
Description: Adrian Machado of Zuplo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on which parts of an API belong at the edge, the data trade-offs, and a slow D1 demo debugged live.
Body:
Rejecting a missing API key should not require a round trip from Japan to Texas. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Adrian Machado](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Adrian_Machado_api_network_distribution), staff engineer at Zuplo, made the case for running the compute-heavy, data-light parts of an API (auth, validation, rate limiting, caching) on the worldwide edge, while the services that touch your database stay close to it.

It is an honest talk. Machado spends as much time on why the edge is not a silver bullet as on why APIs suit it, and his own demo comes out slower than the API it was copying, which he then debugs on stage.

## What "the edge" buys you, and what it costs

A typical API lives in one region, so a user far away pays for every undersea hop, sometimes adding up to seconds. CDNs fixed this for static files. Edge functions, pushed by Cloudflare, Vercel and others through the WinterCG working group, do the same for code: lightweight function-as-a-service runtimes deployed at the CDN's points of presence, typically with a zero millisecond cold start.

The trade-offs are real. Cloudflare's runtime is JavaScript plus some WebAssembly, so Python or Rust services need a Wasm build. Node.js compatibility is partial, and anything that needs raw TCP probably won't work. Bundle sizes are capped. Libraries built for the browser usually run, because the edge is essentially V8.

## Your data is the catch

The bigger problem is that compute is global and data usually isn't. A CRUD call from an edge function pays the edge-to-database round trip, which can be slower than co-locating function and database in one region. Thousands of edge invocations can also exhaust your database connections.

Machado lays out three answers in order of effort:

- **A database proxy** such as Prisma Accelerate or RDS Proxy, which pools connections and can cache, without changing the database.
- **A globally distributed data store** like Cassandra or CockroachDB, or read replicas near the edge, at the price of consistency: async writes give stale reads, sync writes give slow ones.
- **Data that lives at the edge**, such as Cloudflare R2 for blobs, D1 or Upstash for per-region SQLite (handy for GDPR locality), or edge key-value stores for configuration that rarely changes.

## Why APIs are a good fit

Public API users can be anywhere, because you have no control over where your customers deploy. And a lot of API work is compute, not data: authentication and authorisation (especially API keys you validate yourself), logging, request validation with libraries like Ajv or Zod, bot and bad-actor filtering, rate limiting and caching.

Rate limiting at the edge has a bonus effect he points out: rejected requests never reach your central services, which frees them up for legitimate traffic and soaks up some DDoS along the way. His recommended architecture follows from that. Run an edge API gateway for those concerns, and host the actual microservices near the data, ideally replicated across a few regions. The gateway layer is JavaScript or Wasm; your services can be Django or anything else.

## The demo that came out slow

The demo is an ATM locator, a good edge use case because ATM locations are regional, rarely written, and very cacheable. As a baseline he calls Capital One's Nessie hackathon API, which answers in roughly 100 milliseconds. His version uses a Next.js site on Vercel, a Zuplo edge function and route, an edge cache, and Cloudflare D1 holding ATM data he gathered from Capital One's dataset.

The first call took about 1.3 seconds. Rather than hide it, he walks the debugging checklist: is the D1 query itself slow (a latitude/longitude index would help), is the database placed too far away, or is gateway latency to blame. His most likely suspect is placement, since D1 won't necessarily put a low-traffic hobby database close to you, and the practical fix is to cache at the edge so the round trip happens as rarely as possible. It is a better lesson than a perfect demo would have been.

## Who should watch

API engineers modernising a public API, CTOs thinking about API developer experience, and anyone whose global users are paying latency for work that never needed the database. It is a high-level talk, not an introduction to serverless and not a deep tuning session.

Title: Everything in your stack autoscales except the database
Description: Matan Nataf of Rapydo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on why managing database fleets is broken, and a demo of throttling, blocking and caching queries.
Body:
In a cloud-native stack, the database is usually the one tier that doesn't scale out when a noisy neighbour shows up. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Matan_Nataf_rapydo_databases_broken), co-founder of Rapydo, called databases "the stepson of every CloudOps organization" and argued that the way teams run fleets of RDS instances is broken: the people who write the queries aren't the people who get paged for them.

This is a vendor talk with a long live demo of the Rapydo console. The diagnosis in the first half is worth hearing even if you never install anything.

## Developers own the queries, CloudOps owns the consequences

Nataf's framing is organisational before it is technical. Managed services like RDS pushed database responsibility towards developers: they write the queries, pick the ORM, and often a single dev team owns a given database. Developers live in days and sprints, and their code has close to 100% of the impact on the database.

CloudOps and SRE teams live in minutes. They own the infrastructure bill, the database SLA, uptime and performance, and when queries run slow, the customer-facing team calls them. So one group causes the load and another absorbs it, usually without a DBA on the team. He calls that situation not healthy, which is a polite way to describe most on-call rotations that include a database.

## Observability alone leaves you reactive

The first problem with a fleet is visibility. Which instance has the slowest query? Where was the last CPU spike? Which databases are creeping towards the edge of their SLA? He acknowledges the existing observability tools for this, naming Datadog DBM, SolarWinds and New Relic, and argues that seeing the problem is only half the job. The other half is automation: caching queries, shielding the database from CPU spikes, accelerating slow queries and right-sizing the underlying instances.

His case for why it matters is the RDS scaling ladder. Hit a CPU spike, double the instance size, hit the ceiling again, double again. Scaling up is always a 100% step.

## The customer story: from emergency to shrinking instances

Nataf showed a CPU graph from a customer running a couple of hundred RDS instances that had climbed to 8xlarge one emergency at a time. After inserting Rapydo with a few rules, he said, the CPU baseline dropped from 60-100% to 20-30%, and the team then shrank instances step by step until they were 75% smaller than on day one, still below 50% CPU. He put the customer's compute savings at more than half a million dollars a month. Those are the vendor's numbers from a single customer, so treat them as a story, not a benchmark.

## The demo: from bird's-eye view to the offending query

The live part follows one workflow. A master dashboard ranks average query time across the fleet, MySQL and PostgreSQL side by side. Drill into the slowest instance and you find a `SELECT SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` running for 333 seconds. A locks view groups by locking thread and points to a single `UPDATE` causing most of the locks across the fleet.

Then he switches to real time on a database pinned at 100% CPU, with a view that refreshes every three seconds and can scroll back to watch the problem compound, from a handful of concurrent executions to around fifty. Killing the query helps for a minute, then the application sends it again. That is the moment for rules.

## Rules: block, throttle, or cache

Rapydo's rule engine matches query patterns with wildcards and applies an action. You can block a pattern outright, restrict it to certain hours or weekdays so an analytics query only runs at night, or throttle it so only a couple of executions run in parallel. In the demo, the throttle brings the database back from the edge. A second rule caches a query with table-based invalidation: when someone writes to the underlying table, the cache entry is dropped so results stay coherent. Other rules cover database connections and limiting specific users or tenants, which is where the noisy-neighbour problem from the opening gets its answer.

## Who should watch

CloudOps and SRE teams responsible for many MySQL or PostgreSQL instances without a dedicated DBA, especially in multi-tenant SaaS. If your scaling strategy for RDS is "next instance size up", the rule-based throttling and caching ideas are worth knowing whatever tool you use.

- [From Metrics Tsunami to Actionable Insights: Simplifying Database Troubleshooting](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2024_Divine_Odazie_metrics_tsunami_troubleshooting) by Divine Odazie (Severalnines) at Conf42 Observability 2024.

Title: Automating across networks that can't see each other, with Dimensigon
Description: Daniel Moya of Dimensigon at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos open source, decentralised automation with a REST API on every server and proxied transfers.
Body:
Most automation tools assume one control node that can reach every server. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Daniel Moya](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Daniel_Moya_automation_decentralization_orchestration) of Dimensigon demoed the opposite: an open source Python platform that puts a RESTful API on every server, lets any node manage the others, and routes commands and software through bridge nodes when two networks can't talk directly.

The talk is essentially a long hands-on tutorial in Docker, built and narrated live. If you want slides and theory, look elsewhere. If you want to see what using the tool feels like, keystroke by keystroke, this is it.

## A "dimension" is a cluster of servers across subnets

Dimensigon (DM for short) is both the company name and the tool's. It targets a specific, common headache: two or more subnets or data centres connected only through a few specific points, which you still want to manage as one group. That group is called a dimension, and Moya recommends one per lifecycle stage, so production, pre-production and development each get their own, for organisation and security.

The architecture lives in one GitHub repository with three components:

- **dmcore**, a Python Flask service that exposes the RESTful API on each server
- **the elevator**, which detects a new version anywhere in the network and spreads the upgrade
- **dshell**, a command-line client built on prompt_toolkit that turns commands into REST calls, with tab completion everywhere

A web UI is planned. Metadata lives in a distributed database built on SQLAlchemy, with logic to handle split brain during network instability and keep the surviving group consistent.

## The demo network: two subnets and a bridge

The setup is easy to reproduce. Two Docker networks stand in for two data centres, one container is attached to both as a bridge, and the rest live on one side or the other. A new dimension starts with one node, which issues single-use join tokens; every other server joins with its own token, generated from any node that is already a member. From then on, any node can administer the others.

A catalog of actions, orchestrations and software replicates across the dimension with a version watermark. When a node falls behind, `manager catalog refresh` pulls the newest one, and nodes also update automatically in the background.

## Actions, steps and orchestrations

The automation model is layered for reuse. An action is a reusable unit: a shell command, Python, an Ansible playbook, an HTTP request, or one of the built-in internal actions. Steps reference actions, orchestrations are made of steps, and orchestrations can themselves be steps in larger ones. Every step can have an undo, with conditions for when the orchestration counts as failed.

Changing an orchestration creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one, which keeps runs reproducible. Orchestrations export to and import from JSON, and Moya hopes to grow a shared orchestration library. Secrets go in a vault, scoped per environment, and are referenced with double curly braces in the code. The hello-world orchestration runs on three nodes at once and reports success, return code, parameters and elapsed time per server.

## Distributed commands and proxied software transfers

Two features stand out for day-to-day operations. Distributed commands open a shell against a set of target servers so every command you type runs on all of them, handy for pre-flight checks or troubleshooting many hosts. Moya says the idea came from a distributed shell he had used on Oracle Exadata.

The software library is the other. You register a file on any node, and it can be sent to any other node, either one-off or as a step in an orchestration. In the demo, a 200 MB file moves from a server on one network to a server on the other through the bridge, split into chunks and reassembled at the destination. His pitch for it is concrete: no NFS mounts between parts of the company, just a transfer that routes around the network gaps.

Other commands cover log federation (subscribing to a log or directory and replicating it elsewhere), locks for critical orchestrations, server routes and hop costs, and pings that check whether Dimensigon is alive on a node.

## Who should watch

Ops engineers and DBAs managing servers spread across segmented networks, on-prem and cloud, who find SSH jump hosts and a single Ansible control node limiting. It is a tool walkthrough, so watch it with a terminal open.

Title: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025: break it on purpose, everywhere
Description: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 roundup - socio-technical experiments, network faults on Fargate, chaos in platforms, mobile apps, AI monitoring and security.
Body:
Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 ran online on February 20, 2025, with 28 talks, and the theme was scope creep in the best sense. Chaos engineering started with killing instances; in this lineup it reached on-call rotations, internal developer platforms, mobile apps, AI model monitoring, and security controls. The common thread: if you have not watched it fail on purpose, you do not know how it fails.

The talks are all on the [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/ce2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDA4LX-Xal04LBJN52V6C1C).

## The system includes the people

[Benjamin Wilms](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Benjamin_Wilms_reliable_system_unpredictable), co-founder and CEO of gold sponsor Steadybit, gave the keynote-style talk of the day. His definition of a system includes the infrastructure, pipelines, people, and processes around the software, and his best demo tested all of it at once: inject latency into one backend service and take down the gateway, then check that Datadog alerts within 90 seconds, PagerDuty opens an incident, someone acknowledges it, the system recovers, and the incident is resolved. Before any experiment, he also found an availability-zone risk just by colouring Kubernetes deployments by zone. He is clear that the point is the organisation, not blaming whoever was on call.

[Pierluigi Meloni](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Pierluigi_Meloni_success_people_tech), co-founder and CEO of Utterskills, pushed the human angle further: coding alone no longer makes you stand out, and most project failures come from human factors rather than technology. [Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_MihaelaRoxana_Ghidersa_mindset_software_build) of Signant Health looked at how reasoning patterns shape design decisions, and [Vitali Shchur](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vitali_Shchur_qa_mindset_startup) of Check Point Software argued that QA engineers at startups need to think like business analysts and usability experts too.

## Fault injection, hands on

[Sunil Govindankutty](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sunil_Govindankutty_network_resilience_experiments), an Enterprise Support Lead at AWS, opened with Werner Vogels's line that everything fails all the time, then demoed AWS Fault Injection Service experiments on Amazon ECS with Fargate: latency, packet loss, and blackhole conditions against a sample containerised application, so you can see the behaviour before your users do.

[Sayan Mondal](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sayan_Mondal_cultural_mindset_platform), a Senior Software Engineer at Harness and a LitmusChaos maintainer, argued for a chaos-first mindset in platform engineering: make resilience testing part of the internal developer platform and the CI/CD path, with a demo deliberately built to break. [Muhammad Ahmad Saeed](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Ahmad_Saeed_chaos_microservices_engineering) covered designing microservices that hold up under failure, and [Muhammad Rizwan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Rizwan_architecture_systems_event) of Procode showed failure isolation and self-healing with event-driven architecture on Azure Event Grid. [Somaning Turwale](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Somaning_Turwale_resilience_recovery_disaster) of Microsoft took the bigger blast radius, disaster recovery with Azure Site Recovery.

## Chaos beyond the backend

Two talks took controlled failure to places it rarely goes. [Jaspreet Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Jaspreet_Kumar_mobile_apps), Lead Software Engineer at Microsoft, asked the obvious question in his abstract: why not break your mobile app before your users do? [Muddassar Sharif](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_ai_model_systems), co-founder and CTO of Virtuans.ai, applied failure simulation to AI model monitoring, starting from the questions executives and engineering managers ask about LLMs in production and the monitoring concepts the industry already uses.

[Prashanth Reddy Kora](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Prashanth_Reddy_Kora_chaos_cloud_systems) of Centene stress-tested cloud database systems, and [Shashank Reddy Beeravelly](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_ai_data_quality) of Walmart looked at keeping data quality intact when the data itself is chaotic.

## Security as a failure mode

The security track treated breaches as just another failure to rehearse. [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_security_cloud_defense), a Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case for chaos principles in cloud security testing. [Chirag Gajiwala](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Chirag_Gajiwala_resilience_models_security) of Nutanix explored reinforcement learning for adaptive resilience and generative models to simulate vulnerabilities, and [Vamsi Anumolu](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vamsi_Anumolu_security_devsecops_operations) of iCrossing covered DevSecOps across multiple clouds. [Rinku Mohan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rinku_Mohan_signon_design_implementation) of bettercoach went deep on single sign-on design and its integration traps.

## The quiet case for fewer moving parts

A few talks argued that resilience starts with less. [Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Denis_Ermakov_library_fundamentals_need), front-end lead at Techflow (which builds portfolio management software for banks), greeted his "lovely chaotic people" and then made the case against reaching for a shiny auth library in Next.js when the fundamentals already do the job. [Vivek Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vivek_Kumar_apps_vps_docker) compared VPS hosting with Docker, and [Hari Yerramsetty](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Hari_Yerramsetty_cost_optimization_success) of Flexport covered right-sizing, autoscaling, and FinOps.

The rest of the lineup ran from enterprise systems to networks: [Gopikrishna Yeturi](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Gopikrishna_Yeturi_performance_migration_framework) of LTIMindtree and [Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Lurduma_Reddy_Thirumala_Reddy_operations_workloads_scalability) on SAP migrations and SAP on Azure, [Jaya Krishna Vemuri](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Jaya_Krishna_Vemuri_investment_banking_accuracy) of State Street on reconciliation, [Naveen Gowda](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Naveen_Gowda_financial_automation_ecosystems) of Couchbase on financial workflow automation, [Rao Marapatla](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rao_Marapatla_analytics_marketing_insights) of BreakthroughT1D on nonprofit marketing APIs, [Vedant Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_ranking_systems) of Walmart Global Tech on neural ranking, [Sai Charan Madugula](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sai_Charan_Madugula_iot_networking_agility) on SDN for IoT and 5G, and [Dmitrii Nikitin](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Dmitrii_Nikitin_development_maintenance_applications) of Quadcode on white-label Android apps.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsors [Steadybit](https://steadybit.com/), [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continues with [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ce2026) on December 3, 2026. Schedule your next game day accordingly.

Title: Introducing uncertainty before users feel it
Description: Confidence comes from testing
Body:
# Break things. On purpose. Calmly.

Chaos engineering sounds dramatic. Like you’re about to pull cables out of walls and see who panics first.

In reality, it’s much more thoughtful than that. Mostly.

Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 is all about building systems that keep working even when the universe decides to be uncooperative. Network hiccups, failing dependencies, cloud outages, bad configs, expired certificates, and that one service nobody remembers owning. You know the drill.

This conference digs into how teams actually test resilience. Fault injection, chaos experiments, failure scenarios, and learning what really happens under pressure. There are talks on microservices, event-driven architectures, cloud databases, APIs, and what breaks first when things scale faster than expected.

AI shows up here too, because of course it does. Expect sessions on AI model monitoring, AI-driven chaos experiments, and using machine learning to detect issues before users do. Some talks focus on reliability. Others focus on making sure automation doesn’t confidently lead you in the wrong direction.

But chaos isn’t just technical. A big part of the program looks at people, culture, and mindset. Platform teams, leadership, communication, and why throwing more tools at a problem doesn’t magically make systems resilient. Spoiler: humans are still involved.

You’ll also find real-world case studies across cloud, mobile, security, finance, healthcare, and enterprise platforms. From testing disaster recovery to breaking things safely in production, this is chaos engineering where the goal is learning, not drama.

If you like understanding how systems fail before they fail loudly, this one’s for you. Controlled chaos beats surprise chaos. Every time.

Title: A chaos experiment that tests your on-call, not just your pods
Description: Benjamin Wilms of Steadybit at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on testing socio-technical resilience, from pod redundancy to Datadog and PagerDuty response.
Body:
Your redundancy works on paper and your runbook exists in Confluence; neither tells you whether the on-call engineer gets paged within 90 seconds when the gateway falls over. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Benjamin Wilms, co-founder and CEO of Steadybit, argued that a system includes the people and processes around the software, and showed a chaos experiment that verifies both halves at once.

Benjamin has been doing chaos engineering for around nine years. This is a vendor talk: the demos run in Steadybit, wired to Datadog and PagerDuty. The method transfers to other tooling, though, and that is the reason to watch.

## A system is more than its services

The talk starts from a definition. Software runs on infrastructure, is built through a pipeline, and is operated by people inside an organisation with its own processes. Benjamin uses the term socio-technical system for the whole thing. Failures can come from any part of it: a misconfiguration, a human error, an unexpected interaction between services, or two teams with mismatched processes.

He is blunt about the goal. A 100% error-free system will never exist; servers crash, networks lag, dependencies break. What you can do is make the system better at handling failure, and check that it really is.

The demo system is an online shop, with services like a bestseller list, checkout, and a hot deals service, each owned by different teams. Even grouped by area, the dependency bubble chart stays busy, which is his point about complexity.

## Find the risk before you run anything

Steadybit's approach has three phases: uncover risk, understand impact, then increase systemic resilience.

The first phase needs no experiment at all. Benjamin groups the shop's Kubernetes deployments and colours them by availability zone. The cluster spans two zones, the bestseller and checkout services are spread across both, and the hot deals service is not. That is a risk found purely from configuration data. Steadybit's advice feature then flags orange items, such as a checkout deployment that should run more instances, with a snippet to fix it.

The second phase verifies the fix. The experiment does a pre-check that all pods are ready, deletes a pod, and expects it back within 60 seconds while the system keeps serving. Steadybit collects Kubernetes events and deployment readiness into one report. Benjamin stresses running these early, in a pre-production environment, rather than starting in production.

## The experiment that pages a human

The third phase is where the talk earns its title. Benjamin takes a scenario from a past incident: a latency spike in the hot deals backend, followed by a total outage of the central gateway. The hypothesis covers people as well as software:

- Monitoring recognises the problem within 90 seconds and alerts the on-call team via PagerDuty.
- The incident is opened and acknowledged within three minutes.
- The system recovers within three minutes and the incident is resolved within four.

The experiment encodes all of it. Steadybit checks with Datadog that the system is healthy first, injects the latency and the gateway outage, then expects Datadog to report an alert, PagerDuty to show a triggered incident, someone to acknowledge it, Datadog to return to OK, and the incident to be resolved. In the recorded run, every step passed, so the technical recovery and the human response both held up.

He adds a rule worth repeating to any team that runs game days: this is not about how fast one person fixes an outage. Benjamin says he does not like finger pointing; the test measures how well the organisation detects and fixes faults and how its processes are coordinated.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams who already run basic fault injection and want to extend it to alerting and incident response. The "colour by zone" trick is a nice five-minute audit for any Kubernetes cluster. If you have never run a chaos experiment, the talk is accessible, but you will get more from it once you have.

- [Gunnar Grosch on hypothesis-driven resilience modelling](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gunnar_Grosch_hypothesis_development_resilience_modeling) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.
- [Robert Ross on the incident response process](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Robert_Ross_incident_response_process) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.
- [Uma Mukkara on continuous resilience](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Uma_Mukkara_continuous_resilience) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023.

[Watch Benjamin Wilms's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Benjamin_Wilms_reliable_system_unpredictable) from [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ce2025).

Steadybit is a chaos engineering platform for running controlled experiments on Kubernetes and cloud systems, with integrations into monitoring and incident tools such as Datadog and PagerDuty, as shown in the talk.

Title: Conf42 Python 2025 roundup: dunders, concurrency, data and agents
Description: Conf42 Python 2025 in review, from dunder methods, asyncio vs threads and FireDucks to fsspec, FastAPI fraud systems, agentic Django and WebAuthn.
Body:
Iyanuoluwa Ajao introduced a talk at [Conf42 Python 2025](https://www.conf42.com/python2025) by calling Python "the 2nd best language for everything", which is about as honest a summary of the ecosystem as you'll get. The event, streamed online on February 6, 2025, had 51 talks covering both halves of that joke: the language features and libraries that make Python good at so many jobs, and the tricks people use when it isn't fast enough. Speakers came from IBM, Meta, Microsoft, Walmart, Snowflake, Mastercard, Wells Fargo, Qualcomm, NEC and Treeverse.

## The language, used properly

[Eti Ijeoma](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Eti_Ijeoma_python_dunder_methods) (Manufactured Networks) went past `__str__` and `__repr__` to show how dunder methods make APIs feel native and can carry small domain-specific languages. [Iyanuoluwa Ajao](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Iyanuoluwa_Ajao_python_concurrency_patterns) (Fyyne) compared threading, asyncio and multiprocessing, with a practical rule for I/O-bound work: if the libraries you need support async/await, start with asyncio, because threads cost memory and need protecting when they share data; otherwise use threads, and save processes for real parallelism.

[Dmitriy Volkov](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_packaging_busy_people) (Palisade Research) covered Python's packaging oddities for people with no time for them, plus the move towards a GIL-free CPython. When Python itself is the bottleneck, [Hariharan Ragothaman](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_cpp_python_workloads) (athenahealth) offloaded compute-heavy work to C++, and [Sourav Saha](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourav_Saha_firedricks_dataframe_jit) (NEC Corporation) introduced FireDucks, a multithreaded DataFrame library with JIT compilation that detects and optimises common pandas performance problems without code changes.

## Data tooling that hides the plumbing

[Guy Hardonag](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Guy_Hardonag_file_systems_python) (Treeverse) gave hands-on examples of fsspec, the library that lets Pandas, TensorFlow and PyArrow treat local and cloud storage the same way. Anyone who has written `if path.startswith("s3://")` will appreciate it. [Daniel Emakporuena](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Daniel_Emakporuena_data_analysis_streamlit) built an analysis and dashboard tool on Streamlit for people who outgrew Power BI and Tableau, and [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Tim_Spann_vector_databases_python) (Snowflake) combined structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources with Python.

At larger scale, [Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Dileesh_Chandra_Bikkasani_network_performance_automation) (AT&T Labs) used Apache Airflow for network performance automation, [Amarnath Immadisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Amarnath_Immadisetty_python_analytics_realtime) (Lowe's) built real-time customer analytics engines, and [Shashank Reddy Beeravelly](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_data_quality_management) (Walmart) covered AI-assisted data quality checks.

## AI and agents, in plain Python

[Anna Gutowska](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Anna_Gutowska_ai_agents_customizing) (IBM) introduced AI agents that combine LLM reasoning with planning, current information and external tools. [Craig West](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Craig_West_agentic_ai_django) treated agents in Django as "AI as API", building agentic endpoints from scratch, and [Sourabh Gawande](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_ai_applications_practical) (Kusho) shared the practical side of building LLM applications. [Shannon Lal](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shannon_Lal_image_search_python) (Designstripe) combined text search with semantic search for images using Motor, MongoDB and OpenAI. The most fun entry was [Jan Van Wassenhove](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Jan_Van_Wassenhove_code_music_electronic) (Sopra Steria), whose MusicAgent uses generative AI, Python and Sonic Pi to compose and produce electronic music live, album art included.

Search and ranking had a strong showing too: neural ranking for real-time personalisation from [Vedant Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_neural_ranking) (Walmart Global Tech), vector-based semantic search from [Siddharth Pratap Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Siddharth_Pratap_Singh_search_vector_semantic) (Walmart Labs), and context-aware evaluation metrics for search from [Aditya Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Aditya_Singh_precision_metrics_framework). [Parul Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Parul_Gupta_ai_ml_prototyping) (Meta) described the tooling behind fast ML prototyping, and [Shubham Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shubham_Singh_ai_code_review) took AI code review beyond syntax checks.

## Services at scale, and catching fraud

[Aby M Joseph and Jayalekshmi K S](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Aby_M_Joseph_Jayalekshmi_K_S_graphql_microservices_fastapi) (UST) built GraphQL microservices on FastAPI, and [Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sushil_Prabhu_Prabhakaran_python_cloud_scaling) (TCS) orchestrated async workflows with asyncio and FastAPI. Fraud detection got two architecture talks with the same toolbox: [Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Narendra_Bhargav_Boggarapu_fraud_python_transactions) (Wells Fargo) with FastAPI, Ray and MLflow, and [Vinod Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vinod_Upputuri_fraud_ml_numpy) (Mastercard) with PyTorch, Ray and asyncio. [Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Ajay_Krishnan_Prabhakaran_sms_spam_python) (Meta) covered SMS spam detection with NLP.

## Security and operations

[Sairam Durgaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sairam_Durgaraju_fido2_webauthn) (Evernorth Health Services) implemented passwordless, phishing-resistant login in Python with FIDO2, WebAuthn and hardware security keys. [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_secure_cloud_applications) (Microsoft) covered secure-by-design cloud applications, and [Mounika Ponugoti](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Mounika_Ponugoti_device_security_attack) (Qualcomm) cost-effective embedded device security, from secure boot to control-flow integrity. On the ops side, [Justin Dearing](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Justin_Dearing_docker_windows_devcontainers) (Neudesic) showed several free ways to run Windows and Linux containers and devcontainers on Windows without Docker Desktop, built on WSL, and [Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Lurduma_Reddy_Thirumala_Reddy_hana_availability_pacemaker) (Intone Networks) automated SAP HANA high availability with Pacemaker clusters.

## Python outside engineering

[Liv McFarlin](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Liv_McFarlin_python_ux_innovation) (Wheels) showed a UX team using Python for research, prototyping and collaboration, [Vamsi Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vamsi_Upputuri_drug_development_python) (Gilead Sciences) Python in clinical drug development under compliance constraints, and [Rao Marapatla](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Rao_Marapatla_data_warehouses_nonprofits) (BreakthroughT1D) data warehouses for nonprofits.

Thanks to [Arato AI](https://arato.ai/?utm_source=conf42&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Conf42_mail) and [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Python 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBo176Is4wP2F6UCB0yEkWO) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/python2025).

Python stayed the common language across the rest of the year's Conf42 events; [Conf42 MLOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025) is a good next stop.

Title: One language, countless domains
Description: Powered by Python
Body:
# Python is everywhere (again)

Python keeps being that language people “grow out of”.

And then somehow keep using forever.

It’s in data, web, AI, cloud, healthcare, security, automation, embedded systems, and probably running something important you forgot about. Conf42 Python 2025 leans fully into that reality.

This conference covers a lot of ground. There are talks on FastAPI, GraphQL microservices, async workflows, packaging without pain, and scaling Python systems that actually survive production. You’ll also find deep dives into concurrency, distributed file systems, performance tuning, and when Python absolutely should not be doing everything by itself.

AI is, unsurprisingly, everywhere. From AI agents and LLM-powered applications to code review, fraud detection, recommendation systems, and data quality management, Python sits right in the middle of modern machine learning workflows. Some sessions focus on building smarter systems. Others focus on keeping them accurate, explainable, and under control.

There’s plenty beyond AI too. Python in healthcare, finance, IoT, security, and cloud platforms shows up across the schedule. Topics range from embedded device security and zero trust to data warehousing, analytics with Streamlit, and high-throughput financial systems handling millions of events per second.

You’ll also find talks that are just… very Python. Dunder methods. Packaging for busy people. Mixing Python with C++ when performance really matters. And even a reminder that Python can make music, not just dashboards.

If Python is part of your day job, your side projects, or your personality at this point, this one’s for you. It’s practical, wide-ranging, and very comfortable with the fact that Python refuses to stay in one lane.

Title: Conf42 DevOps 2025: caches, flaky tests, Terraform and culture
Description: Conf42 DevOps 2025 roundup - scaling Sofascore with caching, frugal serverless, flaky tests, Terraform supply chain risk, incident response and LLMs in CI/CD.
Body:
Conf42 DevOps 2025 ran online on January 23, 2025, with 58 talks, and it opened the year with a reassuringly practical mix. Yes, LLMs showed up in CI pipelines and Kubernetes troubleshooting. But the talks that stuck were about the fundamentals: caching done right, bills kept small, tests that stop flaking, supply chains that do not hand over your cloud, and people who still have to respond when the pager goes off.

Every session is on the [Conf42 DevOps 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/devops2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCdGhBCZtLYRLD9MT4ddCES).

## Scale is mostly boring, and that's good

[Josip Stuhli](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Josip_Stuhli_scaling_users_performance), CTO of Sofascore, gave the kind of scaling talk that makes you want to look at your own cache config. In the talk he puts Sofascore at more than 28 million monthly active users and 400 billion requests a month, with a peak of 1.6 million requests per second. The early fix for servers falling over at peaks was a full-page memcache, which then hit the classic cache stampede: a missing key, thousands of users asking for it at once, and every request going straight to the database. The talk walks through the fix and other low-hanging fruit that is often overlooked.

[Yan Cui](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Yan_Cui_serverless_saving_tips) of Lumigo, an AWS Serverless Hero who has worked on AWS since 2010, brought a fire hose of money-saving tips for serverless, starting with the one everyone should do on day one: set up billing alarms. They lag by a few hours, but finding out hours late beats finding out when the bill arrives.

Gold sponsor Rapydo tackled the database side. [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Matan_Nataf_db_ops_rapydo), co-founder and CEO of Rapydo, explained why per-instance tools fail for fleets of MySQL and Postgres databases, and demoed throttling a runaway query that kept coming back after it was killed.

## Tests you can trust

Testing got a lot of airtime. [Mike Morgan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) of Buildkite covered how to identify, isolate, and eliminate flaky tests before they erode trust in the pipeline. [Mesut Durukal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mesut_Durukal_agile_automation_test) of Indeed asked whether test automation is a silver bullet (it isn't) and listed the common pitfalls. Analog Devices sent three DevOps engineers with hardware-flavoured problems: [Bianca Popu](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Bianca_Popu_github_infrastructure_testing) on securely wiring public GitHub repositories to private Jenkins test infrastructure, [Stefan Raus](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Stefan_Raus_arm_fpga_testing) on test harnesses for ARM and FPGA-based systems, and [Andreea Andrisan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Andreea_Andrisan_linux_distro_release) on the release strategy for a custom Linux distribution.

## Your supply chain has root access

[Uri Aronovici](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Uri_Aronovici_cloud_terraform_hack), co-founder and CTO of ZEST Security, showed how widely used open-source Terraform providers and modules can be abused to take full control of a cloud production environment, with two attack flows and mitigation practices. If your modules are pinned to whatever latest happened to be, watch this one first.

The security track continued with [Josh Hankins](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Josh_Hankins_devsecops_program_start) of CBTS on starting a DevSecOps program from scratch, [Krishna Chaitanya Rudraraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Krishna_Chaitanya_Rudraraju_threat_modeling_developers) of Microsoft on threat modelling inside DevOps pipelines, [Hariharan Ragothaman](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_deployments_governance_securely) of athenahealth on unifying deployments for governance, and [Sheshananda Reddy Kandula](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Sheshananda_Reddy_Kandula_mobile_security_automation) of Adobe on automating mobile security assessments with MobSF and Jenkins.

## When it breaks anyway

PagerDuty brought two talks on the human side of operations. [Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Daniel_Afonso_incident_response_effective) shared lessons for effective incident response under the banner "Don't Panic!", and [Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mandi_Walls_culture_challenges_devops) argued that culture is still the challenge: when the only tool a team controls is its tooling, every problem looks like a tooling problem.

Observability had its say too. [Dave McAllister](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Dave_McAllister_nginx_metrics_monitor) of NGINX walked through 15 NGINX metrics from the application layer down to the host, [Amir Krayden](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Amir_Krayden_kubernetes_blind_spots) of Senser combined topology with existing observability to find Kubernetes blind spots, [Shyam Sreevalsan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Shyam_Sreevalsan_observability_future_years) of Netdata sketched the next ten years of observability, and [Pradeep Gaddamidi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_cloud_cost_monitoring) of Evernote shared how a budget-tight team built open-source monitoring and logging.

## LLMs join the pipeline

AI talks were plentiful and mostly grounded. [Rajeshwari Ganesan and Chidambaram Ganapathy Sundaram](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Rajeshwari_Ganesan_Chidambaram_Ganapathy_Sundaram_devsecops_automation_systems) of Infosys built a multi-agent LLM system to resolve build failures across more than 100 internal applications. [Kosseila Haddalene](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Kosseila_Haddalene_kubernetes_ai_troubleshooting) of cloudthrill demoed K8sGPT for troubleshooting managed clusters including Oracle OKE, with OpenAI, Cohere, or Ollama behind it. [Nirhoshan Sivaroopan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Nirhoshan_Sivaroopan_ai_accuracy_trust) of WSO2 covered accuracy evaluation for RAG systems, and [Praveen Payili](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Praveen_Payili_ai_data_enterprise) presented AskDataAI, an agent for enterprise data access.

## People, code and the rest

Some of the most-shared talks were not technical at all. [Pawel Zajaczkowski](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pawel_Zajaczkowski_tech_impostor_syndrome) of Xebia tackled impostor syndrome, and [Tomasz Manugiewicz](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Tomasz_Manugiewicz_engineers_power_quiet) of evoke made the case for the quiet engineers whose contributions get missed in extrovert-dominated teams. [Muhammad Ahsan Ayaz](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Muhammad_Ahsan_Ayaz_angular_refactoring_projects) of Scania told the story of refactoring a sprawling estate of Angular projects and what went wrong, [Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Denis_Ermakov_coding_sustainable_development) of Techflow argued that less is more in code, [Tiago Barbosa](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Tiago_Barbosa_api_development_software) of Rely.io made the case for API-first development, and [Caio Medeiros Pinto](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Caio_Medeiros_Pinto_environment_products_innovation) of Citi pitched environments as a service.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsor [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continued with [Conf42 DevOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) and returns as [Conf42 DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/devops2027) on January 21, 2027.

Description: Reliability is the goal
Body:
# DevOps is still a thing (and somehow bigger than ever)

Every year someone declares DevOps “done”, “dead”, or “just how things are now”.

And every year, DevOps quietly adds five more responsibilities, a few new tools, and at least one AI-powered opinion about how you should be doing your job.

Conf42 DevOps 2025 embraces that reality.

This conference is packed. Fifty plus talks across culture, cloud, data, security, testing, observability, incidents, scaling, performance, AI, LLMs, and whatever category your current problem accidentally falls into. If it touches delivery, operations, or keeping systems alive, it’s probably here.

AI shows up everywhere. From generative AI in cloud-native DevOps to AI-assisted monitoring, fraud detection, data pipelines, testing, and even build failure automation. Some talks focus on the promise. Others focus on trust, accuracy, and what happens when AI confidently gives you the wrong answer at scale.

But it’s not all machines. There are plenty of sessions on culture, leadership, impostor syndrome, quiet engineers, and the human side of running complex systems. Because no amount of automation fixes burnout, unclear ownership, or “we’ll just ship it and see”.

You’ll also find deep dives into Kubernetes, serverless, observability, security, incident response, healthcare platforms, and large-scale migrations. From zero to millions of users. From flaky tests to resilient systems. From “why is this slow” to “oh… that’s why”.

If DevOps is your job, your background, or your current identity crisis, this one’s for you. It’s messy, evolving, and still very much not finished.

See you there.

Title: Your app autoscales a thousandfold, your database does not
Description: Matan Nataf of Rapydo at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on managing fleets of MySQL and Postgres databases, with a live demo of throttling a runaway query.
Body:
Kubernetes and autoscaling groups let your application scale out on demand, but the relational database behind it is still one shared-everything box. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Matan Nataf, co-founder and CEO of Rapydo, argued that the tooling for running relational databases in the cloud has not kept up with microservices and multi-tenant architectures, and demoed how Rapydo tackles it.

Rapydo was a gold sponsor of the event, and this is a product talk: roughly half framing, half live demo of the Rapydo console. The framing is useful for anyone running more than a handful of MySQL or Postgres instances.

## From a few databases to thousands

Matan's history lesson is short. On-prem, a company ran a small fleet of databases for a few monolithic apps, with a full DBA team watching them. Load changed by modest percentages, so sizing for the peak was neither hard nor expensive.

Microservices changed that. Teams ship features daily, often on open-source MySQL and Postgres, and the fleet can grow to thousands of instances. Per-instance tools such as Amazon RDS Performance Insights show one database at a time, and with a fleet of 5,000 databases, he points out, looking at one instance at a time makes you reactive by definition.

He also names the uncomfortable part of the ops job: even when you find the bad query, the fix usually lives in legacy code owned by a development team, so all you can do is file it with them and wait.

## Three pillars: observability, resiliency, sane costs

Matan's spec for a modern database management tool has three legs, and he says missing any one of them fails:

- **Fleet-wide observability.** The slowest queries, top CPU and IO consumers, connection shortages, and locks and deadlocks across all instances in one view, with alerts on thresholds.
- **Resiliency without code changes.** Guardrails that protect the database from CPU spikes, runaway queries, repeated identical queries from buggy code, and idle connections eating the pool.
- **Sane costs.** Capacity planning that does not have to assume the worst spike, since he notes managed databases are often the second or third line on a cloud bill.

Rapydo maps onto that with two parts deployed in your own VPC: Scout for observability across Postgres and MySQL, and Cortex, an automation layer that works through a proxy and managed connections to apply caching, throttling, and query rewrites.

## The demo: a query that keeps coming back

The live demo is the best part. The master dashboard shows a 48-hour view of slow queries, top CPU consumers, and locks across the fleet. Grouping the lock view shows the single Postgres instance suffering most, and that two statements, one update and one select, generate most of the locks.

Then the real-time view: a MySQL 8 demo database at 100% CPU with all 250 of its 250 connections in use. Going back 15 minutes shows the same `SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` query running four times in parallel, then 112, then 230, and 237 when he returns to the live view.

Matan kills the query, and the application immediately sends it again, which is the honest moment of the talk: killing queries is a fire extinguisher, not a fix. He considers a cache rule with table-based invalidation, which keeps cached data consistent with the table, then rejects it because the query uses the current date. Instead he applies a throttling rule, with a wildcard on the `LIMIT` clause, that lets that query run only two at a time. The parallel count falls from 75 to 46 to 2, and the database recovers while the app keeps sending the query.

## Who should watch

DevOps and SRE teams who own a large fleet of MySQL or Postgres databases but not the application code hitting them. The framing helps you argue for fleet-level tooling; the demo shows what intervening at the proxy layer looks like. If you run three databases and a DBA, it will feel like someone else's problem, for now.

More database talks from Conf42:

- [Adam Furmanek on observability for PostgreSQL and MySQL](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Adam_Furmanek_observability_postgresql_mysql) at Conf42 DevOps 2024.
- [Lukas Vileikis on lessons from MySQL records](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Lukas_Vileikis_mysql_records_lessons) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

[Watch Matan Nataf's talk](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Matan_Nataf_db_ops_rapydo), part of [Conf42 DevOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/devops2025).

## From Rapydo

Rapydo offers database observability and automation for fleets of MySQL and PostgreSQL databases, deployed in the customer's VPC, with Scout for visibility and Cortex for caching, throttling, and query rewrite rules.

- [Rapydo website](https://www.rapydo.io/)

Title: Where the physical world joins the internet
Description: And starts responding
Body:
# Everything is connected (and somehow it’s your problem)

Once upon a time, the internet lived safely inside computers.

Now it’s in cars, factories, medical devices, oil pipelines, kiosks, fridges, traffic systems, and that one sensor nobody remembers installing but everyone is afraid to touch. Welcome to IoT.

Conf42 Internet of Things 2024 is here to make sense of that world.

This conference covers the full IoT stack, from edge devices and connectivity to cloud platforms, analytics, security, and automation. You’ll find talks on robotics, industrial IoT, real-time analytics, digital twins, Kubernetes at the edge, and what happens when AI meets thousands of devices that never sleep.

AI is everywhere, obviously. Expect sessions on explainable AI for IoT, AI-driven cloud architectures, predictive analytics, automation, and using machine learning to turn massive streams of device data into something resembling a decision. There’s also plenty on observability, telemetry, and figuring out what’s actually going on when things stop behaving.

The use cases go wide. Healthcare, fintech, automotive, logistics, energy, retail, and smart infrastructure all show up. From contact tracing and crisis management to autonomous vehicles and supply chain optimization, this is IoT in the real world, not just diagrams on slides.

Security and reliability get their share of attention too. Identity federation, zero trust, blockchain, multi-layered defenses, and securing connected ecosystems where failure is not an option and “just reboot it” is rarely acceptable.

If your job involves devices, data, clouds, or explaining to someone why a sensor stopped reporting at 3 AM, this one’s for you. IoT is messy, powerful, and very much alive. Let’s talk about it.

Title: When security stops being a checkpoint
Description: And becomes part of the workflow
Body:
# Security wants to be your friend (promise)

DevSecOps is that thing everyone agrees is important and then quietly argues about in pull requests.

Should security shift left? Should it shift everywhere? Should it maybe stop breaking the build five minutes before a release? Big questions. Strong feelings.

Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 is here to unpack all of that.

This one goes wide and deep. There are talks on securing infrastructure, web applications, APIs, and Kubernetes clusters that absolutely did not ask to be exposed to the internet. You’ll hear about secrets management, Git leaks, identity federation, policy as code, and why credentials have a habit of showing up where they really shouldn’t.

AI is very much in the mix. Expect sessions on AIOps, alert noise reduction, AI-driven security assessments, explainable AI, and the slightly terrifying reality of AI being very interested in your secrets. There’s even a panel dedicated to that exact concern, because of course there is.

Beyond tools, the conference also digs into culture, governance, and the human side of security. Soft skills, leadership, compliance, resilience, and what DevSecOps looks like in healthcare, finance, supply chains, and other environments where mistakes are extra expensive.

You’ll find practical talks on Terraform, GitOps, cloud databases, internal developer platforms, and shifting from monoliths to microservices without everything catching fire. There’s also room for bigger conversations about trust, accountability, and what “secure by default” actually means in real teams.

If your job lives somewhere between shipping fast and sleeping at night, this one’s worth your time. DevSecOps isn’t getting simpler, but at least you don’t have to figure it out alone.

Title: Teaching machines by example and constraint
Description: Language does the work
Body:
# So… you talk to machines now

At some point this year, a lot of us realized we’re no longer just writing code.

We’re negotiating. With models. Politely. Repeatedly. Sometimes aggressively. Sometimes with emojis. Sometimes with “no, seriously, do it like this”.

Welcome to prompt engineering.

Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 is all about that strange new layer between humans and machines, where wording matters, context is everything, and a single sentence can be the difference between brilliance and absolute nonsense.

There are talks on securing prompts, preventing injection attacks, and making sure your AI doesn’t spill secrets the moment you look away. Others dig into orchestration, agents completing missions, and turning prompts into actual systems that do useful work instead of just vibing.

You’ll also find plenty of real-world use cases. Healthcare. Retail. Finance. HR. Education. Cloud platforms. Testing. Even SRE perspectives on keeping AI-driven systems reliable when prompts start getting creative at 2 AM.

Some sessions go deep into LLMs, multimodal models, embeddings, vectors, and feedback loops. Others take a more human approach, exploring ethics, bias, hallucinations, and what it means to trust AI output when the stakes are higher than a funny chatbot reply.

If you’ve ever thought “why did the model do that” or “how do I get this thing to behave”, this conference is probably for you. And if prompt engineering has quietly become part of your job title, well… you’re definitely in the right place.

Title: JavaScript: small script, big universe
Description: One more dependency, one more galaxy
Body:
# JavaScript is doing everything now

Once upon a time, JavaScript was just there to make buttons clickable. Cute. Simple. Innocent.

Fast forward a bit and now it’s running in browsers, on servers, inside kiosks, across healthcare systems, helping with AI workloads, securing containers, and probably judging your variable names. Growth, right?

This one covers the whole JavaScript universe. AI in the browser. Built-in AI features. JavaScript in healthcare, utilities, finance, and retail. There’s also plenty on architecture, resilience, zero trust, and reducing false positives, because nothing builds character like being paged for something that wasn’t broken.

Some sessions dive into regulated worlds like healthcare, finance, and utilities, where incidents are extra spicy and “just restart it” is not a valid strategy. Others focus on cloud migrations, Kubernetes security, and the quiet art of keeping systems upright while everyone else is asking what went wrong.

If incidents are part of your job (or your life, at this point), this one’s for you. Bring your curiosity, your scars, and maybe a sense of humor. You’ll probably need it.
